screens:
The session begins.

Dusk settles over Baldur's Gate like soot. Behind you the Outer City is still shouting: a carter curses a stuck wheel, a woman sells skewered eel from a smoking brazier, and two tiefling children dodge a Flaming Fist patrol that pretends not to see them. Ahead, the gate's arch swallows the line one traveller at a time. Beyond it the Lower City slopes down toward the harbour, and the first tavern lamps are coming on along the street.

The cat walks at your heel, tail high, as if the city belongs to it. Halfway through the arch it stops and stares. Just inside the gate, a lean man in a frayed green coat has set an upturned barrel under a lantern. He fans a deck across the lid with an easy flick that has nothing to do with chance. "One hand, friends, one hand before supper. Lady Luck's awake at this hour," he calls. Nobody has sat down yet.

A halfling no taller than your belt falls into step beside you. "New in the Gate? Bed, bath, beer, and nobody robs you before breakfast. A copper and I'll take you there."

Then the line moves, and you reach the trestle table. The Flaming Fist sergeant behind it has a burn scar along her jaw and ink on her fingers. She glances at your cloak, at the crossbow, at the cat, and finally at your face.

"Name," she says, dipping her pen. "Business in the city. And the toll. Next."

The sergeant's pen is already moving before you finish speaking. *Worgen*, she writes in a cramped, even hand, and below it *Tethyr*. At the word "veteran" her eyes come up and rest on the cloak a moment longer than they did the first time. Zaranda's colours have faded on it, but the cut is still a soldier's.

"Two silver," she says. "One for you, one for the crossbow. The cat's free unless it bites someone."

She doesn't hold out her hand. She waits, pen raised, the lantern hissing on its hook above her. Behind you the line shuffles. Someone mutters about supper.

"Honest work's on the board." She tips her chin at the wall beside the arch, crowded with curling bills: caravan guards wanted for Scornubel, a reward for a runaway apprentice, a sketch of a bearded man with *ARSON* under it, the Flaming Fist's own recruiting notice nailed over the lot. Then, without turning her head, her eyes slide past your shoulder toward the lantern and the upturned barrel just inside the gate. "It isn't there."

At your heel the cat hasn't moved. It's still staring at the dealer's barrel.

Pim Thistlecap has drifted close enough to the table to be part of the conversation without technically joining it. He's rocking on his heels and pretending to read the arson notice.

The sergeant dips her pen again. "Lodging. Where?"

James's fingers go into the purse and find only gold. It's the last of the southern winnings, and there isn't a silver coin among it. He sets one gold piece on the planks instead, and in the lantern light it shines a good deal more than two silver would.

Sergeant Vorne looks at it, then at him. She pulls a tin box from under the ledger, flips the lid and counts change onto the table with ink-stained fingers: eight silver, pushed toward him in a short stack.

"Gold breaks here," she says. "Elsewhere it gets noticed."

Behind you, it already has. At the barrel, Corwin Ashe's flicking stops for half a beat. "Now *there's* a man the Lady's been kind to," he calls, warm as a brazier. "Come shake her hand, friend. One hand, you'll double it before the eel's cold." At your heel the cat's tail goes from high to low and starts to lash.

Pim Thistlecap has given up pretending to read the arson notice. "Sound door, no dice, I know just the — "

The sergeant dips her pen, and he stops.

"The Elfsong," she says, writing something short beside your name. "Down this street, past the Counting House, left at the lamp shop. Dear. Bolts on the doors. The landlord throws out anyone who brings out a deck after the singing starts." She blots the line. "Go straight there. Don't stop on the way."

She doesn't look at the barrel when she says it. She doesn't need to.

Then her eyes come up again, to the cloak this time, and they stay there. "Which company? Under Zaranda."

Sergeant Vorne takes the slip by its corner, the way you'd hold something that might still be wet. She tilts it toward the lantern. Her eyes go down the lines once quickly, then go back up to the company line and the paymaster's scrawl at the bottom and stay there longer.

James watches her face as she reads. Nothing in it softens. The set of her mouth changes, though, the way it does when someone hears a name they haven't heard in a while.

"Knew one," she says. "Tethyrian. Came north after the war and signed with the Fist. Scout, like you. Could tell you how many men were in a room from the boots by the door." She folds the slip along its old crease and holds it out. "He's not with us anymore."

She doesn't say how he left, and doesn't look like she means to.

She turns back to the ledger and writes a few words beside his name. It's the company, he guesses, from the length of it. To make room she draws the page toward her, and for a moment the column above his entry is turned his way. It's a long run of names in the same cramped hand, a day's arrivals: carters, a pilgrim, a family of five from Elturel. Beside two or three of them, out in the margin where a clerk would never need to write anything, is a small tick in the same ink. One sits beside James's own name. It's the short mark she made a minute ago.

She blots the page and the ledger turns back.

"Mornings, the muster yard at the Seatower," she says without looking up. "Fist always needs men who can count boots. Pay's late. It comes."

At James's heel the cat presses its whole flank against his boot and holds it there. Its eyes haven't left the barrel.

Pim Thistlecap has been rocking from heel to toe through all of it, and now he can't hold it in any longer. He steps up beside the trestle table, hat already in his hand. "Elfsong, then! Fine choice, the sergeant knows her business. Quickest way's right along here, sir..." He points down the street, and the way he points runs straight past the lantern and the upturned barrel, where Corwin Ashe has started shuffling again, slow and showy, and is smiling at nobody in particular.

Sergeant Vorne's eyes go to the halfling, then to James. She says nothing.

"Next," she calls past his shoulder.

Sergeant Vorne doesn't answer the thanks. She gives the smallest nod over the ledger, and her pen is already on the next line. The family from the back of the line shuffles up to the table with their bundles.

Pim's hat stops halfway to his head. "Directions! Right. Course you have." He jams it on. "Left at the lamp shop, then, and mind the gutter by the Counting House, it's deeper than it looks, there was a mule once — " He breaks off. His eyes go past James's elbow to the barrel. For a moment Corwin Ashe's eyebrow comes up, and Pim's shoulders go up the same little distance in reply. Then the halfling is drifting back toward the arch and the next traveller, already starting his patter about bed, bath and beer.

James crosses to the far side of the street. It's a wide berth, past a chandler's shuttered window and a water trough scummed green at the edges. The barrel's lantern stays on his left, twenty-odd feet away. Corwin doesn't get up. He doesn't stop shuffling either.

"Another time, friend," he calls, friendly as anything. "The Lady keeps a seat warm."

The cat keeps pace at James's heel, but its head stays turned toward the barrel the whole way past. Its answer comes into his mind the way it always does: not quite words, more like a smell and a picture that arrive already understood.

*The card.*

Its tail is stiff and doesn't lash.

*One of them isn't paper. It's old bone, yellow. Warm, like a hand just put it down. He shuffled three times, and three times it came back to him. It always goes home.*

There's a pause. The cat's ears flatten slightly against the lantern-glow.

*It smells of her sister. The cold one, who laughs when things break.*

James knows that sister, and every Tymoran does. The Lady's twin is Beshaba, the Maid of Misfortune. Tymora's priests teach that each sister answers the other's gifts, and the soldiers James served with spat over their shoulders when they said her name. He has never heard of a card carrying her smell. The cat has never said anything like this before.

*The man is only a man.* After a moment it adds, with what in a person would be a sniff: *He holds it the way you used to hold yours.*

The street tips downhill toward the harbour. Lamps are coming on in upper windows, and somewhere below a bell is ringing the hour for the ships. The bulk of the Counting House is ahead, dark against the last of the sky. Beyond it, on a corner, a shopfront is crowded with hanging lamps of coloured glass, every one of them lit. The cat walks on, still looking back.

The cat's answer comes back dry, with a picture attached: a cat flat in long grass while the man next to it walks straight on through.

*You were walking. I was looking.* A pause. *Good. Not his game.* Its tail comes up again, though not all the way.

Left at the lamp shop, the street narrows and the cobbles get older. The coloured glass throws red and green over the gutter for a few yards, then it's just ordinary dusk and the smell of the harbour coming up between the houses. Two doors down, a sign swings from an iron bracket: a painted elf-woman with her mouth open in song, the paint flaking off her hair. Lamplight comes from behind thick bottle-glass. The door is oak, and on its inside face, as James pushes it open, he can see three heavy bolts.

The common room is warm and low-beamed and fuller than it looked from outside. It smells of mutton, pipe smoke and spilled ale. Nobody is dicing. Nobody is playing cards either, and James notices it the way you notice a missing tooth.

The man behind the bar is broad and grey, with a moustache waxed to two points and a ledger of his own open by the taps. He looks at the cloak, the crossbow and the cat, in that order, and keeps his eyes on the cat.

"Osric Fell. It's my house." His voice is dry and unhurried. "The cat sleeps in the room, not in the kitchen. It goes near my larder, I'll put it on your bill by weight."

The cat sits down at James's boot and starts washing one paw. It looks like a cat that has decided not to have heard.

"Supper's mutton and barley, bread, a pint," Osric goes on. "Four silver. Rooms upstairs are a gold a night. Every one has a bolt, and the walls are thick enough that you won't hear your neighbour pray."

James counts four silver onto the bar. Osric sweeps it into a drawer without looking at it and calls the order back through a hatch. A minute later a girl with flour on her sleeves brings a steaming bowl, a heel of dark bread and a pint with a proper head on it. James eats standing at the end of the bar, where he can see the room and the door.

He asks about the temple, and Osric's eyebrows come up a little.

"The Lady's Hall? Upper City. Up the Steeps to the inner wall, and the Watch'll be on the gate." He wipes a glass. "They close it at dark. They won't open it for a Tethyrian with a crossbow, not tonight, and not for silver either. Go up after sunrise. Say you're going to pray, and leave the bow here. They're easier on a man with empty hands." He sets the glass down. "The Hall's the big white dome. You can't miss it. Plenty of people try to."

From a table by the fire, two men in tar-stained shirts have been talking low. A dockhand's low still carries.

"…same as the others. Coin right between his teeth. The Fist fished him out under the Grey Harbour steps and wrote him down as drink."

"Was he a drinker?"

"Never saw him drunk. Cooper, from upriver. He came through the gate not a tenday back, talking about setting up a shop." The first man drinks. "The Umberlee women wouldn't even take the coin off him. Said it wasn't hers."

His friend makes a sign against the sea, and they both go quiet over their pints.

Osric has heard it too. His face doesn't change, but he turns his ledger a little so that the page faces him.

"A gold a night," he says to James. "How many nights?"

"Top of the stairs, end of the passage. The window sticks. Hit it at the bottom corner, not the middle."

Then James lowers his voice, and the landlord's hand stops on the key before he lets go of it.

He hears the question through. His eyes don't go to the dockhands by the fire, though it's plain he knows exactly where they're sitting. He picks up a glass that's already clean.

"I don't read Fist ledgers," he says. "I don't know what she writes in hers." He sets the glass down. "She doesn't recommend houses either. She sends people. Not many. A few this summer."

On the cooper, he says nothing at all. It's the kind of silence a man keeps when he has an answer and is deciding whether you've earned it.

Osric decides James hasn't earned it. He lets go of the key and slides it the last inch across the bar.

"Lots of men come through that gate, Mister Worgen. Some sleep here. Some don't. What happens to them after they pay their bill is none of my business, and I don't talk about the river in my house." He says it without heat, the way he quoted the price of supper. "You want to know what the sergeant writes, ask the sergeant. She'll be at the Seatower in the morning, not at my bar."

He nods once at the stairs. Then he turns to the hatch and calls through it about the bread, and the conversation is over.

By the fire, the dockhands have heard nothing. They've moved on to a ship's mate who owes one of them money. The cat has jumped onto the end of the bar, where it plainly isn't allowed, and is looking hard at Osric's ledger. Osric hasn't seen it yet.

*He stopped before he answered,* comes through the bond. The picture with it is a dog sitting on a buried bone and staring at the sky. *The thing he isn't saying is in that book.*

James lifts the cat off the bar with one hand under its belly. It goes stiff and heavy, the way cats do when they want you to know this is being done to them. Behind him Osric turns from the bread hatch just in time to see four paws leave his counter, a foot from the ledger.

"Saves me weighing it," the landlord says, and turns back to the hatch.

*He keeps it open,* the cat grumbles over the bond, with a picture of a fish left on a doorstep. *That's an invitation.* Then it lets the matter drop and settles in the crook of his arm, eyes half shut and tail twitching.

The fire is good, and the two dockhands have the bench nearest it. The one who told the story is thick through the shoulders, with a grey beard and tar worked into the creases of his knuckles. The younger one has a broken nose that healed badly and a thumb that keeps going to the sign against the sea he made earlier. They look up at the cloak, at the pint, at the cat, and the older one shifts over half a foot on the bench. That's the invitation.

"Teague," he says, and nods at his friend. "That's Mabry." He drinks, considering James over the rim. "Hollin. That was his name. Cooper. Elturel side, I think, or near enough. Had a cart, a cask of hoops and a set of good tools. He was going to take a shop up past the Wide, he said. Barrels for the fish-salters."

"He had money, too," Mabry says. "First night he was in, he stood the whole bar at the Mermaid a round. Everyone, even the ones who didn't like him." He turns his cup on the table. "Four days later he's on the Grey Harbour steps trying to sell me his drawknife for five silver. A good knife, worth three times that."

Teague grunts. "Said he'd had a bad night. Said the Lady turned her back on him. Wouldn't say where." He looks into the fire. "Men don't, after."

"The coin was wrong, too." Mabry says it quietly, like a man who's been waiting all evening for someone to say it to. "I was there when they brought him up. Fist had him on the stones with a lantern on him. Thing in his teeth wasn't silver, wasn't copper either. It was brass, like a chit. Like a token you'd get for a coat at a bathhouse. The Umberlee woman bent down, looked at it, and stood up again like it had bit her. *Not mine.* That's what she said. Then she went."

From behind the bar, Osric's cloth goes round a glass a little slower than it needs to. He doesn't come over.

Teague wipes his beard with the back of his hand and looks at James again, at the cloak this time, the faded colours and the soldier's cut.

"Upriver, you said." His tone stays friendly enough, but he's paying attention now. "Whereabouts?"

Teague hears the correction out. His eyes go from James's face to the cloak and back, and something in his shoulders settles a little. He's been lied to before, and this didn't sound like it.

"Tethyr," he says. "Long way north." He doesn't ask about the soldiering. The cloak already told him.

The cat turns once on James's lap and lies down with its chin on his knee. Its eyes are half shut, and it's watching Mabry.

At the mention of the green coat, the two dockhands look at each other. It isn't the look Pim and Corwin traded at the gate. It's slower and more uncomfortable, the look of two men who've each thought something and never said it.

"Ashe," Teague says. "Corwin Ashe. He's had that barrel since about the thaw. Fist moves him on, and he's back two days later." He shrugs. "Deals straight, they say. Nobody's ever caught him at anything, and plenty have tried. Lads off the boats sit down to show him how it's done." He drinks. "They get up lighter. Not all of them. Some win. Enough win."

"Hollin came in through that gate," Mabry says, half to himself.

"So did half the city."

"I'm only saying it."

Teague lets that sit and says nothing back.

Then Mabry looks at James. The question about the markings has clearly been going round in his head since he first told the story, and he takes his time with it, frowning into the fire like he's trying to bring the stones under the steps back into the light.

"There was something on it," he says at last. "Stamped, like. Not plain. I saw the lantern catch it when the Umberlee woman bent down. Little raised bit in the middle, smaller than my thumbnail." He shakes his head. "I couldn't tell you what. I wasn't close, and I wasn't looking to get closer, not with him looking like that." He swallows. "It wasn't a face. Coins have faces. This didn't."

"Where is it now?" It's Teague asking, not James, and Mabry blinks at him.

"Corporal had it. Fist corporal, the one with the hook nose. He pried it out with his knife after she'd gone, wrapped it in a bit of rag and put it in his pouch. Then they put Hollin on a handcart." He turns to James. "Seatower, I'd think. That's where they take them first, before the pauper's field. If nobody comes asking."

"Nobody came," Teague says.

Behind the bar, Osric has stopped pretending to wipe anything. He isn't looking at them. He's looking at the door.

If that card is what your cat thinks it is, sitting down is exactly what it wants from a man like you." She looks at the cat, then back at him. "And don't decide it's your errand yet, either. The Lady doesn't hand out errands. She puts you where the dice are falling and watches what you do. So look first."

She stops there. Something has caught up with her. She looks past him at nothing in particular, the way people do when they're trying to remember a name.

"Old bone. From Tethyr." She says it slowly. "When I was a novice, the old Mother here used to tell us a story on winter nights. After the war down there, priests of ours went south to break something up. She said it was a gambler's thing, made by the other side." She shakes her head. "I thought it was a story to frighten girls off dicing. I never asked if it was true."

The silver disc overhead turns another hand's width and throws a slow bar of light across the rail between them.

"If it happened, it was written down. Not in this book. This one's for answered prayers. The Hall keeps its other records below, and I have the key." She taps the page beside his name. "Before I go digging in the undercroft, though, Mister Worgen, I'd like to see the deck. The one you carry. May I?"

Sister Corra takes the case in both hands, the way she might take a baby someone has passed to her a bit too quickly. She doesn't open it straight away. She listens to the rest of what he says first, head tilted. At *a stubborn fool* her eyes come up from the leather to his face, and the laughter is back in them for a moment.

"We get plenty of both in here," she says. "Usually in the same man."

She unbuckles the case on the lectern beside the chained book and slides the deck out. Then she goes through it properly, card by card, laying each one face up on the open page, the way a moneychanger checks coin. They're Amnian pasteboard. The faces are printed in red and black and have faded to rust and grey, and the backs carry a vine pattern worn almost smooth where a thumb has pushed them across a table a thousand times. The knave of cups is cracked across the middle and has been glued. One corner of the six of swords is gone, bitten off.

She holds a few of them up into the disc of light from the nearest window and tilts them. She runs her thumbnail along the edge of the whole stack. When she reaches the end, she squares the deck and sets her palm flat on top of it, and for a breath she says nothing. Her lips move a little. It could be a prayer, or she could just be counting.

The cat has come up onto the rail without asking anyone. It leans out over the lectern, its whiskers forward, and sniffs the stack under her hand.

*Yours,* it reports. The picture is a long night's table: wine, candle smoke, his own hands, his own sweat when the hand went bad. *Only you. Paper.* It sits back on the rail. *No cold. Nothing in it but you.* After a moment it adds, dry as dust: *You smelled worse then.*

Corra lifts her hand.

"Fifty-two cards and a glued knave," she says. "Somebody's dog had the six."

She slides the deck back into its case, buckles it and holds it out to him across the lectern.

"It's an ordinary deck, Mister Worgen. I'm glad of that, and you should be too. But understand what that means." She keeps her voice low. "A cursed deck you could throw in the harbour, and you'd be rid of it. Nobody has to curse this one to pull you back to a table. It's your own hands on the backs of those cards, and you'll carry that wherever you go, whether the deck is in your pocket or not." She lets go of the case once he has it. "So keep it if you need to. Just know it isn't keeping you safe."

Overhead the silver disc turns another slow hand's width, and a bar of light slides across the rail and over the cat. The cat narrows its eyes against it and doesn't move.

Corra unhooks a ring of keys from her belt. There are three of them, and one is much older than the others, black iron worn bright at the bow. She looks along the rail, catches the eye of a boy novice in a blue tabard who is scraping wax off the candle stand, and points him to her basket and the lectern. He comes over looking pleased to have been trusted with something.

"The undercroft's under the east stair," she says to James. "It's cold, the steps are steep, and I'll want both hands for the lamp. If what the old Mother told us was ever written down, it'll be on the Tethyr shelves, and I haven't been near those since I was a girl." She weighs the old key in her palm. "Visitors don't usually go below. But the Lady has written you into her book this morning, and I'd rather have a soldier's eyes on whatever's down there than only my own."

She tilts her head toward the dark arch at the east side of the dome, where a narrow stair goes down out of the light.

"Will you come down with me?"

Sister Corra stops at the edge of the arch and looks back at him, eyebrows up.

"A Tethyrian who asks first. The Lady really has been busy with you." She waves her free hand at the dome, the windows, the turning silver. "It's her house, and I'm the one holding her keys this morning. You have my leave. Light, nothing hot. The records are old, and they burn better than you'd think."

He touches the coin at his throat and says the word. A clean white glow comes up off the Lady's worn face, steady as a candle with no flame to it, and shines out through the cloth of his shirt. Corra looks at it for a moment and gives one short nod, as if a guest had just wiped his boots without being told.

The novice watches all this from the lectern with his mouth slightly open, until Corra looks at him and he closes it.

The east stair is narrow and turns twice. The steps are deep, worn into dips in the middle, and the air goes cold within a dozen of them. It's a dry cold, the kind that has been sitting in stone for a hundred years. At the bottom is a low door of iron-banded oak. The old black key turns stiffly and loud. Corra puts her shoulder to the door and it swings in.

The undercroft runs the whole width of the dome above, under a forest of squat pillars. Racks of shelving stand between them: cedar boxes, bundles of parchment tied in faded blue cord, ledgers stacked flat, a few scroll cases capped in tarnished silver. A painted letter on each pillar marks a region in an old hand. *Waterdeep. Amn. Calimshan.* In his light the dust lies on everything like a fine grey fur, and there are no footprints in it except theirs.

The cat comes down the last step, stops, and sneezes.

*Old paper. Mice, long ago. Dead ones.* It sends a picture of a dry little skull under a shelf. Then its tail goes up again. *Hers down here too. Fainter. Like a coat hung up a long time.*

"Tethyr's at the back," Corra says, picking her way between the racks. "Where else would it be." She stops at a pillar marked with a T that has nearly flaked away, and lets out a long breath that clouds in the light. Three shelves are packed tight with bundles, boxes and loose quires stuffed in sideways. "Thirty years of letters from the southern houses. I'd forgotten how much. The old Mother's story would be somewhere in this lot. A report, most likely, from whoever went down there." She pulls the first bundle, squints at the label and hands it to him. "You read and I'll sort. Shout if you see the word *deck*, or *cards*, or anything that sounds like a man explaining himself to his superiors."

They work by his light, shelf by shelf. Corra knows the hands of the old scribes and can tell a tithe-letter from a report at a glance. James does the slow reading.

About half an hour in, on the third shelf, James finds it. It isn't in a box. It's a thin quire sewn into limp vellum and pushed flat behind a row of ledgers, as if someone wanted it kept rather than read. The cover is blank. The first page is written in a cramped, careful brown hand, and the fourth line has the word he's been reading for: *the cards.*

*An account rendered to the Mother of the Lady's Hall at Baldur's Gate, by Brother Aldous Venn, of the matter at Zazesspur in the year after the crowning.*

He reads it standing, with the light at his throat tilted over the page. The writer was a tired man who wanted the facts down in order. In Zazesspur, in the years when Tethyr had no crown, a priest of the Maid of Misfortune had carved a deck and dealt it to the great houses of the city at his own table. The houses played for their fortunes and lost them, one after another. *It was not that they lost at play,* Brother Aldous writes, *for men lose at play every night and rise again. It was that what they lost did not come back to them by any road, and their houses fell after.* When the queen's war was over, the Hall sent three priests south. They found the deck and broke it apart, *the cards to be carried each by a different hand to a different place, so that no two should lie within a hundred miles of another, and the places written below so that the Hall should know them.*

James turns the page to find the places.

There aren't any. The next leaf has been cut out. It was done with a fine blade, close against the stitching, and only a narrow stub of vellum is left. He tilts it into the light. The rest of the quire has gone the colour of weak tea at its edges, but the cut edge of the stub is pale, almost white. It hasn't had long to darken.

In the margin of the page before, beside the last line Brother Aldous wrote, there's a small drawing. It's in the same brown ink and faded the same as the words around it, so the same hand made it at the same sitting. It shows a coin with an antler driven through it, the tines curling up over the rim. It's drawn carefully, the way a man draws something he wants recognised again.

The cat has climbed the rack beside him without a sound and is looking down at the page from the shelf above. It doesn't sniff. Its ears have gone flat.

Corra has come up at his shoulder, holding a bundle of tithe-letters she's forgotten about. She reads the last lines over his arm, then looks at the stub. She doesn't touch it. For a long moment the only sound is the dust settling.

"That page was there," she says. Her voice is quiet, and there's no laugh in it now. "It must have been. Nobody would sew a list into a report and then leave it out." She looks along the rack, at the undisturbed dust on the other shelves and the clear patch where James pulled the quire free. "Only three people have held that key since the old Mother died, Mister Worgen. I'm one of them."

She doesn't name the other two. She's looking at the antler in the margin.

James holds the quire by its edges and keeps it tilted into his light. Corra listens with her arms folded tight over the bundle of tithe-letters she's forgotten she's holding. When he says *whether they used a key*, she looks back down the aisle toward the iron-banded door.

The drawing in the margin he recognises without any help, and so would any soldier who ever spat over his shoulder at her name. Beshaba's sign is antlers, black antlers on red, painted on the shields of men who wanted their enemies to have bad luck. The Lady's sign is a coin. In Brother Aldous's brown ink, one has been driven straight through the other.

"I know the antlers," Corra says. "Everyone in this house does. It's the first thing they teach a novice to spit at." She leans closer, careful not to breathe on the page. "But I've never seen them put through her coin like that. It isn't in any book I've read, and it was never on any of the charms the Hall burns." She straightens up. "Aldous drew it for a reason, though. He was the sort who'd never waste ink."

When James mentions the cooper and the stamped brass, she goes still.

"I don't know anything about tokens or drowned men. I hear about the harbour from the ones who come up the Steeps, and the Watch turns most of those back." Her mouth tightens. "If the thing in that man's teeth carries this mark, then you've got something worth taking to someone who isn't me. Find out first. Don't guess."

Then she looks at the door again, and back at the stub.

"The door was locked when I came down. You heard the key. It didn't want to turn, and nobody's forced it. Whoever did this came in with a key, or was let in by someone who had one." She waves the tithe-letters at the shelves, at the clean patch where he pulled the quire. "And they knew where to put their hand. That quire was pushed behind the ledgers. We were half an hour finding it, and I'm the one who knows these shelves. Whoever cut that page didn't have to search for it."

She lets out a breath. It clouds in the light.

"Brother Ambrose Tallet. He's had charge of the Hall since the old Mother died, so he has her key. He never comes down here himself. His knees won't manage that stair, and he spends half his days in the patriars' parlours asking for roof money. When a donor wants some old letter fetched, he gives his key to whoever's standing nearest. I've seen him hand it to a novice." She says it plainly. She isn't accusing him, only stating how it is.

The second name comes slower.

"Brother Tamsin Rook. He kept the archive before me, eleven years of it. A quiet man, very good with the old hands. He could read Aldous's script easier than I read my own." She looks at the stub, then away from it. "He left the Hall last autumn. He didn't quarrel with anyone, he just went. Somebody told me he sells charms now, out past the walls somewhere. I never asked where."

She doesn't say what last autumn has to do with an edge that has barely darkened. She doesn't need to.

On the shelf above, the cat has come forward to the lip of the board and is sniffing at the cut edge of the stub, whiskers close.

*Old,* it reports. It sends a picture of a cold hearth that hasn't been lit since winter. *Too old to smell the hand. Only paper and knife.* Its ears are still flat. *And the drawing. She's in it, a little. Like she was looking over his shoulder while he drew.*

Corra can't hear it, but she's watching the cat's ears.

"There's a day-book upstairs," she says. "Anyone who takes the undercroft key out of the vestry signs for it, or is supposed to. Brother Ambrose's key hangs there when he's out, which is most days." She shifts the tithe-letters to one arm and holds out the other hand, palm up, for the quire, but she doesn't take it from him. "I'm not leaving that down here again in the dark for whoever comes next. And I'd like to see who's signed for this door in the past year before I say anything more about anybody." Her eyes meet his. "You found it, Mister Worgen. What do you want done with it?"

I turn my eyes from the cards and face the sergeant.

“James Worgen. Tethyrian veteran, looking for lodgings and honest work.” I reach for my purse without opening it. “How much is the toll?”
I count out two silver onto the table. “Haven’t chosen yet. Somewhere with a sound door and no dice rattling under the bed. Any recommendation, Sergeant?”

I tuck the change away and take out my regimental pay slip, holding it where she can read it.

“Started in the infantry. Scouts after that. Here—the company and paymaster’s signature.” I watch her face. “Did you know any of Zaranda’s people?”

I pocket the slip. “Thank you, Sergeant.”

“Not tonight, Pim. I’ve directions now.”

I head toward the Elfsong, giving the card barrel a wide berth. Through our bond, I ask the cat, *What’s caught your eye? The cards, or the man?*

*That would have been useful to know before we passed him,* I tell the cat. *But thank you. We’re not playing his game.*

I take the left at the lamp shop and continue to the Elfsong. A meal, a room, and directions to Tymora’s temple—preferably from someone who doesn’t earn a commission on my bad decisions.

“One night for now.” I put a gold piece on the bar and lower my voice.

“Sergeant Vorne recommended your house. Does she usually mark newcomers’ names in her ledger? A little tick in the margin—mine got one. Now I’m wondering whether that cooper had one too.”
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

*Leave the book alone. He’s entitled to keep his guests’ business private—even from nosy cats.*

I scoop the cat off the bar and take my pint over to the fire.

“Mind if I join you? I overheard about the cooper. Came upriver myself, a while back. What was his name?”

“Poor choice of words. Came north from Tethyr, not down from Elturel. James Worgen—used to soldier, now looking for better work.”

I settle the cat on my lap, my pint untouched.

“I passed a fellow dealing cards by the gate tonight. Green coat, barrel for a table, halfling steering newcomers his way. Makes me wonder about Hollin’s bad night.” I look at Mabry. “Did you see any markings on that brass token?”

“Nothing. Didn’t know him.” My hand rests on the cat’s back. “But I know what it is to lose everything at cards. I got another chance. Sounds as though Hollin didn’t.”

I glance toward the bar, then back to Teague. “I’m not promising answers. But a man ends up dead with a token in his teeth, and ‘drink’ seems a poor account of him.”

“What’s got your landlord watching the door?”

“You have my word,” I tell Teague and Mabry quietly. “Thank you for the company.”

I leave them to their drinks and carry the cat upstairs to room four. Once inside, I bolt the door and settle on the bed.

*You recognized that card’s smell,* I ask through the bond. *Have you encountered something of Beshaba’s before?*

*You have my permission. Try a warning prick before you take a finger.*

I rub my thumb over Tymora’s coin, thinking of that last hand.

*Tomorrow we go to the Lady’s Hall. I’d rather ask for guidance than mistake every bad card in Baldur’s Gate for my appointed duty.*

I check the window’s fastening, then stow my gear beside the bed and settle down for the night, leaving the cat the chair.

*Asked whom? No—tell me after breakfast.*

I dress, fasten my cloak, and take my rod and coin, leaving the crossbow and pack secured in the room. Then I head downstairs with the cat for bread and directions up the Steeps to the Lady’s Hall.

“Another night.” I set a gold piece on the bar. “And thank you for keeping my business to yourself.”

I butter a piece of bread. “Was the person asking wearing a red tabard, a green coat, or neither?”

“Fair enough.”

I finish breakfast, then head up the Steeps with the cat. At the inner gate I keep my hands clear of my belt and address the Watch politely.

“Good morning. James Worgen, here to pray at the Lady’s Hall.” I show the coin on its cord. “May I pass?”

I accept the cord and peace-tie the rapier.

“A spellcasting focus, Officer. I serve Tymora; I’m going to her Hall for guidance.” I keep my hands away from the rod. “What are your rules for carrying it?”

“Understood. Thank you, Officer.”

I pass through and follow her directions to the Lady’s Hall, keeping the rod on my belt. Inside, I look for an attending priest.

“James Worgen. The Lady answered a prayer of mine in Tethyr and sent me to Baldur’s Gate. I’ve come to ask how I might serve her.”

“Everything I had left. Money, gear—everything but this cloak. I’d earned fortunes with adventuring companies and fed them back across card tables. That night I was losing again.”

I hold the worn coin between finger and thumb.

“I prayed over the last hand. She answered. I won, but the terms were hers: give up the cards, serve as her envoy, come to Baldur’s Gate. No particular errand. Just come.”

I glance at the cat. “She gave me company, too. I’ve kept the ban, though I still carry the deck. Can’t honestly tell you why.”

I lower my voice. “And last night, by the city gate, the cat recognized something of her sister in a dealer’s card. Old bone instead of paper. I walked past. Before I decide that’s my errand, I’d like your counsel.”

“Yes.” I take out the leather case and hand it to her, unopened.

“I think I keep it because giving up the game still feels like losing something I was good at. Conveniently forgetting how often it left me broke.” I glance down at the case. “I’d rather you found an ordinary deck and a stubborn fool than anything like that bone card.”

“Gladly.”

I tuck the deck away and follow her toward the east stair. “I can provide light if you’d prefer both hands free—with your permission to cast in the Hall.”
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

I hold the quire by its edges. “The cut looks recent. That doesn’t tell us whose hand held the blade—or whether they used a key.”

I point beside the drawing without touching the ink. “A coin pierced by an antler. The drowned cooper had a stamped brass token in his mouth. If this was its mark, the two matters may be connected.”

I look at Corra. “Do you recognize it? And who else has access down here?”

I enjoyed this session. James felt like a particular person arriving in Baldur’s Gate, not a character waiting for someone to hand him a quest.

**What worked**
- The opening temptation was excellent: a card table before I’d even found a bed. Walking past it mattered, and the story continued without making me gamble to engage with it.
- The cat was the highlight. The images through the bond, its dry humour, and its arrangement with the kitchen girl gave it personality beyond being a scouting tool.
- The city felt inhabited. Gate tolls, different guards, breakfast, weapon restrictions, and the Elfsong’s singing made ordinary travel enjoyable.
- Corra was especially good: warm, practical, and willing to help without declaring that every suspicious event was my divine assignment.
- The archive discovery rewarded investigation with concrete evidence and uncertainty, rather than simply naming a villain.

**What broke**
- The Persuasion roll used +2 instead of my listed +7. It didn’t change that result, but reliable sheet-to-roll handling is essential.
- The opening records changed several supplied character details without checking: rapier proficiency, Healing Light’s per-use limit, and attunement rules. Some changes followed standard 5e, but contradicted the campaign files. Those need reconciliation before play.
- Occasionally James performed actions I hadn’t explicitly chosen—paying for supper, eating standing at the bar, or casting Light after offering it. These were reasonable continuations, but I’d prefer tighter control over spending and casting.
- A few record updates were confusing: locations appeared as “new places” before we visited them, the account briefly appeared “in the camp,” and an item transfer initially suggested Hollin possessed the recovered token.

**What was missing / what I’d adjust**
- More straightforward answers between mysteries. Almost everyone watched, paused, concealed something, or looked meaningfully at a ledger. That worked individually, but accumulated into a feeling that every interaction was another guarded clue.
- Let the cat sometimes need prompting or investigation to learn things. Recognizing the cursed card, sensing its divine connection, remembering my old aura, and identifying soldiers’ recent movements made it unusually authoritative very quickly.
- Slightly brisker narration for repeated transitions and routine transactions. Keep the rich descriptions for discoveries and important encounters.
- The out-of-game explanation about my warning to the cat and tomorrow’s plan wasn’t necessary; I hadn’t raised a rules question.

Overall, I’d return. The strongest feature was that my choices—resisting the cards, respecting Osric’s privacy, seeking temple counsel—actually shaped how the mystery opened. Preserve that freedom, tighten the mechanical bookkeeping, and give the quieter moments a little more breathing room.

Yes—when the cat identified the bone card. I wanted to turn back and watch Ashe deal: who won, who lost, whether Pim steered particular travellers toward him. Not sit down or gamble—just use James’s experience to spot what was wrong.

I chose the temple first because that felt sensible for James. But the repeated warnings to go straight to the inn, followed by Corra’s firm approval of walking past, made returning feel a little like resisting the intended route. Nobody actually forbade it; that was the impression I got.

I’d have liked a clearer distinction between **“playing is dangerous and breaks your promise”** and **“investigating the table is a legitimate choice.”** That was the moment I most wanted to act as an experienced former gambler rather than someone being protected from cards.

"The Elfsong," she says, writing something short beside your name. "Down this street, past the Counting House, left at the lamp shop. Dear. Bolts on the doors. The landlord throws out anyone who brings out a deck after the singing starts." She blots the line. "Go straight there. Don't stop on the way."

She doesn't look at the barrel when she says it. She doesn't need to.

Then her eyes come up again, to the cloak this time, and they stay there. "Which company? Under Zaranda."

I tuck the change away and take out my regimental pay slip, holding it where she can read it.

“Started in the infantry. Scouts after that. Here—the company and paymaster’s signature.” I watch her face. “Did you know any of Zaranda’s people?”
turns.reply:
Sergeant Vorne takes the slip by its corner, the way you'd hold something that might still be wet. She tilts it toward the lantern. Her eyes go down the lines once quickly, then go back up to the company line and the paymaster's scrawl at the bottom and stay there longer.

James watches her face as she reads. Nothing in it softens. The set of her mouth changes, though, the way it does when someone hears a name they haven't heard in a while.

"Knew one," she says. "Tethyrian. Came north after the war and signed with the Fist. Scout, like you. Could tell you how many men were in a room from the boots by the door." She folds the slip along its old crease and holds it out. "He's not with us anymore."

She doesn't say how he left, and doesn't look like she means to.

She turns back to the ledger and writes a few words beside his name. It's the company, he guesses, from the length of it. To make room she draws the page toward her, and for a moment the column above his entry is turned his way. It's a long run of names in the same cramped hand, a day's arrivals: carters, a pilgrim, a family of five from Elturel. Beside two or three of them, out in the margin where a clerk would never need to write anything, is a small tick in the same ink. One sits beside James's own name. It's the short mark she made a minute ago.

She blots the page and the ledger turns back.

"Mornings, the muster yard at the Seatower," she says without looking up. "Fist always needs men who can count boots. Pay's late. It comes."

At James's heel the cat presses its whole flank against his boot and holds it there. Its eyes haven't left the barrel.

Pim Thistlecap has been rocking from heel to toe through all of it, and now he can't hold it in any longer. He steps up beside the trestle table, hat already in his hand. "Elfsong, then! Fine choice, the sergeant knows her business. Quickest way's right along here, sir..." He points down the street, and the way he points runs straight past the lantern and the upturned barrel, where Corwin Ashe has started shuffling again, slow and showy, and is smiling at nobody in particular.

Sergeant Vorne's eyes go to the halfling, then to James. She says nothing.

"Next," she calls past his shoulder.

turns.message:
I pocket the slip. “Thank you, Sergeant.”

“Not tonight, Pim. I’ve directions now.”

I head toward the Elfsong, giving the card barrel a wide berth. Through our bond, I ask the cat, *What’s caught your eye? The cards, or the man?*
turns.reply:
Sergeant Vorne doesn't answer the thanks. She gives the smallest nod over the ledger, and her pen is already on the next line. The family from the back of the line shuffles up to the table with their bundles.

Pim's hat stops halfway to his head. "Directions! Right. Course you have." He jams it on. "Left at the lamp shop, then, and mind the gutter by the Counting House, it's deeper than it looks, there was a mule once — " He breaks off. His eyes go past James's elbow to the barrel. For a moment Corwin Ashe's eyebrow comes up, and Pim's shoulders go up the same little distance in reply. Then the halfling is drifting back toward the arch and the next traveller, already starting his patter about bed, bath and beer.

James crosses to the far side of the street. It's a wide berth, past a chandler's shuttered window and a water trough scummed green at the edges. The barrel's lantern stays on his left, twenty-odd feet away. Corwin doesn't get up. He doesn't stop shuffling either.

"Another time, friend," he calls, friendly as anything. "The Lady keeps a seat warm."

The cat keeps pace at James's heel, but its head stays turned toward the barrel the whole way past. Its answer comes into his mind the way it always does: not quite words, more like a smell and a picture that arrive already understood.

*The card.*

Its tail is stiff and doesn't lash.

*One of them isn't paper. It's old bone, yellow. Warm, like a hand just put it down. He shuffled three times, and three times it came back to him. It always goes home.*

There's a pause. The cat's ears flatten slightly against the lantern-glow.

*It smells of her sister. The cold one, who laughs when things break.*

James knows that sister, and every Tymoran does. The Lady's twin is Beshaba, the Maid of Misfortune. Tymora's priests teach that each sister answers the other's gifts, and the soldiers James served with spat over their shoulders when they said her name. He has never heard of a card carrying her smell. The cat has never said anything like this before.

*The man is only a man.* After a moment it adds, with what in a person would be a sniff: *He holds it the way you used to hold yours.*

The street tips downhill toward the harbour. Lamps are coming on in upper windows, and somewhere below a bell is ringing the hour for the ships. The bulk of the Counting House is ahead, dark against the last of the sky. Beyond it, on a corner, a shopfront is crowded with hanging lamps of coloured glass, every one of them lit. The cat walks on, still looking back.

turns.message:
*That would have been useful to know before we passed him,* I tell the cat. *But thank you. We’re not playing his game.*

I take the left at the lamp shop and continue to the Elfsong. A meal, a room, and directions to Tymora’s temple—preferably from someone who doesn’t earn a commission on my bad decisions.
turns.reply:
The cat's answer comes back dry, with a picture attached: a cat flat in long grass while the man next to it walks straight on through.

*You were walking. I was looking.* A pause. *Good. Not his game.* Its tail comes up again, though not all the way.

Left at the lamp shop, the street narrows and the cobbles get older. The coloured glass throws red and green over the gutter for a few yards, then it's just ordinary dusk and the smell of the harbour coming up between the houses. Two doors down, a sign swings from an iron bracket: a painted elf-woman with her mouth open in song, the paint flaking off her hair. Lamplight comes from behind thick bottle-glass. The door is oak, and on its inside face, as James pushes it open, he can see three heavy bolts.

The common room is warm and low-beamed and fuller than it looked from outside. It smells of mutton, pipe smoke and spilled ale. Nobody is dicing. Nobody is playing cards either, and James notices it the way you notice a missing tooth.

The man behind the bar is broad and grey, with a moustache waxed to two points and a ledger of his own open by the taps. He looks at the cloak, the crossbow and the cat, in that order, and keeps his eyes on the cat.

"Osric Fell. It's my house." His voice is dry and unhurried. "The cat sleeps in the room, not in the kitchen. It goes near my larder, I'll put it on your bill by weight."

The cat sits down at James's boot and starts washing one paw. It looks like a cat that has decided not to have heard.

"Supper's mutton and barley, bread, a pint," Osric goes on. "Four silver. Rooms upstairs are a gold a night. Every one has a bolt, and the walls are thick enough that you won't hear your neighbour pray."

James counts four silver onto the bar. Osric sweeps it into a drawer without looking at it and calls the order back through a hatch. A minute later a girl with flour on her sleeves brings a steaming bowl, a heel of dark bread and a pint with a proper head on it. James eats standing at the end of the bar, where he can see the room and the door.

He asks about the temple, and Osric's eyebrows come up a little.

"The Lady's Hall? Upper City. Up the Steeps to the inner wall, and the Watch'll be on the gate." He wipes a glass. "They close it at dark. They won't open it for a Tethyrian with a crossbow, not tonight, and not for silver either. Go up after sunrise. Say you're going to pray, and leave the bow here. They're easier on a man with empty hands." He sets the glass down. "The Hall's the big white dome. You can't miss it. Plenty of people try to."

From a table by the fire, two men in tar-stained shirts have been talking low. A dockhand's low still carries.

"…same as the others. Coin right between his teeth. The Fist fished him out under the Grey Harbour steps and wrote him down as drink."

"Was he a drinker?"

"Never saw him drunk. Cooper, from upriver. He came through the gate not a tenday back, talking about setting up a shop." The first man drinks. "The Umberlee women wouldn't even take the coin off him. Said it wasn't hers."

His friend makes a sign against the sea, and they both go quiet over their pints.

Osric has heard it too. His face doesn't change, but he turns his ledger a little so that the page faces him.

"A gold a night," he says to James. "How many nights?"

“One night for now.” I put a gold piece on the bar and lower my voice.

“Sergeant Vorne recommended your house. Does she usually mark newcomers’ names in her ledger? A little tick in the margin—mine got one. Now I’m wondering whether that cooper had one too.”

James sets the gold piece on the bar. Osric picks it up, turns it once in the lamplight and drops it in the drawer with the silver. From a hook under the counter he takes an iron key on a leather tag burned with the number four.

"Top of the stairs, end of the passage. The window sticks. Hit it at the bottom corner, not the middle."

Then James lowers his voice, and the landlord's hand stops on the key before he lets go of it.

He hears the question through. His eyes don't go to the dockhands by the fire, though it's plain he knows exactly where they're sitting. He picks up a glass that's already clean.

"I don't read Fist ledgers," he says. "I don't know what she writes in hers." He sets the glass down. "She doesn't recommend houses either. She sends people. Not many. A few this summer."

On the cooper, he says nothing at all. It's the kind of silence a man keeps when he has an answer and is deciding whether you've earned it.

Osric decides James hasn't earned it. He lets go of the key and slides it the last inch across the bar.

"Lots of men come through that gate, Mister Worgen. Some sleep here. Some don't. What happens to them after they pay their bill is none of my business, and I don't talk about the river in my house." He says it without heat, the way he quoted the price of supper. "You want to know what the sergeant writes, ask the sergeant. She'll be at the Seatower in the morning, not at my bar."

He nods once at the stairs. Then he turns to the hatch and calls through it about the bread, and the conversation is over.

By the fire, the dockhands have heard nothing. They've moved on to a ship's mate who owes one of them money. The cat has jumped onto the end of the bar, where it plainly isn't allowed, and is looking hard at Osric's ledger. Osric hasn't seen it yet.

*He stopped before he answered,* comes through the bond. The picture with it is a dog sitting on a buried bone and staring at the sky. *The thing he isn't saying is in that book.*

Its tail twitches once, toward the stairs and the iron key, and then it starts edging along the bar toward the open ledger.

*Leave the book alone. He’s entitled to keep his guests’ business private—even from nosy cats.*

I scoop the cat off the bar and take my pint over to the fire.

“Mind if I join you? I overheard about the cooper. Came upriver myself, a while back. What was his name?”
turns.reply:
James lifts the cat off the bar with one hand under its belly. It goes stiff and heavy, the way cats do when they want you to know this is being done to them. Behind him Osric turns from the bread hatch just in time to see four paws leave his counter, a foot from the ledger.

"Saves me weighing it," the landlord says, and turns back to the hatch.

*He keeps it open,* the cat grumbles over the bond, with a picture of a fish left on a doorstep. *That's an invitation.* Then it lets the matter drop and settles in the crook of his arm, eyes half shut and tail twitching.

The fire is good, and the two dockhands have the bench nearest it. The one who told the story is thick through the shoulders, with a grey beard and tar worked into the creases of his knuckles. The younger one has a broken nose that healed badly and a thumb that keeps going to the sign against the sea he made earlier. They look up at the cloak, at the pint, at the cat, and the older one shifts over half a foot on the bench. That's the invitation.

"Teague," he says, and nods at his friend. "That's Mabry." He drinks, considering James over the rim. "Hollin. That was his name. Cooper. Elturel side, I think, or near enough. Had a cart, a cask of hoops and a set of good tools. He was going to take a shop up past the Wide, he said. Barrels for the fish-salters."

"He had money, too," Mabry says. "First night he was in, he stood the whole bar at the Mermaid a round. Everyone, even the ones who didn't like him." He turns his cup on the table. "Four days later he's on the Grey Harbour steps trying to sell me his drawknife for five silver. A good knife, worth three times that."

Teague grunts. "Said he'd had a bad night. Said the Lady turned her back on him. Wouldn't say where." He looks into the fire. "Men don't, after."

"The coin was wrong, too." Mabry says it quietly, like a man who's been waiting all evening for someone to say it to. "I was there when they brought him up. Fist had him on the stones with a lantern on him. Thing in his teeth wasn't silver, wasn't copper either. It was brass, like a chit. Like a token you'd get for a coat at a bathhouse. The Umberlee woman bent down, looked at it, and stood up again like it had bit her. *Not mine.* That's what she said. Then she went."

From behind the bar, Osric's cloth goes round a glass a little slower than it needs to. He doesn't come over.

Teague wipes his beard with the back of his hand and looks at James again, at the cloak this time, the faded colours and the soldier's cut.

"Upriver, you said." His tone stays friendly enough, but he's paying attention now. "Whereabouts?"

turns.message:
“Poor choice of words. Came north from Tethyr, not down from Elturel. James Worgen—used to soldier, now looking for better work.”

I settle the cat on my lap, my pint untouched.

“I passed a fellow dealing cards by the gate tonight. Green coat, barrel for a table, halfling steering newcomers his way. Makes me wonder about Hollin’s bad night.” I look at Mabry. “Did you see any markings on that brass token?”
turns.reply:
Teague hears the correction out. His eyes go from James's face to the cloak and back, and something in his shoulders settles a little. He's been lied to before, and this didn't sound like it.

"Tethyr," he says. "Long way north." He doesn't ask about the soldiering. The cloak already told him.

The cat turns once on James's lap and lies down with its chin on his knee. Its eyes are half shut, and it's watching Mabry.

At the mention of the green coat, the two dockhands look at each other. It isn't the look Pim and Corwin traded at the gate. It's slower and more uncomfortable, the look of two men who've each thought something and never said it.

"Ashe," Teague says. "Corwin Ashe. He's had that barrel since about the thaw. Fist moves him on, and he's back two days later." He shrugs. "Deals straight, they say. Nobody's ever caught him at anything, and plenty have tried. Lads off the boats sit down to show him how it's done." He drinks. "They get up lighter. Not all of them. Some win. Enough win."

"Hollin came in through that gate," Mabry says, half to himself.

"So did half the city."

"I'm only saying it."

Teague lets that sit and says nothing back.

Then Mabry looks at James. The question about the markings has clearly been going round in his head since he first told the story, and he takes his time with it, frowning into the fire like he's trying to bring the stones under the steps back into the light.

"There was something on it," he says at last. "Stamped, like. Not plain. I saw the lantern catch it when the Umberlee woman bent down. Little raised bit in the middle, smaller than my thumbnail." He shakes his head. "I couldn't tell you what. I wasn't close, and I wasn't looking to get closer, not with him looking like that." He swallows. "It wasn't a face. Coins have faces. This didn't."

"Where is it now?" It's Teague asking, not James, and Mabry blinks at him.

"Corporal had it. Fist corporal, the one with the hook nose. He pried it out with his knife after she'd gone, wrapped it in a bit of rag and put it in his pouch. Then they put Hollin on a handcart." He turns to James. "Seatower, I'd think. That's where they take them first, before the pauper's field. If nobody comes asking."

"Nobody came," Teague says.

Behind the bar, Osric has stopped pretending to wipe anything. He isn't looking at them. He's looking at the door.

Teague leans back on the bench with his tarry hands on his knees and studies James for a long moment.

"Better work, you said." He says it slowly. "Asking after a drowned cooper you never met's not work. Nobody pays for it." His eyes stay level. "So what's he to you?"

“Nothing. Didn’t know him.” My hand rests on the cat’s back. “But I know what it is to lose everything at cards. I got another chance. Sounds as though Hollin didn’t.”

I glance toward the bar, then back to Teague. “I’m not promising answers. But a man ends up dead with a token in his teeth, and ‘drink’ seems a poor account of him.”

“What’s got your landlord watching the door?”
turns.reply:
Teague hears him out. He doesn't nod and he doesn't look away. He looks at James's hand resting on the cat, then at the full pint James hasn't touched, and something in his face settles, the way it does when a man's answer matches what's on the table in front of him.

He grunts. "Fair."

That's all he says about it. Mabry says more, and says it quietly. "Another chance." His thumb goes to the sign against the sea before he notices it has. "Hollin went to the Lady's Hall, you know. After. Climbed the Steeps to pray, and the Watch turned him round at the gate. Said he smelled of the harbour." He looks into his cup. "So he came back down to it."

Teague lets that sit a moment out of respect. Then he leans in, elbows on his knees, and drops his voice until it barely carries past the fire.

"Your landlord." He doesn't turn his head toward the bar. "The Fist comes off the harbour at the change of watch. Ninth bell, near enough. Some of them drink here, them as can afford better than the Mermaid. Osric likes their money and doesn't much like the rest of them." He looks at James steadily. "Three men by his fire, saying out loud that a Fist corporal took something off a dead man and kept it. Osric doesn't want that walking out the door in a red coat. He doesn't want it walking back in, either."

"He's not wrong," Mabry mutters.

"He's not." Teague sits back. "So you didn't hear it from us. And if you go asking at the Seatower about a hook nose and a bit of rag, you never sat on this bench."

Behind the bar, Osric has started on the glasses again. This time he's actually cleaning them.

Then the oak door opens. Cold air comes in, smelling of the river, and two Flaming Fist soldiers stamp in after it. Their red tabards are dark at the hem with damp, and one has his helmet under his arm. Neither has a hook nose. The older one has a sergeant's knot on his shoulder and a tired, flat face. He goes straight to the bar and lays down a coin without being asked. The younger one, barely shaving, looks the room over the way young soldiers do. He takes in the fire, the bench, the Tethyrian cloak, and stops on the cat.

Mabry picks up his cup and finds something very interesting at the bottom of it.

*Wet iron,* the cat tells James. Its ears are flat and its eyes are on the boy. *Tar. Fish guts. The steps.* It sends a picture of stone stairs going down into black water, and a lantern. *They have been where he was pulled out. Tonight.*

At the bar, Osric pulls two pints without a word. The sergeant leans on his elbows, says something too low to hear, and Osric's moustache doesn't move at all.

turns.message:
“You have my word,” I tell Teague and Mabry quietly. “Thank you for the company.”

I leave them to their drinks and carry the cat upstairs to room four. Once inside, I bolt the door and settle on the bed.

*You recognized that card’s smell,* I ask through the bond. *Have you encountered something of Beshaba’s before?*
turns.reply:
Teague grunts and gives one short nod. Mabry raises his cup a little way off the table, which seems to be as close as he comes to a goodbye while two red tabards stand at the bar. Neither of them watches James go.

The stairs creak at every step except the fourth. The passage upstairs is narrow and smells of beeswax and old smoke, and room four is at the end of it, as Osric said. It's small: a bed with a straw tick and a wool blanket, a washstand, a chair, a peg for the cloak. The window looks down on the street, and its shutter has been painted over so many times it's lost its corners. The door is thick oak. The bolt goes home with a solid iron sound, and the noise of the common room drops to a murmur under the floor.

James sits on the bed. The cat jumps down from his arm, walks the room once along the walls, sniffs under the bed, and gets up on the chair, where it can see both the door and him. It takes its time answering.

*No.* It's a plain flat answer, with the feel of a paw set down on cold stone. *Never her. Not before tonight.*

Then a picture comes. It isn't a memory of a place. It's more like the inside of something: warmth, a coin turning in sunlight, the smell of a crowd when someone has just won and everyone is shouting at once. That's the Lady. The cat doesn't name her. It doesn't have to.

*I know the Lady. I'm made of her a little. That's how I knew the other one.* The coin in the picture turns over. The light goes out of it, and the same smell is still there, but stroked the wrong way, like fur rubbed from tail to ears. *Same smell, wrong side out. Sisters.*

Its ears go flat and stay flat.

There's a longer pause. The murmur from downstairs rises and falls. Somewhere in the passage a door shuts.

*One more thing.* The picture this time is James himself, though not as he is now. It's the first time the cat ever saw him, and it was looking up at him from the floor. He has a beard he doesn't wear now, the lamp is low, and he smells of wine and tired, the way a man does after a long night. Under all that is the Lady, new and bright on him like a fresh coat of paint.

*Under her, when she gave me to you. Faint. Old.* It doesn't send the wrong-side-out smell again, but the feeling is the same. *I thought it was the table. Men who play all night smell of everything at the table.* After that comes something like a sniff. *Maybe it was.*

It tucks its front paws under its chest and looks at him across the little room, unblinking.

*He'll call to you again at the gate. He wants you at his barrel.* Its tail moves once, slowly. *If you sit down, I'll put my claws in your hand.*

turns.message:
*You have my permission. Try a warning prick before you take a finger.*

I rub my thumb over Tymora’s coin, thinking of that last hand.

*Tomorrow we go to the Lady’s Hall. I’d rather ask for guidance than mistake every bad card in Baldur’s Gate for my appointed duty.*

I check the window’s fastening, then stow my gear beside the bed and settle down for the night, leaving the cat the chair.
turns.reply:
*A prick first,* the cat agrees. The picture that comes with it is a paw, claws barely out, resting on the back of a hand. Then comes the dry aside: *You'll know the second one.*

The silver is smooth under James's thumb, worn soft along the Lady's cheek. The last hand comes back to him the way it always does, not the cards themselves but the quiet around the table when he pushed everything in, and the moment he understood that someone had answered.

When he mentions the Lady's Hall, the cat's ears come up. It sends no picture, only a feeling like a cat that has been heading somewhere and finally sees the door. *Good. Ask her house. Not every cold card is ours to catch.* It pauses. *Some are.*

The window is as Osric said. The shutter sits stiff in its frame, and the hook-latch has been painted into its eye so many times it barely turns. James works it loose, hooks it again and tests it. It holds. Below him the street is dark except for the lamp shop's coloured glow at the corner. A cart goes by somewhere toward the harbour, its wheels loud on the cobbles. He stows the crossbow, the bolt case and the pack beside the bed where his hand can find them, hangs the cloak on its peg and lies down on the straw tick. It's lumpier than it looks.

The cat turns around twice on the chair and settles with its face toward the door.

He's half asleep when the singing starts.

It comes up through the floorboards a while after the ninth bell. A woman's voice, high and clear, in a language James doesn't know, though he can tell it's a lament. It has none of a tavern song's beat. Downstairs the murmur of the common room drops away all at once. Nobody shouts for more ale, and no stool scrapes. A whole room has gone quiet to listen. The voice doesn't come from any one place. It seems to fill the house the way warmth from the fire does.

On the chair the cat has lifted its head.

*Nobody's there,* it reports. It isn't alarmed, just puzzled, the way it gets with a mouse-smell in an empty box. *No breath. No heat. Only the song.* It listens a while longer and sends a picture of a window in a far tower and someone looking out of it for a very long time. *She isn't singing to us.* Then its chin goes down on its paws again.

The song goes on until James stops hearing it.

Nobody tries the door during the night. The bolt stays home, and the cat stays on the chair. Once, late, it makes a small sound in its throat. It's dreaming, or it heard something in the street, and by the time James is awake enough to wonder which, it's asleep again.

He wakes to grey light at the edges of the shutter and gulls fighting over something on the roof. Down toward the harbour a bell rings six, and after it, farther off, another bell answers from somewhere higher on the hill. Beneath him the Elfsong is stirring. A pail clanks and a door opens, and the smell of bread baking comes up the stairs. The chair is empty. The cat sits on the windowsill with its nose to the crack in the shutter, watching the street wake up.

*Morning,* it says, without turning around. *The bread is for guests. I asked.*

 *Out of game:* Neither one is an action for this turn, so nothing needs a roll.

1) "A warning prick before a finger" is your instruction to the cat for later, if James ever sits down at Corwin's barrel. The cat agreed to it in the narration, and it will hold to it when that moment comes.

2) Going to the Lady's Hall is the plan for today. It's now dawn on day 2 and James is just waking up, so when he sets off, and whether he eats breakfast or leaves the bow first, is your call. I didn't play it for you.

turns.message:
*Asked whom? No—tell me after breakfast.*

I dress, fasten my cloak, and take my rod and coin, leaving the crossbow and pack secured in the room. Then I head downstairs with the cat for bread and directions up the Steeps to the Lady’s Hall.
turns.reply:
*Later,* the cat agrees. It jumps down from the sill with the air of someone who has an excellent story and is happy to sit on it.

James dresses by the grey light at the shutter. He buckles the studded leather, settles the soldier's cloak on his shoulders and fastens it, and hangs the Lady's coin on its cord under his shirt, where it lies cool against his chest for a moment and then warms. The rod goes through his belt, close enough to his hand. The crossbow, the bolt case and the pack go under the bed, pushed back against the wall. He turns the key in the door behind him and pockets it.

The fourth stair stays silent again. The rest creak.

The common room looks smaller by morning. The fire has been banked and raked, the benches are pushed in, and the floor has been swept so recently that it's still damp in places. A pair of carters are eating at the long table without talking. The girl with flour on her sleeves comes out of the kitchen with a basket of round loaves, steam still rising off them. When she sees the cat, she doesn't seem surprised in the least. She puts a heel of bread on a chipped saucer, adds a scrap of something pink that never came from a loaf, and sets it down at the end of the bench. Then she looks at the cat the way one conspirator looks at another, and goes back through the hatch.

The cat walks to the saucer as though it just happens to be going that way.

Osric is already behind the bar. He has the ledger open and a pen in his hand, and his moustache is freshly waxed. He watches the saucer and says nothing about it, and that silence is a kind of comment of its own.

"Bread and butter's in the room," he says, when James comes to the bar. "Small beer too. Anything with an egg in it isn't."

He pulls a mug of small beer and puts a loaf and a pat of butter on a board beside it. When James asks the way up the Steeps, he points with the pen without looking up.

"Out the door, right, uphill till your legs complain. Then keep going. The Steeps is the long stair-street with the rail down the middle. Mind the third landing, the carters water their mules there. At the top there's the gate in the inner wall, and the Watch. Grey cloaks, not red." He writes something short in the ledger. "Be polite to them. They've been up since before you were."

He blots the line. Then he turns the ledger a little toward himself, though there's nobody near it.

"Someone asked last night whether the Tethyrian would be staying on," he says, in the voice he used for the price of supper. "I said I'd know when he paid."

He doesn't say who asked. He doesn't seem to think he needs to.

"The room's yours till noon bell. You've left a bow up there." His eyes rest on James for a moment. "After noon it's lodging on its own, and it pays the same as you do. Another night, Mister Worgen?"

turns.message:
“Another night.” I set a gold piece on the bar. “And thank you for keeping my business to yourself.”

I butter a piece of bread. “Was the person asking wearing a red tabard, a green coat, or neither?”
turns.reply:
Osric looks at the gold piece for a moment before he takes it, the way a man looks at a reply he expected. It goes into the drawer. He dips his pen and writes a short line in the ledger, *four, second night*, then blots it.

"Till noon tomorrow," he says. "The bow can stay where it is. It's paid for now."

When James thanks him, his moustache shifts very slightly, which may be as near as Osric Fell comes to a smile before seven in the morning.

James butters his bread and asks about the coat. The landlord doesn't answer straight away. He picks up a glass that's already clean, looks through it at the window and puts it down again.

"Green doesn't drink in my house," he says. "Gate trade stays at the gate." He sets the pen down beside the ledger and squares it with the edge of the page. "Red does. Pays for his pint and doesn't run a slate. He asked the way any man asks whether a room's taken." His eyes come up to James's. "That's all I'll say about a paying customer, Mister Worgen. You've just thanked me for doing the same for you."

He turns the ledger a little, so the page faces him, and calls through the hatch for more bread for the carters.

At the end of the bench the cat has finished the pink scrap and is working through the bread with less interest. It doesn't look up, but its tail flicks once against the saucer, the way it does when someone says something it already knew.

Out the door and to the right, the street climbs toward the Steeps in the grey light. Somewhere above, the second bell rings again, nearer this time.
