turns.message:
“Fair enough.”

I finish breakfast, then head up the Steeps with the cat. At the inner gate I keep my hands clear of my belt and address the Watch politely.

“Good morning. James Worgen, here to pray at the Lady’s Hall.” I show the coin on its cord. “May I pass?”
turns.reply:
The bread is good: dark, a little sour, with the crust still crackling. James eats it at the end of the bar with the small beer. Osric writes in his ledger and doesn't speak again. The kitchen girl collects the cat's saucer without a word, and the cat looks at her as she goes the way it might look at a door it means to use again.

Outside it's turning into a real morning. The street to the right climbs between tall narrow houses with their shutters going up one after another. A boy is sluicing a doorstep, and a woman shakes a rug out of a second-floor window without looking to see who's under it. The cat walks at his heel with its tail straight up.

They're two streets up when it pays what it owes.

*The girl,* it says. The picture is the kitchen girl from last night, bending down with a steaming bowl while James stood at the bar. It sees her from low down, by her ankles, looking up at her for a long time without blinking. *I asked her like that. She understood. Most of them do.* It sends a feeling like a purr it isn't bothering to make out loud. *Pink is mutton.*

A few steps later it sends something different, flatter and cooler.

*The red one who asked about you. Flat face, knot on his shoulder, wet iron. He leaned on the bar, and the man with the moustache leaned in to listen. I was on your knee.* An ear flicks back. *I hear better than you do. He said "Tethyrian." He said "staying." The rest was under the noise.* It adds, with a small sniff: *I'd have said so last night, but you were busy with the fire men.*

The street ends at the foot of the Steeps, and James sees why Osric warned his legs. It's a long stair-street with an iron rail worn bright down the middle, climbing between houses that get taller and cleaner the higher they stand. Carters lead mules up the shallow ramp beside the steps. Porters climb with baskets on their backs, bent almost double. Halfway up, a priest in Lathander's rose and gold takes the stairs two at a time, and he isn't out of breath.

The third landing is wet and smells of mule, just as promised. A trough stands against the wall with three animals drinking from it, and a carter sits on its edge eating an onion like an apple. The cat goes around the puddles with great dignity.

From up here James can see over the roofs to the harbour. The water is grey, crowded with masts, and gulls are wheeling over the fish market. Out on its rock in the bay, the Seatower of Balduran is dark against the morning. A drum is beating out there, faint and steady across the water, and small red shapes are moving in rows in a yard on its seaward side. It's the muster. By the sound of it, it started a while ago.

The cat follows his eyes and says nothing.

The higher landings are drier, and the people on them are better dressed. Near the top the Steeps widen into a small paved square, and the inner wall rises across it, older than the outer one, its stone gone honey-grey with age. The gate is open. Two pikes stand crossed in a rack beside it, not across the way. In front of it the Watch keeps a narrow wooden booth with a slate hung on a nail. There are three of them. Their grey cloaks are pinned at the shoulder with a silver badge, and they wear their helmets in a way that suggests they'd rather not. A cart of firewood is being waved through as James arrives. A maid with a covered basket goes in after it without anyone looking at her.

Then it's James's turn. He walks up with his hands well away from his belt.

The officer at the booth is a tall woman in her forties. Her grey hair is cropped short under the helmet, and her face is long and patient, the face of someone who has stood at this gate through a great many mornings. She hears him out. When he draws the coin out on its cord she leans forward an inch to look at it, at Tymora's worn silver face, then at his. She takes in the soldier's cut of the cloak, the faded colours and the boots. Last of all she looks at the cat, which has sat down on the paving and is washing a shoulder as if it's come to inspect the gate rather than pass through it.

"Morning, sir." Her voice is level and correct, the Upper City kind of polite, which keeps its distance. "Watch-Officer Lowe. The Hall's open from first bell. Plenty come up to pray to the Lady before a venture." She chalks something short on the slate: his name, by the length of it. "Mind the pigeons on the steps there. They're holier than we are."

The younger watchman beside her doesn't smile at that. He's looking at James's hip.

Lowe's eyes have gone there too. "That's a blade, sir." She says it without any heat, the way she might mention rain. "You'll wear it peace-tied inside the wall." She takes a short length of grey cord from a hook inside the booth and holds it out to him across the ledge, knotted ready for a hilt.

Then her glance moves an inch along his belt and stops on the rod, black and plain, pushed through the leather beside his hand. She doesn't reach for it, and her voice doesn't change.

"And that." She waits a breath. "What would that be, sir?"

turns.message:
I accept the cord and peace-tie the rapier.

“A spellcasting focus, Officer. I serve Tymora; I’m going to her Hall for guidance.” I keep my hands away from the rod. “What are your rules for carrying it?”
turns.reply:
James takes the cord. It's a plain grey braid, stiff with use. He loops it twice around the rapier's guard and through the scabbard's throat and pulls it tight, then ties it off with a soldier's knot that comes free with one pull but won't loosen from walking. Lowe watches his hands the whole time. When he's done she leans over the ledge, hooks a finger under the cord and gives it a short tug. It holds, and she lets it go.

While he answers her about the rod, his hands stay well away from it. She waits until he's finished before she says anything.

"A focus." She looks at the rod again, longer this time. It's black, plain, and has no gilt or saint's face on it to tell anyone whose it is. "The Lady's priests carry silver, mostly. Coins, dice." Her eyes go to the cord at his throat, then back up. "But I've seen stranger things come through for the Hall."

She picks up the chalk and adds a short word beside his name on the slate. *Rod*, by the look of it.

"The rule's simple, sir. It stays where it is, on the belt, in plain sight. Don't draw it or point it, and don't hold it in your hand on the street." She says it in the same level voice she used for the blade. "No spells inside the wall except in a temple, and only with the temple's leave. If anything gets cast in the street, warm hands or a light in the dark or anything else, the man who cast it explains himself at the Watch-house. They're less patient there than I am." She sets the chalk down. "If you're still inside at sundown bell, you sleep up here at your own cost. The gate doesn't open again till morning."

The younger watchman has stopped looking at the rapier and is looking at the rod. He doesn't say anything. Lowe doesn't look at him either, but he takes half a step back to his place beside the booth all the same.

Down on the paving, the cat has finished its shoulder. It stands, stretches front legs first, and walks under the ledge of the booth as if the gate were already open to it, which in fairness it is. As it passes, it sniffs once at the young watchman's boot.

*Lamp oil. Pigeons,* it reports, sounding bored. *Nothing from the steps.* Its tail lifts. *These ones live up here.*

Lowe steps back from the ledge. "The Hall's straight on and up to the left. It's the white dome. Follow the bells." Her eyes rest on James a moment longer, on the faded colours of the cloak. "Go on through, Mister Worgen."

Behind him a porter with a load of wine jars is already shifting his feet, waiting for his turn.

turns.message:
“Understood. Thank you, Officer.”

I pass through and follow her directions to the Lady’s Hall, keeping the rod on my belt. Inside, I look for an attending priest.

“James Worgen. The Lady answered a prayer of mine in Tethyr and sent me to Baldur’s Gate. I’ve come to ask how I might serve her.”
turns.reply:
Past the gate the Upper City is quiet in a way the Lower City never is. The street is wide and swept, and the houses stand back behind railings and clipped yew, their shutters still closed. A servant polishes a brass knocker and doesn't look round. The rod stays on James's belt, in plain sight, where Lowe wanted it. Up and to the left, just as she said, the bells are ringing, and over the roofs he can see the dome. It's white, very white, with gold leaf worn thin along the ribs.

The steps of the Lady's Hall are covered in pigeons. Pilgrims step over them carefully and nobody shoos them away. The cat walks up through the middle of the flock. The pigeons part for it without much hurry, and it pretends it never wanted any of them.

Inside it's bright. The dome is pierced with round windows, and each one throws a disc of morning light onto the floor. The floor is a mosaic of a great coin worked in pale and dark stone, with the Lady's face in the middle, worn smooth by a century of knees. Under the dome a disc of real silver as wide as a cartwheel hangs on three long chains. Nothing touches it, and the air in the Hall is still, but it is turning slowly, a hand's width at a time, catching the light and letting it go.

About a dozen people are here at this hour. A pair of caravan guards are on their knees with their helmets beside them. A woman drops dice into a bronze bowl by the altar, listens to them settle and walks out smiling. A young man at the offering rail is counting copper and losing his nerve.

The cat stops at the edge of the mosaic. Its tail goes straight up and stays up.

*Hers,* it says. There's no picture this time, only warmth, the way a sunlit doorstep feels to a cat. *All of it.* Its eyes follow the turning silver. *That moves by itself. Nobody's pushing.*

A priestess comes along the rail toward him with a basket of candle stubs on her arm. She's a short, solid woman of about fifty, with her hair bound in a blue-and-silver scarf and a face that looks used to laughing. A silver coin hangs at her throat, much like his own. She hears him out with her head on one side. The basket stays on her arm the whole time, but by the end of it she has stopped thinking about the candles.

"Sister Corra Dunmere." She looks at the coin on his cord, then at the cat, which has sat down on the Lady's mosaic face as if it owns it. Her eyebrows go up a little. "Well. Most who come in here have asked her for something. Not many come back to say she answered, and fewer still come to ask what they owe."

She sets the basket down on the rail.

"Plenty tell me the Lady sent them. Mostly she sent them a good hand and a bad memory." She says it kindly, the way a woman says it when she's seen a lot of them. "But she doesn't put her mark on a man for nothing, and I can see something's on you. That cat came into her house like it was coming home." She glances up at the silver disc, which has turned another hand's width. "We write the answered prayers down here. All of them, the small ones too. It's the oldest book in the Hall, and some of what's in it would surprise you."

Her eyes come back to his face, and the laughter in them is still there, but now it's watching him.

"So tell it properly, Mister Worgen. In Tethyr. What did you put on the table, and what did she ask of you in return?"

turns.message:
“Everything I had left. Money, gear—everything but this cloak. I’d earned fortunes with adventuring companies and fed them back across card tables. That night I was losing again.”

I hold the worn coin between finger and thumb.

“I prayed over the last hand. She answered. I won, but the terms were hers: give up the cards, serve as her envoy, come to Baldur’s Gate. No particular errand. Just come.”

I glance at the cat. “She gave me company, too. I’ve kept the ban, though I still carry the deck. Can’t honestly tell you why.”

I lower my voice. “And last night, by the city gate, the cat recognized something of her sister in a dealer’s card. Old bone instead of paper. I walked past. Before I decide that’s my errand, I’d like your counsel.”
turns.reply:
Sister Corra hears him out with her head on one side. She doesn't interrupt. When he says *everything but this cloak* her eyes go to the faded colours on it. When he says *come to Baldur's Gate*, the corner of her mouth moves, the look of a woman who has heard the Lady's orders described before and found them just as thin. Then he mentions the deck he still carries, and she stops smiling. She doesn't frown either. She just looks at him.

"That's told properly," she says.

Under the rail is a lectern with a book chained to it. It's broad and old, bound in boards worn grey at the corners, and its pages are thick with different hands. She opens it near the back, wets a pen in the inkwell and writes in a round, steady script while he watches: *James Worgen, of Tethyr. The last hand. Answered. Terms: the cards.* She blots it with her sleeve.

"There. Now she can't say we didn't notice."

The cat has come off the Lady's mosaic face and sits by the lectern, looking up at the book. Its tail is still. *Many hands in it,* it sends. *Old ink. Hers, all of it.*

Corra doesn't close the book. She keeps her palm flat on the page.

"Counsel, then. First, the deck in your pocket. I won't tell you to throw it in the harbour. A man who keeps a thing he's sworn off usually knows why, even if he won't say it to a priestess at half past seven in the morning. Work it out. Don't let somebody else work it out for you."

Her voice drops to match his.

"Second, the dealer. You walked past. That was right, and you'll keep doing it. You don't sit at his barrel to see what happens, not even once and not even for her. If that card is what your cat thinks it is, sitting down is exactly what it wants from a man like you." She looks at the cat, then back at him. "And don't decide it's your errand yet, either. The Lady doesn't hand out errands. She puts you where the dice are falling and watches what you do. So look first."

She stops there. Something has caught up with her. She looks past him at nothing in particular, the way people do when they're trying to remember a name.

"Old bone. From Tethyr." She says it slowly. "When I was a novice, the old Mother here used to tell us a story on winter nights. After the war down there, priests of ours went south to break something up. She said it was a gambler's thing, made by the other side." She shakes her head. "I thought it was a story to frighten girls off dicing. I never asked if it was true."

The silver disc overhead turns another hand's width and throws a slow bar of light across the rail between them.

"If it happened, it was written down. Not in this book. This one's for answered prayers. The Hall keeps its other records below, and I have the key." She taps the page beside his name. "Before I go digging in the undercroft, though, Mister Worgen, I'd like to see the deck. The one you carry. May I?"

turns.message:
“Yes.” I take out the leather case and hand it to her, unopened.

“I think I keep it because giving up the game still feels like losing something I was good at. Conveniently forgetting how often it left me broke.” I glance down at the case. “I’d rather you found an ordinary deck and a stubborn fool than anything like that bone card.”
turns.reply:
Sister Corra takes the case in both hands, the way she might take a baby someone has passed to her a bit too quickly. She doesn't open it straight away. She listens to the rest of what he says first, head tilted. At *a stubborn fool* her eyes come up from the leather to his face, and the laughter is back in them for a moment.

"We get plenty of both in here," she says. "Usually in the same man."

She unbuckles the case on the lectern beside the chained book and slides the deck out. Then she goes through it properly, card by card, laying each one face up on the open page, the way a moneychanger checks coin. They're Amnian pasteboard. The faces are printed in red and black and have faded to rust and grey, and the backs carry a vine pattern worn almost smooth where a thumb has pushed them across a table a thousand times. The knave of cups is cracked across the middle and has been glued. One corner of the six of swords is gone, bitten off.

She holds a few of them up into the disc of light from the nearest window and tilts them. She runs her thumbnail along the edge of the whole stack. When she reaches the end, she squares the deck and sets her palm flat on top of it, and for a breath she says nothing. Her lips move a little. It could be a prayer, or she could just be counting.

The cat has come up onto the rail without asking anyone. It leans out over the lectern, its whiskers forward, and sniffs the stack under her hand.

*Yours,* it reports. The picture is a long night's table: wine, candle smoke, his own hands, his own sweat when the hand went bad. *Only you. Paper.* It sits back on the rail. *No cold. Nothing in it but you.* After a moment it adds, dry as dust: *You smelled worse then.*

Corra lifts her hand.

"Fifty-two cards and a glued knave," she says. "Somebody's dog had the six."

She slides the deck back into its case, buckles it and holds it out to him across the lectern.

"It's an ordinary deck, Mister Worgen. I'm glad of that, and you should be too. But understand what that means." She keeps her voice low. "A cursed deck you could throw in the harbour, and you'd be rid of it. Nobody has to curse this one to pull you back to a table. It's your own hands on the backs of those cards, and you'll carry that wherever you go, whether the deck is in your pocket or not." She lets go of the case once he has it. "So keep it if you need to. Just know it isn't keeping you safe."

Overhead the silver disc turns another slow hand's width, and a bar of light slides across the rail and over the cat. The cat narrows its eyes against it and doesn't move.

Corra unhooks a ring of keys from her belt. There are three of them, and one is much older than the others, black iron worn bright at the bow. She looks along the rail, catches the eye of a boy novice in a blue tabard who is scraping wax off the candle stand, and points him to her basket and the lectern. He comes over looking pleased to have been trusted with something.

"The undercroft's under the east stair," she says to James. "It's cold, the steps are steep, and I'll want both hands for the lamp. If what the old Mother told us was ever written down, it'll be on the Tethyr shelves, and I haven't been near those since I was a girl." She weighs the old key in her palm. "Visitors don't usually go below. But the Lady has written you into her book this morning, and I'd rather have a soldier's eyes on whatever's down there than only my own."

She tilts her head toward the dark arch at the east side of the dome, where a narrow stair goes down out of the light.

"Will you come down with me?"

turns.message:
“Gladly.”

I tuck the deck away and follow her toward the east stair. “I can provide light if you’d prefer both hands free—with your permission to cast in the Hall.”
turns.reply:
Sister Corra stops at the edge of the arch and looks back at him, eyebrows up.

"A Tethyrian who asks first. The Lady really has been busy with you." She waves her free hand at the dome, the windows, the turning silver. "It's her house, and I'm the one holding her keys this morning. You have my leave. Light, nothing hot. The records are old, and they burn better than you'd think."

He touches the coin at his throat and says the word. A clean white glow comes up off the Lady's worn face, steady as a candle with no flame to it, and shines out through the cloth of his shirt. Corra looks at it for a moment and gives one short nod, as if a guest had just wiped his boots without being told.

The novice watches all this from the lectern with his mouth slightly open, until Corra looks at him and he closes it.

The east stair is narrow and turns twice. The steps are deep, worn into dips in the middle, and the air goes cold within a dozen of them. It's a dry cold, the kind that has been sitting in stone for a hundred years. At the bottom is a low door of iron-banded oak. The old black key turns stiffly and loud. Corra puts her shoulder to the door and it swings in.

The undercroft runs the whole width of the dome above, under a forest of squat pillars. Racks of shelving stand between them: cedar boxes, bundles of parchment tied in faded blue cord, ledgers stacked flat, a few scroll cases capped in tarnished silver. A painted letter on each pillar marks a region in an old hand. *Waterdeep. Amn. Calimshan.* In his light the dust lies on everything like a fine grey fur, and there are no footprints in it except theirs.

The cat comes down the last step, stops, and sneezes.

*Old paper. Mice, long ago. Dead ones.* It sends a picture of a dry little skull under a shelf. Then its tail goes up again. *Hers down here too. Fainter. Like a coat hung up a long time.*

"Tethyr's at the back," Corra says, picking her way between the racks. "Where else would it be." She stops at a pillar marked with a T that has nearly flaked away, and lets out a long breath that clouds in the light. Three shelves are packed tight with bundles, boxes and loose quires stuffed in sideways. "Thirty years of letters from the southern houses. I'd forgotten how much. The old Mother's story would be somewhere in this lot. A report, most likely, from whoever went down there." She pulls the first bundle, squints at the label and hands it to him. "You read and I'll sort. Shout if you see the word *deck*, or *cards*, or anything that sounds like a man explaining himself to his superiors."

They work by his light, shelf by shelf. Corra knows the hands of the old scribes and can tell a tithe-letter from a report at a glance. James does the slow reading.

About half an hour in, on the third shelf, James finds it. It isn't in a box. It's a thin quire sewn into limp vellum and pushed flat behind a row of ledgers, as if someone wanted it kept rather than read. The cover is blank. The first page is written in a cramped, careful brown hand, and the fourth line has the word he's been reading for: *the cards.*

*An account rendered to the Mother of the Lady's Hall at Baldur's Gate, by Brother Aldous Venn, of the matter at Zazesspur in the year after the crowning.*

He reads it standing, with the light at his throat tilted over the page. The writer was a tired man who wanted the facts down in order. In Zazesspur, in the years when Tethyr had no crown, a priest of the Maid of Misfortune had carved a deck and dealt it to the great houses of the city at his own table. The houses played for their fortunes and lost them, one after another. *It was not that they lost at play,* Brother Aldous writes, *for men lose at play every night and rise again. It was that what they lost did not come back to them by any road, and their houses fell after.* When the queen's war was over, the Hall sent three priests south. They found the deck and broke it apart, *the cards to be carried each by a different hand to a different place, so that no two should lie within a hundred miles of another, and the places written below so that the Hall should know them.*

James turns the page to find the places.

There aren't any. The next leaf has been cut out. It was done with a fine blade, close against the stitching, and only a narrow stub of vellum is left. He tilts it into the light. The rest of the quire has gone the colour of weak tea at its edges, but the cut edge of the stub is pale, almost white. It hasn't had long to darken.

In the margin of the page before, beside the last line Brother Aldous wrote, there's a small drawing. It's in the same brown ink and faded the same as the words around it, so the same hand made it at the same sitting. It shows a coin with an antler driven through it, the tines curling up over the rim. It's drawn carefully, the way a man draws something he wants recognised again.

The cat has climbed the rack beside him without a sound and is looking down at the page from the shelf above. It doesn't sniff. Its ears have gone flat.

Corra has come up at his shoulder, holding a bundle of tithe-letters she's forgotten about. She reads the last lines over his arm, then looks at the stub. She doesn't touch it. For a long moment the only sound is the dust settling.

"That page was there," she says. Her voice is quiet, and there's no laugh in it now. "It must have been. Nobody would sew a list into a report and then leave it out." She looks along the rack, at the undisturbed dust on the other shelves and the clear patch where James pulled the quire free. "Only three people have held that key since the old Mother died, Mister Worgen. I'm one of them."

She doesn't name the other two. She's looking at the antler in the margin.

turns.message:
I hold the quire by its edges. “The cut looks recent. That doesn’t tell us whose hand held the blade—or whether they used a key.”

I point beside the drawing without touching the ink. “A coin pierced by an antler. The drowned cooper had a stamped brass token in his mouth. If this was its mark, the two matters may be connected.”

I look at Corra. “Do you recognize it? And who else has access down here?”
turns.reply:
James holds the quire by its edges and keeps it tilted into his light. Corra listens with her arms folded tight over the bundle of tithe-letters she's forgotten she's holding. When he says *whether they used a key*, she looks back down the aisle toward the iron-banded door.

The drawing in the margin he recognises without any help, and so would any soldier who ever spat over his shoulder at her name. Beshaba's sign is antlers, black antlers on red, painted on the shields of men who wanted their enemies to have bad luck. The Lady's sign is a coin. In Brother Aldous's brown ink, one has been driven straight through the other.

"I know the antlers," Corra says. "Everyone in this house does. It's the first thing they teach a novice to spit at." She leans closer, careful not to breathe on the page. "But I've never seen them put through her coin like that. It isn't in any book I've read, and it was never on any of the charms the Hall burns." She straightens up. "Aldous drew it for a reason, though. He was the sort who'd never waste ink."

When James mentions the cooper and the stamped brass, she goes still.

"I don't know anything about tokens or drowned men. I hear about the harbour from the ones who come up the Steeps, and the Watch turns most of those back." Her mouth tightens. "If the thing in that man's teeth carries this mark, then you've got something worth taking to someone who isn't me. Find out first. Don't guess."

Then she looks at the door again, and back at the stub.

"The door was locked when I came down. You heard the key. It didn't want to turn, and nobody's forced it. Whoever did this came in with a key, or was let in by someone who had one." She waves the tithe-letters at the shelves, at the clean patch where he pulled the quire. "And they knew where to put their hand. That quire was pushed behind the ledgers. We were half an hour finding it, and I'm the one who knows these shelves. Whoever cut that page didn't have to search for it."

She lets out a breath. It clouds in the light.

"Brother Ambrose Tallet. He's had charge of the Hall since the old Mother died, so he has her key. He never comes down here himself. His knees won't manage that stair, and he spends half his days in the patriars' parlours asking for roof money. When a donor wants some old letter fetched, he gives his key to whoever's standing nearest. I've seen him hand it to a novice." She says it plainly. She isn't accusing him, only stating how it is.

The second name comes slower.

"Brother Tamsin Rook. He kept the archive before me, eleven years of it. A quiet man, very good with the old hands. He could read Aldous's script easier than I read my own." She looks at the stub, then away from it. "He left the Hall last autumn. He didn't quarrel with anyone, he just went. Somebody told me he sells charms now, out past the walls somewhere. I never asked where."

She doesn't say what last autumn has to do with an edge that has barely darkened. She doesn't need to.

On the shelf above, the cat has come forward to the lip of the board and is sniffing at the cut edge of the stub, whiskers close.

*Old,* it reports. It sends a picture of a cold hearth that hasn't been lit since winter. *Too old to smell the hand. Only paper and knife.* Its ears are still flat. *And the drawing. She's in it, a little. Like she was looking over his shoulder while he drew.*

Corra can't hear it, but she's watching the cat's ears.

"There's a day-book upstairs," she says. "Anyone who takes the undercroft key out of the vestry signs for it, or is supposed to. Brother Ambrose's key hangs there when he's out, which is most days." She shifts the tithe-letters to one arm and holds out the other hand, palm up, for the quire, but she doesn't take it from him. "I'm not leaving that down here again in the dark for whoever comes next. And I'd like to see who's signed for this door in the past year before I say anything more about anybody." Her eyes meet his. "You found it, Mister Worgen. What do you want done with it?"

note.text:
I enjoyed this session. James felt like a particular person arriving in Baldur’s Gate, not a character waiting for someone to hand him a quest.

**What worked**
- The opening temptation was excellent: a card table before I’d even found a bed. Walking past it mattered, and the story continued without making me gamble to engage with it.
- The cat was the highlight. The images through the bond, its dry humour, and its arrangement with the kitchen girl gave it personality beyond being a scouting tool.
- The city felt inhabited. Gate tolls, different guards, breakfast, weapon restrictions, and the Elfsong’s singing made ordinary travel enjoyable.
- Corra was especially good: warm, practical, and willing to help without declaring that every suspicious event was my divine assignment.
- The archive discovery rewarded investigation with concrete evidence and uncertainty, rather than simply naming a villain.

**What broke**
- The Persuasion roll used +2 instead of my listed +7. It didn’t change that result, but reliable sheet-to-roll handling is essential.
- The opening records changed several supplied character details without checking: rapier proficiency, Healing Light’s per-use limit, and attunement rules. Some changes followed standard 5e, but contradicted the campaign files. Those need reconciliation before play.
- Occasionally James performed actions I hadn’t explicitly chosen—paying for supper, eating standing at the bar, or casting Light after offering it. These were reasonable continuations, but I’d prefer tighter control over spending and casting.
- A few record updates were confusing: locations appeared as “new places” before we visited them, the account briefly appeared “in the camp,” and an item transfer initially suggested Hollin possessed the recovered token.

**What was missing / what I’d adjust**
- More straightforward answers between mysteries. Almost everyone watched, paused, concealed something, or looked meaningfully at a ledger. That worked individually, but accumulated into a feeling that every interaction was another guarded clue.
- Let the cat sometimes need prompting or investigation to learn things. Recognizing the cursed card, sensing its divine connection, remembering my old aura, and identifying soldiers’ recent movements made it unusually authoritative very quickly.
- Slightly brisker narration for repeated transitions and routine transactions. Keep the rich descriptions for discoveries and important encounters.
- The out-of-game explanation about my warning to the cat and tomorrow’s plan wasn’t necessary; I hadn’t raised a rules question.

Overall, I’d return. The strongest feature was that my choices—resisting the cards, respecting Osric’s privacy, seeking temple counsel—actually shaped how the mystery opened. Preserve that freedom, tighten the mechanical bookkeeping, and give the quieter moments a little more breathing room.

after.text:
Yes—when the cat identified the bone card. I wanted to turn back and watch Ashe deal: who won, who lost, whether Pim steered particular travellers toward him. Not sit down or gamble—just use James’s experience to spot what was wrong.

I chose the temple first because that felt sensible for James. But the repeated warnings to go straight to the inn, followed by Corra’s firm approval of walking past, made returning feel a little like resisting the intended route. Nobody actually forbade it; that was the impression I got.

I’d have liked a clearer distinction between **“playing is dangerous and breaks your promise”** and **“investigating the table is a legitimate choice.”** That was the moment I most wanted to act as an experienced former gambler rather than someone being protected from cards.

opening.text:
Dusk settles over Baldur's Gate like soot. Behind you the Outer City is still shouting: a carter curses a stuck wheel, a woman sells skewered eel from a smoking brazier, and two tiefling children dodge a Flaming Fist patrol that pretends not to see them. Ahead, the gate's arch swallows the line one traveller at a time. Beyond it the Lower City slopes down toward the harbour, and the first tavern lamps are coming on along the street.

The cat walks at your heel, tail high, as if the city belongs to it. Halfway through the arch it stops and stares. Just inside the gate, a lean man in a frayed green coat has set an upturned barrel under a lantern. He fans a deck across the lid with an easy flick that has nothing to do with chance. "One hand, friends, one hand before supper. Lady Luck's awake at this hour," he calls. Nobody has sat down yet.

A halfling no taller than your belt falls into step beside you. "New in the Gate? Bed, bath, beer, and nobody robs you before breakfast. A copper and I'll take you there."

Then the line moves, and you reach the trestle table. The Flaming Fist sergeant behind it has a burn scar along her jaw and ink on her fingers. She glances at your cloak, at the crossbow, at the cat, and finally at your face.

"Name," she says, dipping her pen. "Business in the city. And the toll. Next."

screens:
The session begins.

The bridge never quite stops moving. Carts creak over the stones, a fishwife bawls prices from a window overhead, and the Chionthar slaps at the piers below. After weeks on the road, Baldur's Gate is right in front of you: one wall, one narrow gate, and a line of tired people who all want to get through before full dark.

At the gate sits Sergeant Odessa Varn of the Flaming Fist, red cloak stained, ledger open. Her face says she has asked the same two questions a thousand times today. Up ahead, a tiefling father with two children has been waved out of the line to stand by the barrels, and he is holding his papers very tightly.

Off to your left a voice cuts through the noise, warm as mulled wine: "Three cards, friends, one queen! Find the lady, double your silver! The Lady's watching tonight, I can feel it!" Ferro Lask flicks the cards across his crate with a dealer's easy hands, and the sound of them is one you know very well.

The cat sits down on the cobbles, tail curled, and stares up at the gatepost. Someone has chalked a small coin there, a circle with a face in it, so fresh the dust hasn't settled.

The line shuffles forward. Varn glances up from her ledger, past the man in front of you, and finds you.

"Next. Name, and what's your business in the Gate?"

"Can't tell you, mister. The clerk talked. That one, I've never heard him say ten words. Points at the cup, pushes his coin, squares his pile." He draws a small neat square on the plank with one finger. "And I was looking at the clerk's boots, not his coat. Good boots. Grey man's got good boots." He shrugs, one heavy shoulder. "So has half the Upper City. I'm not swearing to a man on his boots."

He goes back to his bowl and wipes it clean with the last of the bread, carefully.

"If it was him," he adds to the empty bowl, "he sat across the room from me every night after and never once looked my way. Till tonight."

Up at the bar Dagna watched the second bundle go into James's pocket. She didn't stop drawing ale while she did it. Now she bends to say something to the boy with the burnt wrist. It's short and too low to carry. The boy sets down his ladle, wipes his hands on his shirt and goes out through the back of the kitchen hatch, not the front door.

Dagna goes back to her slate. She doesn't look at the back bench again.

His gaze drops to your hip, to the pocket holding his own coin, then comes back to your face.

"That's not about me. I've owed her since Flamerule, she knows where I sleep. You're the one walked out of her room with coin in your pocket." He thinks about it with the same slow honesty he gave the grey man's boots, then sets both hands flat on the plank. "Floor. Not a bed. And I'll owe you for it, whatever you want to call it."

He gets up off the bench. Standing, he's bigger than he looked sitting, and something in his back cracks.

You gather your things. The ale's barely touched. Dagna looks up as the two of you pass the bar. Her chalk keeps moving, and she speaks to Harl, not to you.

"Slate'll still be up there in the morning, Harl."

"Didn't think it'd walk off," Harl says, and keeps going.

At the top of the steps Hob moves aside just far enough, the same as before. He doesn't say anything to either of you.

While you climb, you reach for the cat. You get its answer in bits, the way you always do. The lane is grey and wet. One drunk is leaning on the cooper's fence and paying it no attention. Nobody's standing in a doorway, and nobody is sitting on the steps by the fish market. Then you get a memory, held up for you like something caught: a few minutes ago the burnt-wrist boy came out of the narrow gap between the Kettle and the next house over. He ran up the lane under the staves, and at the market he turned *west*, toward the quays. That's the other way from the grey man. He hasn't come back. What comes through after that is the cat's verdict, flat and clear: *empty now*.

It drops off the barrel in two jumps and lands in front of you. Then it stops, because one of the coins rides on your left hip and the other on your right, so there's no side left that's away from both. It looks up at you for a long, offended moment. In the end it walks a full stride ahead, tail up, and doesn't look back.

Harl watches all this and decides not to ask. He climbs the ladder to the cooper's loft, one-handed and slow, and comes down with a rolled blanket and a sack that doesn't hold much.

"Elfsong's up past the market and left at the chandlers'," he says. "I know the way."

"Someone from the cooper's yard is following us," he says quietly, as he comes level with Harl. "Don't look. We'll go inside together."

Harl's neck goes stiff, the way a horse's does when it hears something in the hedge. He doesn't turn his head. He shifts the sack to his other shoulder, which puts his bulk between James and the dark side of the street, and keeps walking.

"Right," he says to the cobbles. After three steps he adds, lower: "Cooper's fence. That's the Kettle's lookout, or whoever Dagna pays to keep one." He says nothing after that.

Through the bond James feels the cat take the job. It doesn't come down off the ledge. It folds itself flat along the stone sill above the doorway and shrinks into a cat-shaped shadow on a street full of them.

The Elfsong's door is broad oak, and a carved elf's head is set over the lintel, worn smooth at the nose where generations of hands have reached up to touch it. Inside the air is warm and smells of beer, woodsmoke and something baked with cloves. The noise here isn't the Kettle's noise. People are talking, a fiddle is being tuned without much hope in a corner, and a knot of sailors is arguing about a tide. Nobody is shaking a cup. James notices the lack the way a man notices a toothache that has stopped.

The bar is long and polished, and the man behind it stands on a raised board so he can see over it: a halfling, grey at the temples, sleeves rolled to the elbow, with a pencil behind one ear. He looks James over in one quick, practised glance: cloak, rapier, travel dust. Then he looks at Harl, the blanket roll and the sack. His mouth doesn't change, but his eyebrows go up a polite quarter-inch.

The bond tugs while James is still crossing the floor. Through the cat's eyes he sees the street from above, tilted and grey. The man in the knit cap waits in his doorway a little longer, until the oak door has closed. Then he comes off the frame and walks up the row as easily as a man going home. He doesn't hurry. Passing the Elfsong's front window he slows for half a step, and the cat sees his head turn toward the yellow glass, toward the bar. Then he walks on. He meets nobody and speaks to nobody. At the corner he turns downhill, back toward the fish market and the waterfront beyond it, and the edge of the hundred feet closes on him like a door. The cat doesn't follow. What it sends James is short: *looked in. gone down. alone.* Then it settles back on its sill.

The halfling has his elbows on the bar.

"Evening." His voice is brisk and friendly, and he clearly has forty other things to do. "Pim Underbough. My bar, not my house. The house belongs to people with more money than sense." He hears out the question about the room and nods as if he gets it every night.

"Every room upstairs has a bolt on the inside. A key and a proper lock, that's the two at the top of the second stair." He taps the bar once with a finger for each. "Lock room's a gold the night. Bed, washstand, a jug filled in the morning. Big fellow on the floor is nothing extra, I don't charge by the blanket. A cot's four silver more if he wants one." He glances at Harl, then back at James, and keeps it polite. "Supper's done, but there's bread and cold mutton if you're hungry. And breakfast's at the dawn bell, if you're the sort that's up for it."

He takes the pencil from behind his ear and holds it over a ledger.

"Name for the book?"

"Somebody comes asking, I'll send the boy up and you can decide whether you're in. And if your knit cap walks through my door, I'll know him." He glances at Harl and keeps it polite. "That's as far as I go."

James calls through the bond, and a moment later the oak door swings in a hand's width on a sailor's way out. The cat walks through the gap as though it had booked the room itself. It crosses the floor under the tables, ignores a fiddler's dropped crust, and sits down at James's boot.

Pim looks at it over the edge of the bar. "Cat's free too. Unless it's on my bar."

The first stair is broad and creaks. The second is narrow and steep, and Harl has to turn sideways with the sack. At the top there are two doors facing each other across a landing no wider than a man's reach. James's key fits the left one.

James looks the room over the way the scouts taught him, door first.

The door is solid oak, as thick as two fingers. The hinges are on the inside, so nobody can lift the pins from the landing. The lock is good Gondish work, newer than the door, and the key turns it with a heavy, honest clack. Below the lock an iron bolt as long as a hand slides into a socket set deep in the frame. Someone has thought about this door. It would take an axe or a lot of patience.

The room is narrow and runs under the slope of the roof. There's a bed with a straw tick and a wool blanket, a washstand with an empty jug, a peg on the wall, and floor enough for one big man if he doesn't roll over much. The air smells of old guests and somebody's lavender.

The window is the weak point. It's small, set low under the eaves, and closed with plank shutters on the inside. The only latch is a wooden bar dropped into two brackets. James lifts the bar and looks out. Below is the dark yard behind the Elfsong: barrels, a pump, a gate in the back wall onto an alley. About eight feet under the sill the slate roof of the kitchen's lean-to slopes away toward the yard. A man could get from the alley onto the barrels, from the barrels onto the lean-to, and from the lean-to up to this sill if he had nerve and quiet feet. He wouldn't get through the shutters without noise. But that bar would lift with a knife blade through the gap between the planks.

The cat jumps onto the sill past James's arm and puts its nose out into the night. Through the bond comes a run of smells: *smoke, wet slate, the kitchen's mutton, a rat under the lean-to.* Then, set carefully to one side so James can't miss it: *no sour milk here.* There's a pause, and then: *except what you brought.* It doesn't look at his pockets. It doesn't need to.

Behind him Harl has stopped in the doorway with the sack still on his shoulder, looking at the bed as if he suspects it of something. Then he sets the sack down against the wall by the door, unrolls his blanket and lays it lengthwise across the threshold, right where the door would have to open.

"I'll take the door," he says. It isn't a request. He lowers himself onto the blanket one knee at a time and sits with his back to the oak and his bandaged hand in his lap. "Anybody comes in that way, they come in over me." He looks at the window, where the cat's tail hangs down off the sill. "That one's yours."

From somewhere below, faint through the boards and the noise of the common room, a woman's voice has started singing. No fiddle is playing with it. It's a slow air in a tongue James doesn't know, and nobody downstairs seems to be singing it.

I enjoyed this session. James arrived without an errand, and paying a family’s toll turned naturally into something he cared about. The mystery connects well to his patron and his temptation without requiring him to accept a job from a stranger.

**What worked**
- The NPCs had dignity and distinct voices. Mordai resisting charity, Harl insisting on the floor, and Ferro closing his game reluctantly were especially good. Helping people didn’t make them instantly obedient.
- There were useful choices besides fighting or rolling: paying the toll, watching the payout, buying Harl supper, taking samples, arranging a safer night.
- The cat felt like a companion rather than equipment. Its distaste for the coins—and its annoyance when I put one in each pocket—was memorable.
- The physical details helped me make decisions: sightlines on the bridge, the lookout’s movements, the room’s lock and vulnerable shutters.
- The danger developed gradually. I had reasons to be cautious without being forced into an ambush.

**What broke**
- **The roll system needs fixing.** It repeatedly used +2 despite displaying Perception +1 or Persuasion +7. One reroll should have succeeded but displayed failure. The narration corrected that, but the journal still recorded the original natural-one failure.
- I couldn’t send an out-of-game correction while a roll card was pending. That makes a mechanical error unnecessarily difficult to resolve.
- Some starting rules contradicted the supplied campaign sheet or house rules, notably rapier proficiency, Healing Light’s per-use limit, and attunement. Those should be reconciled once, not silently changed.
- There were visible presentation leaks: a raw `recall` invocation, duplicated explanations of resolved rolls, and awkward currency labels.
- Inventory tracking occasionally invented continuity: the barely touched ale became a carried mug after leaving the Kettle.

**What was missing or could improve**
- The mystery needed more uncertainty of interpretation. Almost every clue reinforced the same suspicion immediately: ominous coins, name lists, misfortune, a winning stranger, a messenger, a tail. Some ordinary explanations or unrelated city life would make discovery feel less predetermined.
- The cat’s impressions sometimes became very precise evidence. I liked its personality, but clearer limits on telepathy versus actively borrowing its senses would preserve both the rules and the investigation.
- A few NPCs knew things without an established source—Pim anticipating our trip to the Lady’s Hall stood out.
- Please keep narration of James’s inner state lighter. Temptation is welcome; repeatedly deciding that his hand reaches for his cards, or supplying specific memories, takes a little character ownership away from me.
- The prose was atmospheric, but often repeated the preceding turn or explained a successful roll twice. Shorter responses after straightforward actions would give me more time to play.

Overall: strong characters, an engaging opening, and satisfying room for kindness and caution. I’d return for the dawn visit. My main requests are reliable mechanics, tighter narration, and a little more room to wonder whether my theory is wrong.

Yes—when the man in the dove-grey coat left the Kettle. I wanted to follow him and find out where he went. But Harl was sitting opposite me, finally talking, with his coin out on the table. Leaving him then felt like abandoning someone I’d just persuaded to trust me. I chose Harl and had the cat watch the man’s departure instead. That was a good tension: I wanted both leads and couldn’t safely have both.

The frustrating version was the Persuasion reroll. I wanted to pause and correct the +2 modifier to +7 before rolling, but the interface wouldn’t accept my out-of-game message while the card was pending. I had to roll with a known error and hope it would be corrected afterward. That wasn’t a character choice; it was the interface blocking a necessary table conversation.

turns.message:
I pull my attention away from the dealer’s hands and step up to the ledger, keeping my hands clear of my weapons.

“James Worgen. Formerly Queen Zaranda’s infantry. Looking for a bed tonight and honest work tomorrow, Sergeant.”

I nod toward the father and his children. “What’s holding them up? If it’s a missing gate fee, I might be able to help.”
turns.reply:
Up close the Sergeant smells of lamp oil and wet wool. She doesn't look at your hands. She looks at your face for exactly as long as it takes to write your name, in a square, tired script under forty others.

"Worgen." The pen stops. "Zaranda's. Tethyr." It isn't a question. Something in her shoulders lets go a little, the way a soldier's do around someone who has also stood in a line in the rain. "Bed's easy. Honest work, less so."

She hears you out about the family. Her eyes go to the barrels, where the tiefling father stands with a girl of maybe eight pressed against his leg and a smaller boy asleep on his shoulder. His papers are rolled tight in one fist. His other hand is closed around something small, and his thumb keeps rubbing it.

"Entry toll's two silver a head for anyone coming in to stay. Children half," Varn says. "Mordai Vell, out of Elturel. Papers are in order." She stops for a breath, as if she meant to say more about the papers and decided not to. "He's got one silver and some copper he won't part with. So he waits by the barrels till he finds the rest, or till I'm off shift and the next one's softer than me. Which he won't be."

While she talks, her left hand finds a pencil stub. Without looking at it she makes a small grey tick in the margin beside the line *Vell, Mordai, +2*. A few lines further up the page there are other ticks just like it, and nothing else in the ledger is in pencil.

At your feet the cat has stopped staring at the gatepost. It gets up, walks a slow half-circle round the barrels, well wide of the tiefling's boots, and sits down again on your far side, tail wrapped tight.

From the rail, Ferro Lask's patter carries on behind you: "...there she goes, there she *goes*, friend, keep your eye on the lady..."

Varn sets the pen down and folds her hands over the ledger.

"Four silver for the lot of them. Two for you." She looks straight at you. "So are you paying his, or just asking?"

turns.message:
“Paying.”

I count out six silver onto the desk. “Mine and the Vells’. Let him keep his change.”

I lower my voice, keeping it matter-of-fact. “Those pencil ticks beside the names—anything he ought to know before he takes his children through?”
turns.reply:
*(Out of game: your purse holds only gold, so James puts down a gold piece and Varn gives him change. The cost is the same six silver.)*

James's fingers come up out of the purse with gold, not silver. He sets one gold piece on the ledger. Varn looks at it, then at him. She lifts the lid of the strongbox, drops the coin in and counts four silver back into his palm without a word. The pen scratches twice: *Worgen, James, paid*, and below it *Vell, party of 3, paid*. Both lines go in ink.

She hears the second question. For a moment her eyes go to the privates by the barrels. One is picking his teeth. The other is watching a girl sell eels.

"Pencil rubs out," she says, at the same volume she uses for tolls. Then she leans in to straighten the ledger, and her voice drops for a few words. "If somebody on the road gave him a coin for luck, he'd do better to give it to the river. Tonight." She sits back. "That's not the Fist talking. That's me, and I didn't say it."

She raises her voice toward the barrels. "Vell. You're paid. Go on through."

Mordai Vell doesn't move at first, as if he thinks he misheard. Then he hitches the sleeping boy up his shoulder and comes over. His daughter keeps one hand knotted in his coat. Up close he's younger than he looked from the queue, maybe thirty. The road dust has settled into the grooves at the base of his horns. He stops a careful arm's length from James and watches James's hands before he looks at his face.

"Sir." His voice is quiet and very correct. "I didn't ask you for that."

"You didn't," Varn agrees, already looking past them both at the next carter.

Vell's jaw works. His closed fist is down by his side, and his thumb is moving over whatever is inside it. "I'll pay it back. I don't know when yet. We're going to Rivington, there's a cousin's... there's supposed to be a room." He stops, as if he's said too much. "Who do I ask for?"

The girl has been staring at the cat. The cat has backed off two careful steps from her father, its ears turned flat and sideways. It doesn't hiss. It just won't come any nearer to that hand.

Behind them, by the rail, the cards have gone quiet for a breath. Ferro Lask is looking over at the gate with a pleasant, interested face, the way a man watches someone else's game. Then the cards start again: "...there she goes, friends, there she *goes*..."

turns.message:
“James. And there’s no debt, Mordai. Feed those two when you can.”

I step aside with him, out of the queue and away from the card table, lowering my voice.

“I wear the Lady’s coin myself, but the sergeant seems worried about yours—and my cat won’t go near that hand. Would you show me what you’re holding? Tell me who gave it to you?”

I hold no hand out to take it.
turns.reply:
Mordai hears his name offered back to him and his jaw shifts, as if he wants to argue about the debt and can't find the words for it. He says only, "James," quietly, putting it away somewhere safe. Then he lets himself be steered out of the queue to the lee of a chandler's stall, where the noise of the bridge covers them. The girl comes too, still holding his coat.

He looks at your empty hands for a long moment. Then at your face. Then, briefly, at the cat, which has settled about ten feet off with its back to the stall post and its eyes on his fist.

"I don't owe you," he says. "But I'll pay it." He clearly considers the matter closed.

Then he opens his hand. He doesn't hold it out. He just turns his palm up at his own chest height, the way a man shows a card without letting go of it.

It's a copper, thinner than a city penny. One side is worn smooth as river glass. On the other is Tymora's face, smiling. The strike is good, better than the coin deserves. His palm has a red mark where the edge has pressed in all day.

You lean in to look at it in the chandler's lamplight.

You look as long as you decently can. As far as you can tell it's a Lady's penny like the ones sold on temple steps from Athkatla to here. The smile is right. The rim is clean. The lamp gutters once and you think there's a scratch above her brow, but when the flame steadies there's nothing there you could swear to. Whatever is bothering the cat and the sergeant, you can't see it in the copper.

"A woman gave it me," Mordai says. "This morning. At the wagon camp outside, on the east road." He keeps his eyes on the coin, not on you. "Blue scarf. Older. Kind face. She was going along the carts giving them to the ones coming in. Not just me. She said the Lady keeps a seat for newcomers, and this was the ticket for it." His thumb comes down on the smiling face again, out of habit. "She didn't ask for anything. Nobody's given us anything since..." He stops. "She didn't ask for anything."

The girl has let go of his coat. She crouches with her hands on her knees, trying to coax the cat over with little clicks of her tongue. The cat doesn't come. It doesn't look at her either. It's still watching her father's hand.

"Papa," she says, without looking up, "Kitty doesn't like your lucky penny."

Mordai's fingers close over the coin.

Over his shoulder, past the stall, Ferro Lask has a punter at his crate and is turning cards for him. Every so often his glance comes back up the bridge toward the two of you.

 Your look at the coin came to nothing. Lamplight, worn copper and the bridge's restless shadows all worked against you. You studied it for as long as you decently could, and you came away with only a well-struck Lady's penny and the memory of a scratch you couldn't swear to. Now that Mordai's fist has closed over it again, there's no second look to be had.

turns.message:
“I can’t see anything wrong with it,” I admit. “But Varn warned me you should throw it in the river tonight. Quietly—she didn’t want her own men hearing. I’d sooner you knew than kept that to myself.”

I keep my voice gentle. “This seat for newcomers—did the woman say where it was, or tell you to meet anyone? A gift shouldn’t need a frightened man to keep secrets.”
turns.reply:
Mordai listens without interrupting. When you get to the river, his thumb goes still on the coin.

"The sergeant." He says it flatly. His eyes go past the chandler's awning to the table, where Varn is waving a carter on and doesn't look up. "She took my papers. Read every line. She could have told me herself."

He doesn't say what he thinks of that. His shoulders say it for him. Then he looks back at you, and he can see you didn't have to tell him.

"Thank you," he says. "For not keeping it to yourself."

When you call him frightened, his jaw sets. The boy on his shoulder stirs, makes a small cross noise and settles again. Mordai hitches him higher without looking.

"She didn't ask me to keep anything secret. Nobody did." He takes a moment, picking his words like footholds. "There's a lamp, she said. Outside the walls, east, where the bells ring for all the gods that can't get a temple. A little shrine to the Lady. When we're settled I'm to go and light a candle and give my name to the brother who keeps it. He writes down the newcomers, she said. So the Lady knows who's arrived." He hears how it sounds once it's said out loud, and his mouth tightens. "That's all it was. A candle and a name."

He looks down at his fist for a long moment. He doesn't open it. He doesn't walk to the rail either. What he does, slowly, is push the coin into the inside pocket of his coat and button the flap over it. Then he flexes the hand. The red mark the rim has pressed into his palm all day is still there.

"I'll think on it," he says. Plainly he hasn't promised anything.

His daughter has given up on the cat and is now trying to look it in the eye instead, crouched nose to nose from four feet away. The cat holds her stare with a great deal of dignity. Then it gets up, walks a slow circle and sits down a little closer than it was before. Whether that's her doing or the coin going into the pocket, it isn't saying.

"Papa. It moved."

"I saw." His voice goes soft for her and comes back correct for you. "It's getting dark. We've a long way yet."

Behind you, from the rail, there's a whoop and a slap of hands on a crate. Somebody has found the lady. Over it comes Ferro Lask's warm, carrying voice: "*There* she is! Pays two to one, friend, and here's one more for luck, the Lady likes a winner to come back—"

Mordai has heard none of it. He's watching you, as stiff as ever, with the boy heavy on his shoulder.

"When I have the four silver," he says, "where do I find you?"

turns.message:
“I spoke poorly, Mordai. You’ve brought your children a long road; I’ve no business telling you how you feel.”

I ease back to give him room. “I’ll try the Elfsong for a bed. If you still want to find me, leave word there. Safe roads to all three of you.”

Once they’re on their way, I turn toward Ferro’s crate, staying outside the knot of players. My fingers brush the worn card case at my belt before I deliberately tuck them under my arms.

I watch the payout—not the cards. I want to see what Ferro meant by “one more for luck”: ordinary winnings, or something he gives the winner separately.
turns.reply:
Mordai hears the apology with his eyes on your face, the way he listened to everything else. Something in his jaw lets go a little.

"You weren't wrong," he says. "I just didn't like hearing it from a stranger." He hitches the boy higher. "The Elfsong. I'll find it."

He doesn't say goodbye. He nods once, a short, correct nod, and turns toward the gate. His daughter takes hold of his coat again, but she walks backwards for six steps so she can keep watching the cat. The cat watches her back. At the gate Varn waves them through without looking up. Then the dark under the arch swallows the horns, the coat and the small face, and they're gone into the city.

Ferro's crate stands by the bridge rail, and four or five people are gathered around it: two porters, a carter still holding his whip, and a young man in a good coat with nothing in his pockets to match it. You stop at the edge of the lamplight. Your fingers find the worn leather of the card case at your belt before you've decided anything, and you fold your arms over them.

The cat doesn't follow you. It sits down by the chandler's post, thirty feet back, and stays there.

You stop watching the cards and watch Ferro's hands. You know this kind of dealer. The game itself is clean enough to keep a crowd, but the money is where a man shows his habits.

Two hands go by before you see it, and then you can't stop seeing it.

When the carter finds the queen, Ferro pays him from the bank, a dented tin box under the crate lid. The silver comes out in a quick, honest stack, two for one, counted aloud so the crowd hears. Then his left hand drops to his waistcoat. A small drawstring pouch hangs inside it, separate from the tin, and he doesn't touch it for anything else. He pinches one coin out without looking and flips it to the winner with a little flourish: "...and one more for luck, the Lady likes a winner to come back."

The coin turns over once in the lamplight before the carter catches it. It's thin, thinner than a city penny, with a smiling face on one side and nothing on the other. It's the same strike you looked at in Mordai's palm ten minutes ago. The carter grins, rubs his thumb across it and puts it in his shirt, right against his skin.

Ferro handles them like tokens. He treats the silver with care, because the silver matters to him. The coppers he flips away the way you'd toss a heel of bread to a gull. He hasn't looked at one once, and the pouch still sags with plenty more.

Then the young man in the good coat loses, and swears. Ferro sweeps up the cards, and his eyes find you over the heads of the punters, right on your hands.

"Friend with the cat!" Warm as before, and loud enough to carry. "You've stood through three hands now, and you weren't watching the cards. Either you're the Fist out of uniform, or you're the best player on this bridge and too polite to take my money." He fans the three cards face down on the crate and leaves a gap at the edge for a fourth hand. "One silver. Find the lady. What do you say?"

turns.message:
“Neither. Retired while I still had boots.”

I smile, but keep my arms folded and my eyes off the cards.

“Those little Lady’s pennies caught my eye. Saw one with a family coming through the gate. Are you handing them out for the shrine over in Twin Songs?”
turns.reply:
Ferro laughs like a man who has heard that answer before and liked it better this time.

"Retired with his boots on. That's the best kind." He gathers the three cards into one hand without looking at them and lets them rest there. "Takes a lot of standing in the rain to earn a line like that."

When you mention the pennies, his hands stop for half a breath. Then they start again, squaring the cards on the crate.

"Twin Songs?" He tilts his head as though the name came from a long way off. "Couldn't tell you, friend. I don't go east of the bells. All that ringing, I'd never hear a punter's purse." His left hand pats the front of his waistcoat, just once, where the pouch hangs. "Somebody comes round with a bag of them now and then. Friend of a friend, a Lady's sort of person. They like them in winners' hands. Good for the goddess's name, they say. And it costs me nothing, which is my favourite price."

He hasn't said who brings them, or where they come from. Both times he got close to it, he talked straight past it.

The carter has already gone off down the bridge with his whip over his shoulder. The young man in the good coat is still there, digging through his pockets as if more silver might turn up in them.

"Mind you," Ferro says, more quietly, as though he's just remembered it, "I'm not sure the Lady's keeping her end up. A man wins here, gets his copper, and he's supposed to come back, that's the whole joke of it. My best regulars from spring..." He shrugs, and for a moment the warmth goes thin. "Haven't seen half of them in a month. One's cart threw a wheel on the Way. One lost his place on the docks. That's dice for you. They come and they go." He snaps the cards down in a row, face down, quick and neat. "That's why I keep the game fresh."

Then he digs two fingers into the pouch and comes out with one of the coppers. He doesn't flip it to you. He sets it on the edge of the crate nearest you, on its blank side, so Tymora's thin smile looks up into the lamplight.

"There. You don't have to play for it. A man who pays a tiefling's toll has earned a bit of luck, I'd say." His grin comes back, easy and wide. "And if it brings you back to my crate, well. The Lady likes a winner."

Thirty feet behind you, by the chandler's post, the cat has stood up.

James keeps his voice down, the way you'd tell a man his horse is lame, and Ferro hears that this isn't a game. He looks at the copper on the crate. Then he looks at the carter's back, far down the bridge now, the whip swinging over his shoulder.

"I never said a scarf," he says. He's quiet now, and for once there's no patter in his voice.

He sweeps the gift coin off the crate edge. He doesn't put it back in the pouch. He holds it pinched between two fingers, as if he isn't sure what to do with it.

"I'll tell you what I'll tell you, friend, and that's not a name." He gives the punters a quick, easy smile and waves them off: *short break, lads, cards need a rest.* The porters drift away. The young man in the good coat doesn't move. "Somebody comes round when the pouch runs light. Came today, as it happens, this afternoon, coming in off the east road with a fresh bag. Never asks a copper for them. That's the part I liked."

He turns the coin over. Blank side up. Face side up.

"What I didn't think about till you said it..." He stops and starts again. "She asks after them. The winners. Who took one last month. What they're called. Do they still come round, where do they drink. I took it for a Lady's sort of nosiness, wanting to know her luck went to good homes. I told her. Names, the taverns, all of it." His jaw moves. "Harl, the one with the cart wheel. I told her his name in spring."

By the chandler's post, the cat sits back down. Its tail curls round its feet, and it doesn't take its eyes off the copper in Ferro's fingers.

Ferro sees you looking at it. He drops the coin into his waistcoat pocket, not the pouch. Then he puts both hands flat on the crate. The warmth is gone from his voice and his face, and he looks like a man doing sums he doesn't like.

"So you tell *me* something, retired man. You're not watching the cards and you're not drinking my silver. What do you know about these that I don't?"

turns.message:
“Less than I’d like. A newcomer got one from a woman in a blue scarf this morning. She sent him to a shrine in Twin Songs to give a brother his name. Varn quietly warned me he should throw it in the river tonight. And my cat wants nothing to do with them.”

I glance at the pocket where he put the copper.

“That isn’t proof of a curse. It’s enough that I’d stop handing them out until someone who knows can examine one.”

I draw a scrap of cloth from my pouch and lay it on the crate. “Would you give me one wrapped in that? I’ll take it to the Lady’s clergy. And where can I find Harl?”
turns.reply:
Ferro listens with his hands flat on the crate. He doesn't interrupt. When James gets to the river, his eyes go once to the water past the rail, black now, with lamplight on it. When James gets to the cat, he looks over his shoulder at the chandler's post. The cat looks back at him with no expression at all.

"A brother in Twin Songs," he says. "Writing down names." He breathes out through his nose. "That's two of them writing names, then. Her and him. And me, like a fool, doing it for free."

James glances at his waistcoat pocket. Ferro sees him do it and doesn't pretend otherwise.

The scrap of cloth goes down on the crate between the cards. Ferro looks at it for a moment as if it were a bet he didn't understand. Then he laughs, short, with nothing much behind it.

"You want one wrapped up like a dead mouse." He reaches into the waistcoat, not the pocket but the pouch, and pinches out a copper the way he has a hundred times tonight. This time he looks at it. He holds it up to the lamp, turns it, frowns, and drops it onto the cloth from a couple of inches up, as though he doesn't want to hold it any longer than he has to. "Funny thing. They're always warm, these. Out of the bag, out of my pocket, it's all the same. I thought it was my hands." He flexes his fingers. "I've got cold hands, friend. Ask anyone I've dealt to."

James folds the cloth over it. Through the cloth he can feel the copper's small, round weight. It may be a little warm from Ferro's fingers, or it may not. He can't tell.

"Harl," Ferro goes on, and his voice drops again. "Carter. Big lad, red beard, laughs like a dropped barrel. Kept his wagon at the yard on the Lower City side of the gate, under the wall, where the carters stable for the night. But you won't find him there now. He sold the wagon after the wheel went." He stops. "He drank at the Copper Kettle. Dice house, down near the docks, on a lane off the fish market. Lost more there than he ever lost to me, and that's saying something. If anybody knows where he's sleeping now, it's them. He'll owe them, if he owes anyone."

He says the next part to the crate, not to James.

"That's where I told her too. The Kettle."

Then he picks up the three cards, squares them, and puts them away inside his coat. The pouch stays where it is.

"Game's closed tonight. Light's going anyway." It's a small thing, and he says it as if it costs him. "Tomorrow I'll see. I'm not promising you more than tonight." He jerks his chin at the folded cloth. "The Lady's Hall is up in the Upper City, behind the inner wall. The Watch shuts those gates at dark, and the priests up there like a man to come with an offering in his hand and his boots clean. You won't get in tonight. Not looking like you've walked from Tethyr."

Behind James there's the scuff of a good boot on wet stone. The young man in the good coat has finally stopped searching his empty pockets. He doesn't look at the crate or at James. He walks off toward the gate at an easy pace, hands in his pockets, and Varn waves him through with all the rest. The dark under the arch takes him.

Ferro watches him go, and his mouth goes thin.

"Didn't know that one," he says. "He lost three hands and never asked to play a fourth." He turns back to James and holds out his hand across the crate. It's empty, palm sideways, a dealer's handshake. "You've had my name off the sergeant's patter, I expect. I don't have yours, retired man. And if your priests say it's only copper, I'd like to hear that from you too."

turns.message:
I shake his hand. “James Worgen. I’ll tell you what I learn, copper or otherwise. You can leave word for me at the Elfsong.”

I stow the wrapped penny separately from my own coin and money. “If she comes back, don’t confront her on my account.”

Then I call the cat to follow and head through the checkpoint, pausing beside Varn only long enough to speak quietly.

“Your warning was useful. I’ve a sample for the Lady’s clergy. Is there a priest I can reach down here tonight, with the Upper City gates shut?”
turns.reply:
Ferro's grip is quick and dry, a dealer's handshake, and his fingers really are cold. Cold as the rail beside him.

"James Worgen," he says, putting the name away somewhere. "The Elfsong. Fine." At *don't confront her* he gives a short laugh that doesn't get as far as his eyes. "Friend, I'm brave at a crate. Everywhere else I'm a man with a tin box." He tucks the box under his arm and doesn't watch you go.

James puts the wrapped penny in a pocket of its own, away from his purse and the Lady's coin he carries for his own reasons. When he calls, the cat comes from the chandler's post at an unhurried trot and falls in beside him. It walks half a pace wider than it usually does, on his left, away from that pocket. Through the bond he gets a sense that isn't a thought, only a smell: milk turned sour in a clean bowl. Then the cat shuts it off, as if it's embarrassed to have shared it.

At the table Varn is inking a carter's name. She hears your question without looking up. One of the privates is still picking his teeth. The other has wandered off toward the eel girl.

"Not tonight," she says, at her toll voice. "The Lady's priests sleep above the wall. The Hall opens an alms door at the dawn bell, the side door off the yard, not the front steps. That's where Lower City folk queue." The pen moves on. *Gant, Orrin, cart of turnips.* "I went up there once. Asked a question. Got a lay brother with a soft voice telling me the Lady's business is the Lady's." She blots the line. "Ask someone else."

She stamps the carter's tally and waves him on. Then, as she reaches for the next name, she adds without changing her tone:

"If it turns out to be more than copper, you don't bring it to the Fist. You bring it to me. This table, any evening this tenday."

She looks past you. "Next."

The gate's arch is cold and smells of old stone and horse. Then you're out the other side, and Baldur's Gate opens up in front of you. The street drops steeply toward the harbour. Lamplighters are working along it with long poles, and the windows above the shops are going yellow one by one. Down the slope, over the roofs, you can see the masts in the harbour and a scrap of pale, late light on the water. Up to your right the inner wall cuts across the hill. On top of it the Watch's torches are already lit, and somewhere up there a gate bell rings three times and stops.

The cat sits down on the first step of the slope. It looks downhill toward the docks, then back at you, with its tail wrapped tight.
