turns.message:
“The docks, then,” I murmur to the cat. “Let’s see if Harl’s bad luck has left him anything to eat.”

I ask a lamplighter for directions to the Copper Kettle and make my way there. As I walk, I keep an eye out for the young man in the good coat who lingered through our conversation at Ferro’s crate.
turns.reply:
James asks the first lamplighter he passes, a stooped woman with a pole twice her height and a tin of oil on a strap. She doesn't stop working. She hooks the little door of the lamp open and trims the wick while she talks.

"Kettle. Down Fishgate to the market, then the lane with the smell, past the cooper's, look for the pot hung over the door." The wick catches and the glass goes yellow. "If you're going to lose money, lose it early. They get worse after the tenth bell." She shuts the lamp and moves on to the next one.

The street drops toward the water in short, steep runs, with steps cut in wherever the hill was too much for carts. The cat goes down them ahead of James in neat little jumps. It still keeps to his left, away from the pocket. The city is full at this hour: porters going home, sailors going out, a Fist patrol of three in red cloaks walking with the boredom of men near the end of a shift. James studies every back in a good coat as he passes it, the way a scout once taught him on a hillside in Tethyr. Look at the walk, not the coat.

He doesn't find him. He sees half a dozen good coats between the gate and the water: a clerk with ink on his cuff, a tall man arguing with a woman, a boy who has plainly borrowed his father's. None of them walks with that easy, unbothered pace, hands in pockets. If the young man is still on this street, either he isn't wearing that coat or he isn't in front of James. James can't tell which, and he doesn't like not knowing.

By the time the street flattens out at the fish market, the light over the harbour has gone from pale to grey. The stalls are shuttered. The cobbles are slick with scales and the gulls have them to themselves, walking about like customs men. The lane is easy to find: you follow your nose. It runs behind the market between leaning houses, past a cooper's yard where staves are stacked like ribs, to a door two steps below the street. A dented copper kettle hangs on a chain above it, black with old smoke.

You hear the place before you reach it. Under the voices there's the dry rattle of dice in a leather cup, the knock as they're turned out on wood, then a groan or a shout. James knows that sound better than he knows his own name. His hand drifts to the card case at his belt again before he notices it, and he leaves it hanging at his side.

The cat stops at the top of the steps. It stretches its neck toward the doorframe and sniffs along the wood at the height where a hand would rest. Its whiskers go forward, then flat. Through the bond comes a faint thread of that same smell, the sour milk in the clean bowl, thinner than on the bridge but there. It sits down on the top step and doesn't come any further.

The doorway is filled by a man as wide as the door, bald, his forearms crossed over a leather apron. He looks at James's boots, then the cloak, then the rapier, and last of all at the cat.

"Steel stays on you, hands stay off it. Cat's your trouble, not mine." His voice is flat and bored. He's said it a thousand times. "Playing or drinking?"

Somewhere between the gate and the fish market, James lost the crowd. He looked hard at every back that went past him, and none of them was the young man. If he's still out there, still watching, James walked the whole way down to the docks without catching him at it. He has no idea whether anyone followed him to this door.

The doorman is still waiting on his answer.

turns.message:
“Drinking. And buying supper for Harl, if he’s here. Red beard, used to keep a wagon—Ferro sent me this way.”

I keep my hands loose and clear of my weapons. “Has he been in tonight?”

Through the bond, I ask the cat to stay somewhere safe near the entrance and warn me if it notices the young man from the bridge.
turns.reply:
The doorman hears Ferro's name and doesn't react to it. He reacts to Harl's: his eyes go flat for a moment, like a man looking at an old bill.

"Drinking's at the bar." He uncrosses his arms slowly. "Harl's in. He's always in. He doesn't eat on his own coin, I'll tell you that for free." He leans aside just enough to let a man past and no more. "You buy his supper, buy his supper. His slate's the house's business. Don't go paying on it at the bar without talking to Dagna first, or she'll think you're making a point."

Then he goes back to studying the lane.

Through the bond James feels the cat take in the request. It doesn't answer the way a person would. It just goes. It crosses the lane in three neat jumps and climbs the stacked staves in the cooper's yard opposite, well clear of the doorframe. Up there it folds into a loaf on the top barrel, where it can see both the Kettle's door and the mouth of the lane back toward the fish market. Through the bond comes something like *settled*, with a cold edge of *watching*. Nothing else for now.

Two steps down, the Kettle is warm, low and brown. Pipe smoke hangs under the beams in a flat layer. There are four tables, each with its own cluster of players and its own leather cup going round, and the sound James heard from the street is much louder in here: the rattle, the knock on the wood, then the groan or the shout. A bar of black planks runs along one wall. Behind it a broad grey-haired woman, Dagna by the doorman's description, is drawing ale with one hand and chalking a long slate with the other. The slate is covered in names and little rows of marks. James knows what a slate like that is without needing to read it.

At the nearest table someone throws a pair of sixes. The cheer goes through James's chest like a struck bell. His hand has started toward his belt again before he catches it.

Harl isn't hard to find, because Ferro described him well. Getting the size of him right is harder. He's on a bench at the back, near the cold end of the hearth, under the slate. He's a big man gone soft and hollow at once. His red beard is untrimmed and has grey in it that a man his age shouldn't have. In front of him there's a mug and no plate. His left hand is wrapped in a dirty linen strip across the knuckles. He isn't playing. He's watching the far table, the busiest one, the way a man watches a fire he used to warm himself at.

There's one player at that far table James's eye keeps coming back to without his meaning it to. He's a neat, narrow man in a dove-grey coat, and the coins in front of him are stacked more tidily than anyone else's. He throws, and the table groans. He doesn't smile when he wins. He just reaches out and squares the stack.

Harl hasn't noticed James yet. Dagna has. She doesn't stop chalking, but she's looking at the newcomer with the rapier, and she isn't trying to hide it.

turns.message:
I go to the bar, turning my back on the dice tables.

“Evening. An ale and two hot suppers, please—one for me, one for Harl. What’ll that cost?”

I nod toward his bench. “Your doorman was clear about the slate. I’m only buying a meal, not settling anyone’s accounts.”
turns.reply:
The bar is black planks rubbed shiny by elbows. When James turns his back on the room, the noise of the dice doesn't get any quieter. It's behind him now, and that's no better. He sets his hands on the wood.

Dagna finishes drawing the ale she's on, slides it down to a porter without looking where it lands, and comes along the bar to him. She brings the chalk with her. Her eyes go over him once, the same way the doorman's did, but slower, and they stop on the rapier longer than they stop on his face.

She hears him out. When he nods at the bench and talks about the slate, one grey eyebrow goes up a little.

"Hob told you that, did he." She doesn't sound annoyed. She sounds like a woman crossing an item off a list. "Good. Saves us a talk."

She taps the chalk twice against the edge of the slate.

"Ale's four copper. Stew's six a bowl, bread with it. Sixteen the lot." A bowl of something brown and steaming is already being ladled at the hatch behind her by a thin boy with a burnt wrist. "Harl's goes to him, not to the table. Nobody eats a stake in my house."

While she talks, a potboy comes in from the far side of the room with a little pewter dish. It's the house's cut from the busiest table, the one with the man in the dove-grey coat. He puts it down at her elbow. Mostly it's silver, and a couple of tired gold pieces. Mixed in with them are three or four thin coppers that look wrong beside the city pennies. They're too thin, and too well struck. Dagna tips the whole dish into a stone jar under the bar without sorting it and puts the lid back on.

James feels something against his hip at about the same moment. It's the pocket where the wrapped copper rides, away from his purse. It might be warm. It might just be the hearth and the crowd and a long walk down the hill. Still, it's a small, steady warmth through the cloth, like a coin a man has been holding in his fist, and it wasn't there out on the bridge.

At the back of the room Harl has noticed the stew coming out of the hatch. He isn't looking at James. He's looking at the bowl, like a man who has taught himself not to hope it's for him.

Dagna puts the chalk down at last, which seems to be a courtesy, and leans on the bar.

"So. Sixteen copper." Her eyes don't leave his. "What's Harl to you, that you'd walk in off the street and feed him?"

turns.message:
I put two silver on the bar. “Ferro knows him. Said he’d had a rough run. I’ve eaten a few meals on someone else’s kindness myself.”

I nod toward the bowls. “I’d like a word with him, if he’s willing. Supper’s his either way.”

Once I have my ale and change, I carry my bowl over to Harl’s bench. “Harl? James Worgen. Ferro pointed me your way. Mind if I sit?”
turns.reply:
Dagna looks at the two silver, then at James, and takes her time over it. She sweeps the coins off the bar into her palm, drops them in a box under the counter and counts four city pennies back onto the wood. They are round and dull and nothing about them is wrong.

"Kindness," she says, the way she might name a coin she doesn't see often. "Fine." She jerks her chin at the boy, who sets a second bowl on the hatch next to the first and a heel of dark bread across each. "Talk's free. Don't go putting ideas in his head about winning it back. He's had enough of those."

She draws the ale and slides it over. Then she goes back to her slate. Her eyes follow James across the room all the same.

The bench at the back is out of the hearth's reach. The air there is noticeably cooler, as if the fire has given up on that end. James sets the bowl down in front of Harl, puts his own beside it and the ale between them.

Up close Harl is younger than his beard. He might be thirty-five. The grey has come in in streaks, the way it does on men who've had a fright, and there are pouches under his eyes like bruises. The linen round his left hand is brown at the knuckles. He looks at the bowl first and at James second, and for a moment he doesn't move at all.

"That's mine?"

He doesn't wait for an answer. He gets the spoon into his good hand and eats the first three mouthfuls fast, bent low over the bowl like a man guarding it. Then he makes himself slow down, and that seems to cost him more. He tears the bread with his teeth because he can't do it one-handed.

"Ferro." He says it to the stew. His voice is big, built for shouting across a carters' yard, and he keeps it down to a mumble, which only makes it sound broken. "He still on the bridge? With the crate?" A breath goes out of him that might once have started as a laugh. "Took two silver off me every Moonday since Greengrass and I'd thank him for it. Good game. Honest, mostly. You know where you are with three cards."

He wipes his beard with the back of the bandaged hand and winces.

"Caught it in the wagon tongue. Week after the wheel." He says it flatly, as if he's told it too often. "Then the buyer for the wagon shorted me eight gold and I couldn't prove it. Then the room. Then..." He lifts the spoon an inch toward the slate above his head and lets it fall. "It's a run, that's all. Runs end."

As he says it, his good hand leaves the spoon. Without his seeming to notice, it goes to the front of his shirt, to a lump under the cloth where a cord might hang, and his thumb presses it once through the wool. The hand comes back to the bowl.

At James's hip, in the pocket on its own, the warmth hasn't gone. If anything it's steadier at this cold end of the room than it was at the bar.

Harl finally looks up properly. His eyes are pale, red-rimmed and wary.

"Nobody feeds me for Ferro's sake, mister. Ferro doesn't owe me and I don't owe Ferro." He has the spoon in a tight grip. "So what is it you want?"

Across the room, at the busiest table, the man in the dove-grey coat throws, wins and squares his stack. While his hands are busy his eyes lift for a moment toward the back bench, then go back to the dice.

“To find out whether someone’s been passing off harm as the Lady’s kindness.”

“Ferro’s been giving winners thin copper pennies. Lady’s face on one side, blank on the other. The woman supplying them asks him for the winners’ names and where they drink. He told her yours. He’s worried now.”

Harl stops eating when you say *harm*. He doesn't put the spoon down. He just holds it over the bowl while you talk, and a drop of stew falls back in.

When you get to Ferro telling the woman his name, his eyes come up off the bowl. At *he's worried now*, his mouth twists inside the beard.

"Ferro's worried." His voice is flat. "That's something."

For a while he doesn't answer the question. He looks at the slate over his head, then at the busy table across the room, then at nothing. Then his good hand goes into the neck of his shirt and comes out with a greasy brown cord. On the end of it, warm from his chest, hangs a thin copper with a smiling face. The edge has worn a ring of green into his skin where it rests.

"Moonday after Greengrass," he says. "Found the lady three times running. Ferro flipped me this on top, like he does. *Lady likes a winner to come back.*" He turns it in the poor light without letting go of the cord. "Wheel went near two months after. I was carrying it then. I've carried it since."

He keeps his voice low. You can hear what it costs a man that size.

"Early summer a woman found me here. Older. Kind face. Had a scarf on her head, I couldn't tell you the colour. She sat where you're sitting and asked was the Lady still with me. I said not so you'd notice. She said that's how the Lady tests a man, and if I wanted her to know me I should go out east past the walls, where the bells are, and give my name at the little shrine." He breathes out through his nose. "So I went. Brother there wrote me in a book. Soft hands. Smelled of candle fat. He told me to wear it against my skin, because that's where the Lady hears you. He gave me the cord." He lifts it an inch. "Didn't charge me for that either."

He stops long enough that you think he's done. He isn't.

"Last tenday a fellow comes by this bench. Neat sort, talked like a clerk. I never looked at his face, I was looking at his boots, they were better than mine. He says there's friends of the Lady who'll stand a man's slate, once she's done testing him. All of it. I'd only to go round to the shrine and make my mark in the book again." His jaw works. "I told him I pay my own way. He said the offer keeps."

His thumb moves over Tymora's face, and he notices it this time. He stops.

"Don't know what they do, you said." He looks at the coin as if he's never seen it before. "But you're sitting here asking me."

Then, without hurry, he squares his stack one last time, sweeps it into a purse, pushes a couple of coins across to the potboy and stands up. He takes a dove-grey hat from the peg and heads for the steps to the door.

Harl hasn't seen him. He's still holding the cord out over the stew, and his pale, red-rimmed eyes are on you.

"So what do I do with it, mister?"

Close to, it smells of tallow, the cheap kind that gutters. That's the candle fat Harl talked about, worked right into the twist of it. The new bundle is as warm through the cloth as the first one. Now James can feel the same small, steady heat on both sides of him.

At *you don't owe him a conversation*, something like a grin moves in Harl's beard and dies before it gets anywhere.

"Never did," he says. "Told him so." He picks up the spoon and goes back to the stew, slower now.

James eats too. The stew is better than the room deserves, mostly barley with some mutton in it. He asks about the man in the dove-grey coat, and Harl's spoon stops halfway to his mouth. He looks past James at the busy table. A carter has taken the empty stool, and the dice go round as if nobody had ever sat there.

"Him." Harl puts the spoon down. "In most nights, since spring, about. That table, that stool. Dagna keeps it for him." He considers that for a moment. "Never seen him lose a night. A throw, sure. Never a night."

He rubs his bandaged knuckles with his thumb and thinks it over honestly, which takes him a while.

"Can't tell you, mister. The clerk talked. That one, I've never heard him say ten words. Points at the cup, pushes his coin, squares his pile." He draws a small neat square on the plank with one finger. "And I was looking at the clerk's boots, not his coat. Good boots. Grey man's got good boots." He shrugs, one heavy shoulder. "So has half the Upper City. I'm not swearing to a man on his boots."

He goes back to his bowl and wipes it clean with the last of the bread, carefully.

"If it was him," he adds to the empty bowl, "he sat across the room from me every night after and never once looked my way. Till tonight."

Up at the bar Dagna watched the second bundle go into James's pocket. She didn't stop drawing ale while she did it. Now she bends to say something to the boy with the burnt wrist. It's short and too low to carry. The boy sets down his ladle, wipes his hands on his shirt and goes out through the back of the kitchen hatch, not the front door.

Dagna goes back to her slate. She doesn't look at the back bench again.

turns.message:
“Fair. I’d rather an honest ‘don’t know’ than the wrong man’s name.”

I set down my spoon. “I’m heading to the Elfsong for a room. You’re welcome to share it tonight—my expense, no slate. We can walk to the Hall together.” I lower my voice. “Dagna’s just sent her boy out the back after watching me take your coin. Might be ordinary business. I’d rather not leave you here to find out.”

Through the bond, I ask the cat whether the lane is clear while I gather my things to leave.
turns.reply:
Harl watches the spoon go down. He hears the offer through to the end without moving. Then he hears the part about the boy, and his eyes go to the kitchen hatch. The thin lad's ladle is still lying where he left it.

"The back." He says it the way he'd read a mark off the slate. "She sends him out the back for two things, mister. A barrel's run dry, or somebody wants a word with somebody." He doesn't look at the barrels. "Nothing's run dry."

His gaze drops to your hip, to the pocket holding his own coin, then comes back to your face.

"That's not about me. I've owed her since Flamerule, she knows where I sleep. You're the one walked out of her room with coin in your pocket." He thinks about it with the same slow honesty he gave the grey man's boots, then sets both hands flat on the plank. "Floor. Not a bed. And I'll owe you for it, whatever you want to call it."

He gets up off the bench. Standing, he's bigger than he looked sitting, and something in his back cracks.

You gather your things. The ale's barely touched. Dagna looks up as the two of you pass the bar. Her chalk keeps moving, and she speaks to Harl, not to you.

"Slate'll still be up there in the morning, Harl."

"Didn't think it'd walk off," Harl says, and keeps going.

At the top of the steps Hob moves aside just far enough, the same as before. He doesn't say anything to either of you.

While you climb, you reach for the cat. You get its answer in bits, the way you always do. The lane is grey and wet. One drunk is leaning on the cooper's fence and paying it no attention. Nobody's standing in a doorway, and nobody is sitting on the steps by the fish market. Then you get a memory, held up for you like something caught: a few minutes ago the burnt-wrist boy came out of the narrow gap between the Kettle and the next house over. He ran up the lane under the staves, and at the market he turned *west*, toward the quays. That's the other way from the grey man. He hasn't come back. What comes through after that is the cat's verdict, flat and clear: *empty now*.

It drops off the barrel in two jumps and lands in front of you. Then it stops, because one of the coins rides on your left hip and the other on your right, so there's no side left that's away from both. It looks up at you for a long, offended moment. In the end it walks a full stride ahead, tail up, and doesn't look back.

Harl watches all this and decides not to ask. He climbs the ladder to the cooper's loft, one-handed and slow, and comes down with a rolled blanket and a sack that doesn't hold much.

"Elfsong's up past the market and left at the chandlers'," he says. "I know the way."

turns.message:
“Lead on. Main streets, where there’s light.”

I walk beside Harl, keeping my hands free and checking behind us at turns rather than staring over my shoulder all the way. Through the bond, I ask the cat to warn me if anyone keeps following us.

“And it’s James,” I add quietly. “‘Mister’ makes me look around for an officer.”
turns.reply:
Harl takes the lead without saying anything. He goes the way a carter goes, keeping to the middle of the street where the cobbles are flattest. At the mouth of the lane he turns away from the dark run along the waterfront and heads uphill toward the market's lamps. He walks slowly, mostly because of the sack and the blanket, and it suits you. A man who is hurrying gets noticed.

You ask the cat. It answers with a flick of attention, and then it's off ahead of you, up onto a low wall, along a shop's awning and down again, always a couple of houses in front and one roof higher. Through the bond you catch a street seen from above, the lamplight in pools and the gaps between them.

At the first turn, where the fish market gives way to the chandlers' row, you stop to retie a boot lace you don't need to retie, and you look back the way you came.

He's there. And once you've seen him, you can't stop seeing him.

He's about a hundred feet back, on the dark side of the street where the lamps don't reach. He's wiry, about forty, with a knit sailor's cap pulled low and a coat too thin for the night. You know him before you've finished looking, because the cat showed him to you not a quarter of an hour ago: the drunk propped against the cooper's fence, paying the Kettle no attention. Now he isn't drunk. A drunk's feet wander and look for the wall. This man's feet go straight, quiet, heel to toe, and they stopped when yours did. He has turned in to a doorway and is fumbling at its latch like a man trying to get into his own house. The door isn't his. His hand isn't really on the latch, and his head is turned just far enough to keep you at the edge of his eye.

A sergeant on a hillside in Tethyr once told you that a good tail is never the one who looks at you. He's the one who stops looking at the same moment you stop walking. This one has done it twice.

The cat has seen it too, from the bond and from your sudden stillness. It drops off the awning onto a window ledge directly above the doorway, as if that had been its plan all along. It hangs over the edge with its nose down. What comes back to you is a smell, laid out for you: *tar, wet wool, old fish, a knife's oil.* Then a second thing, put down beside the first so you notice what's missing: *no sour milk*. Whatever this man is carrying, there's no Lady's coin on him.

He doesn't look up at the cat. Cats sit on ledges all over this city.

Harl has stopped a pace ahead, sack on his shoulder, waiting for your boot. He hasn't seen anything. He's still chewing over what you said before the turn.

"James," he says, trying it out. It sounds strange in his big voice, as if he's set down a load that was easier to carry. "Right." He looks up the chandlers' row. Three doors on, a lamp hangs over a wide door with a carved elf's head, and noise and warm light spill out of it onto the street. "That's it. The Elfsong."

Behind you, the man in the knit cap has given up on the latch. He's leaning against the doorframe the way a man waits for someone to let him in. He's waiting for you to move.

*(Out of game: that was a natural 20. You spotted him for certain, and as far as you can tell he doesn't know you have.)*

turns.message:
I straighten from my boot and keep walking, without another glance back.

“Someone from the cooper’s yard is following us,” I tell Harl quietly. “Don’t look. We’ll go inside together.”

Through the bond, I ask the cat to watch whether the man follows us into the Elfsong or meets anyone outside, staying hidden and within range.

I enter with Harl and approach the bar. “Evening. Have you a lockable room for two, and what’s the price?”
turns.reply:
James gets up from his boot and walks on at the same easy pace. He doesn't look back.

"Someone from the cooper's yard is following us," he says quietly, as he comes level with Harl. "Don't look. We'll go inside together."

Harl's neck goes stiff, the way a horse's does when it hears something in the hedge. He doesn't turn his head. He shifts the sack to his other shoulder, which puts his bulk between James and the dark side of the street, and keeps walking.

"Right," he says to the cobbles. After three steps he adds, lower: "Cooper's fence. That's the Kettle's lookout, or whoever Dagna pays to keep one." He says nothing after that.

Through the bond James feels the cat take the job. It doesn't come down off the ledge. It folds itself flat along the stone sill above the doorway and shrinks into a cat-shaped shadow on a street full of them.

The Elfsong's door is broad oak, and a carved elf's head is set over the lintel, worn smooth at the nose where generations of hands have reached up to touch it. Inside the air is warm and smells of beer, woodsmoke and something baked with cloves. The noise here isn't the Kettle's noise. People are talking, a fiddle is being tuned without much hope in a corner, and a knot of sailors is arguing about a tide. Nobody is shaking a cup. James notices the lack the way a man notices a toothache that has stopped.

The bar is long and polished, and the man behind it stands on a raised board so he can see over it: a halfling, grey at the temples, sleeves rolled to the elbow, with a pencil behind one ear. He looks James over in one quick, practised glance: cloak, rapier, travel dust. Then he looks at Harl, the blanket roll and the sack. His mouth doesn't change, but his eyebrows go up a polite quarter-inch.

The bond tugs while James is still crossing the floor. Through the cat's eyes he sees the street from above, tilted and grey. The man in the knit cap waits in his doorway a little longer, until the oak door has closed. Then he comes off the frame and walks up the row as easily as a man going home. He doesn't hurry. Passing the Elfsong's front window he slows for half a step, and the cat sees his head turn toward the yellow glass, toward the bar. Then he walks on. He meets nobody and speaks to nobody. At the corner he turns downhill, back toward the fish market and the waterfront beyond it, and the edge of the hundred feet closes on him like a door. The cat doesn't follow. What it sends James is short: *looked in. gone down. alone.* Then it settles back on its sill.

The halfling has his elbows on the bar.

"Evening." His voice is brisk and friendly, and he clearly has forty other things to do. "Pim Underbough. My bar, not my house. The house belongs to people with more money than sense." He hears out the question about the room and nods as if he gets it every night.

"Every room upstairs has a bolt on the inside. A key and a proper lock, that's the two at the top of the second stair." He taps the bar once with a finger for each. "Lock room's a gold the night. Bed, washstand, a jug filled in the morning. Big fellow on the floor is nothing extra, I don't charge by the blanket. A cot's four silver more if he wants one." He glances at Harl, then back at James, and keeps it polite. "Supper's done, but there's bread and cold mutton if you're hungry. And breakfast's at the dawn bell, if you're the sort that's up for it."

He takes the pencil from behind his ear and holds it over a ledger.

"Name for the book?"

turns.message:
“James Worgen. Lock room, please.” I put one gold on the bar. “We’ll be out before breakfast.”

I lower my voice. “A man in a knit sailor’s cap followed us from the fish market and looked through your window just now. He’s gone downhill again. I’m not asking you to fight my troubles, but please don’t give our room number to callers. Send for me instead.”

Through the bond, I call the cat inside. Then I take the key and head upstairs with Harl to inspect the room’s door and windows before we settle in.
turns.reply:
Pim's pencil moves before James has finished his name. *Worgen*, in a quick round hand, and a small *2* beside it. The gold piece goes under the bar without Pim looking at it twice.

"Out before breakfast. Fine. I'll have the boy leave bread on the stair for you, so you don't go to the Lady hungry." He doesn't ask how James knows where they're going. Then James drops his voice, and Pim's face doesn't change, but his eyes go once to the front window. The yellow glass shows the street, a lamp and nobody under it.

"Knit cap." He keeps his voice at bar level and taps the polished wood once. "Thin coat?" James nods, and he taps again. "Nobody gets a room number out of me but the one who paid for it. That's not a favour, that's the house." He takes a heavy iron key off a hook under the bar and lays it in front of James. Its bow is stamped with a small worn leaf. "Somebody comes asking, I'll send the boy up and you can decide whether you're in. And if your knit cap walks through my door, I'll know him." He glances at Harl and keeps it polite. "That's as far as I go."

James calls through the bond, and a moment later the oak door swings in a hand's width on a sailor's way out. The cat walks through the gap as though it had booked the room itself. It crosses the floor under the tables, ignores a fiddler's dropped crust, and sits down at James's boot.

Pim looks at it over the edge of the bar. "Cat's free too. Unless it's on my bar."

The first stair is broad and creaks. The second is narrow and steep, and Harl has to turn sideways with the sack. At the top there are two doors facing each other across a landing no wider than a man's reach. James's key fits the left one.

James looks the room over the way the scouts taught him, door first.

The door is solid oak, as thick as two fingers. The hinges are on the inside, so nobody can lift the pins from the landing. The lock is good Gondish work, newer than the door, and the key turns it with a heavy, honest clack. Below the lock an iron bolt as long as a hand slides into a socket set deep in the frame. Someone has thought about this door. It would take an axe or a lot of patience.

The room is narrow and runs under the slope of the roof. There's a bed with a straw tick and a wool blanket, a washstand with an empty jug, a peg on the wall, and floor enough for one big man if he doesn't roll over much. The air smells of old guests and somebody's lavender.

The window is the weak point. It's small, set low under the eaves, and closed with plank shutters on the inside. The only latch is a wooden bar dropped into two brackets. James lifts the bar and looks out. Below is the dark yard behind the Elfsong: barrels, a pump, a gate in the back wall onto an alley. About eight feet under the sill the slate roof of the kitchen's lean-to slopes away toward the yard. A man could get from the alley onto the barrels, from the barrels onto the lean-to, and from the lean-to up to this sill if he had nerve and quiet feet. He wouldn't get through the shutters without noise. But that bar would lift with a knife blade through the gap between the planks.

The cat jumps onto the sill past James's arm and puts its nose out into the night. Through the bond comes a run of smells: *smoke, wet slate, the kitchen's mutton, a rat under the lean-to.* Then, set carefully to one side so James can't miss it: *no sour milk here.* There's a pause, and then: *except what you brought.* It doesn't look at his pockets. It doesn't need to.

Behind him Harl has stopped in the doorway with the sack still on his shoulder, looking at the bed as if he suspects it of something. Then he sets the sack down against the wall by the door, unrolls his blanket and lays it lengthwise across the threshold, right where the door would have to open.

"I'll take the door," he says. It isn't a request. He lowers himself onto the blanket one knee at a time and sits with his back to the oak and his bandaged hand in his lap. "Anybody comes in that way, they come in over me." He looks at the window, where the cat's tail hangs down off the sill. "That one's yours."

From somewhere below, faint through the boards and the noise of the common room, a woman's voice has started singing. No fiddle is playing with it. It's a slow air in a tongue James doesn't know, and nobody downstairs seems to be singing it.

note.text:
I enjoyed this session. James arrived without an errand, and paying a family’s toll turned naturally into something he cared about. The mystery connects well to his patron and his temptation without requiring him to accept a job from a stranger.

**What worked**
- The NPCs had dignity and distinct voices. Mordai resisting charity, Harl insisting on the floor, and Ferro closing his game reluctantly were especially good. Helping people didn’t make them instantly obedient.
- There were useful choices besides fighting or rolling: paying the toll, watching the payout, buying Harl supper, taking samples, arranging a safer night.
- The cat felt like a companion rather than equipment. Its distaste for the coins—and its annoyance when I put one in each pocket—was memorable.
- The physical details helped me make decisions: sightlines on the bridge, the lookout’s movements, the room’s lock and vulnerable shutters.
- The danger developed gradually. I had reasons to be cautious without being forced into an ambush.

**What broke**
- **The roll system needs fixing.** It repeatedly used +2 despite displaying Perception +1 or Persuasion +7. One reroll should have succeeded but displayed failure. The narration corrected that, but the journal still recorded the original natural-one failure.
- I couldn’t send an out-of-game correction while a roll card was pending. That makes a mechanical error unnecessarily difficult to resolve.
- Some starting rules contradicted the supplied campaign sheet or house rules, notably rapier proficiency, Healing Light’s per-use limit, and attunement. Those should be reconciled once, not silently changed.
- There were visible presentation leaks: a raw `recall` invocation, duplicated explanations of resolved rolls, and awkward currency labels.
- Inventory tracking occasionally invented continuity: the barely touched ale became a carried mug after leaving the Kettle.

**What was missing or could improve**
- The mystery needed more uncertainty of interpretation. Almost every clue reinforced the same suspicion immediately: ominous coins, name lists, misfortune, a winning stranger, a messenger, a tail. Some ordinary explanations or unrelated city life would make discovery feel less predetermined.
- The cat’s impressions sometimes became very precise evidence. I liked its personality, but clearer limits on telepathy versus actively borrowing its senses would preserve both the rules and the investigation.
- A few NPCs knew things without an established source—Pim anticipating our trip to the Lady’s Hall stood out.
- Please keep narration of James’s inner state lighter. Temptation is welcome; repeatedly deciding that his hand reaches for his cards, or supplying specific memories, takes a little character ownership away from me.
- The prose was atmospheric, but often repeated the preceding turn or explained a successful roll twice. Shorter responses after straightforward actions would give me more time to play.

Overall: strong characters, an engaging opening, and satisfying room for kindness and caution. I’d return for the dawn visit. My main requests are reliable mechanics, tighter narration, and a little more room to wonder whether my theory is wrong.

after.text:
Yes—when the man in the dove-grey coat left the Kettle. I wanted to follow him and find out where he went. But Harl was sitting opposite me, finally talking, with his coin out on the table. Leaving him then felt like abandoning someone I’d just persuaded to trust me. I chose Harl and had the cat watch the man’s departure instead. That was a good tension: I wanted both leads and couldn’t safely have both.

The frustrating version was the Persuasion reroll. I wanted to pause and correct the +2 modifier to +7 before rolling, but the interface wouldn’t accept my out-of-game message while the card was pending. I had to roll with a known error and hope it would be corrected afterward. That wasn’t a character choice; it was the interface blocking a necessary table conversation.

opening.text:
The bridge never quite stops moving. Carts creak over the stones, a fishwife bawls prices from a window overhead, and the Chionthar slaps at the piers below. After weeks on the road, Baldur's Gate is right in front of you: one wall, one narrow gate, and a line of tired people who all want to get through before full dark.

At the gate sits Sergeant Odessa Varn of the Flaming Fist, red cloak stained, ledger open. Her face says she has asked the same two questions a thousand times today. Up ahead, a tiefling father with two children has been waved out of the line to stand by the barrels, and he is holding his papers very tightly.

Off to your left a voice cuts through the noise, warm as mulled wine: "Three cards, friends, one queen! Find the lady, double your silver! The Lady's watching tonight, I can feel it!" Ferro Lask flicks the cards across his crate with a dealer's easy hands, and the sound of them is one you know very well.

The cat sits down on the cobbles, tail curled, and stares up at the gatepost. Someone has chalked a small coin there, a circle with a face in it, so fresh the dust hasn't settled.

The line shuffles forward. Varn glances up from her ledger, past the man in front of you, and finds you.

"Next. Name, and what's your business in the Gate?"

The session begins.

The sun drops behind the masts downriver, and Wyrm's Crossing fills with lantern light and the smell of frying fish. The bridge is less a road than a street built on stone. Shutters bang, a fishwife haggles over the last eels, and a porter swears at a mule that will not move. At the far end a barrier of rough planks blocks the way, painted with the Flaming Fist's red gauntlet. Behind it a broad-shouldered sergeant with ink on her fingers works through the queue. She asks each traveller the same question, takes their coppers, scratches a line in a ledger and waves them on.

The cat walks the parapet beside you as if it owns the bridge. At the barrier post it stops and sniffs a chalk mark on the stone. The mark is fresh, not yet smudged by rain or boots, and it is Tymora's coin-sign, face up. Nobody in the queue looks at it.

Just past the barrier, under a hanging lantern, a gnome in a patched velvet coat shuffles a deck with practised fingers on an upturned crate. "One hand, friends, just one, Lady Luck's awake tonight!" The cards whisper as they fall.

The merchant ahead of you pays and steps through. The sergeant dips her pen, looks up and fixes you with a tired, measuring stare. "Next. Name, and what's your business in the Gate?"

Your fingers find no coppers. The purse holds only gold, so a single gold piece rings on the plank instead. The sergeant looks at it, then at you, and doesn't share your smile.

"Save that for the gnome." She sweeps the coin into a tin box, counts change back onto the plank without looking at it, nine silver and eight copper, and dips her pen. "Toll's two copper. Worgen. W-O-R?"

You spell it. She writes in a square, plain hand, and you read it upside down: *Worgen, James. Human. Tethyr, ex-soldier. On foot. One cat.* She really did write the cat. The column above is all names and ticks, dozens of them, and she writes fast enough that nothing else on the page stands out.

"Work." She keeps writing. "The Fist's hiring. Pay's three months late, so the Fist is always hiring. Recruiting table's at the Seatower, mornings. Caravan masters want men with papers, they hire at the Friendly Arm, a day south. Docks pay day rates, if you don't mind a Guild man taking a cut." She blots the line. "Bed. Mother Thessaly's, up the hill, second left past the cooperage. Clean, cheap, and she won't rob you. Ask for the back room, it's quieter."

You glance down at the chalk coin by her post. When you look up, she's already following your eyes to it.

She looks at the mark a moment longer than she needs to. "Wasn't there at noon." She shuts the ledger halfway, over her thumb. "Temple brats draw those on the Lady's steps for luck. Not usually on mine." She looks at you again, more carefully this time, the way she might at a crate with a loose lid. Then her chin jerks toward the open road behind the barrier. "Go on. Next."

The cat hops down off the parapet and crosses into the Outer City ahead of you, tail up. It goes straight past the gnome's crate without a look. Behind you a porter starts arguing about his mule's toll.

As you step through, the cards stop whispering. "Soldier!" the gnome calls, bright as a bell, knuckles resting on his deck. "Steady hand, you said? Steady hands win. First hand's free for veterans of any queen you like!"

Over at the post the cat has its nose to the stone. What reaches you down the bond isn't words. It's a jumble of things it noticed: plain chalk, the cheap kind sold by the stick; a child's sweat; tallow; and underneath, something sharp and bitter, like horn left too close to a fire. Then the cat moves off, low and quick, through the legs of the queue, and drags the smell along behind it like a thread.

The landing is a shelf maybe 15 feet across, and the dark piers of the span rise around it. James can't tell whether the darker patches against the pier are shadow, weed or stonework. He tries for a full minute and the dark beats him. He can't make out any door or doorway from up here. There's something pale near the bottom step, low down at the waterline. James leaves the cat on the top step. It folds its paws under itself and turns its head toward the gap and the lantern light, away from the river. Down the bond comes something like a shrug. *Watching.*

He goes down slowly. The wall under his left palm is cold and slimy with river damp, and every step is worn hollow in the middle by years of feet. He puts his weight on the edge of each one before trusting it. Twice the stone gives a gritty slide under his heel, and twice he holds still until it settles. The boots don't make a sound. On the last step the bridge lanterns still reach, he stops and breathes. The river sucks at the piers. Downstream the slow, uneven knock goes on. Nothing else moves.

The coin is warm from his skin when he draws it out. He closes his fist around it and speaks the word under his breath. Light swells inside his hand, turning his knuckles red at the edges, and one thin blade of it slips out between two curled fingers. He tilts it down at the steps and follows it.

At the bottom the pale thing turns into what it looked like: a torn scrap of coarse grey wool, about the size of his palm. It's snagged on a rough corner of the lowest step, just above where the water slaps up and runs back. It isn't a shawl, only a piece torn off one, with loose threads still hanging from the tear. He crouches without touching it, and even from a foot away he catches a faint, greasy smell of tallow and, under that, something bitter and scorched. It's the same smell the cat dragged him here by.

There's more on that step, right at the waterline. Someone drew a chalk circle on the stone, and the river has been licking at it for a long time. Half of it has washed away to a ghost. The half that's left still shows the shape clearly: Tymora's coin-sign, the same one that was on the sergeant's post. This one has been drawn the other way up, face down. Under his thin light the chalk looks old. It's been wetted and dried and wetted again, and it's weeks old, not hours.

He lets the light creep a little wider, low over the landing, keeping it away from the open water.

Bit by bit his slow sweep of the light picks the landing out of the dark.

The weed on the stone shelf has been trodden. A wide strip of it runs from the water's edge toward the pier, bruised flat and dark, and that comes from many feet over many nights, not one. Closer in, it's been torn fresh in two places, with pale green showing where a heel skidded on it. Those were small feet, as small as a child's.

At the very lip of the landing an iron mooring ring is set into the stone, crusted orange with rust everywhere except one side. The lane is dark between the leaning houses. A few doors short of the lamp, James lets the Mask go. Nothing shows from outside. The weight of the broken nose and the grey beard simply goes, and the face under the hood is his own again: thirty-four, tired, and rough with a day's stubble. He pushes the hood back, and the night air is cold on his ears.

Down the hill the barrier lamp is a smudge of yellow at the end of the street. The chalk coin can't be seen from here.

*I saw. Face up all night. Somebody wants me to know she's watching. Or someone is using her sign and wants me to think so.*

The cat sits on the scrubbed step, tail around its feet, and takes a while to answer. When it does, the answer isn't about the goddess.

*Chalk smelled of the stair.* After a moment: *Same hands.*

Then it turns its face back to the bell-pull as if that settles it.

James gives the cord one short tug. Somewhere deep in the house a small bell goes *tink* once and stops. He steps back off the step onto the cobbles, hands open at his sides, so the lamp in the niche shows him, his empty palms and the cat, and nothing else.

Nothing happens for long enough that the lane's cold starts to creep in. Then a board creaks overhead. A light moves behind a shutter on the first floor, and someone comes down the stairs in no hurry. At eye height in the door a small square grille slides open. Behind it are an eye, part of a lamp, and a grey plait over a shoulder.

The eye looks at his hands first. Then at his face. Then down at the cat, for a good while.

James gives his piece in a low voice: the hour, Sergeant Marsh, clean and cheap and won't rob you, the back room, his name, no dice and no drink, four nights paid ahead, a cat that's house-trained and better company than he is.

The grille stays open while she thinks it over.

"Marsh," the woman behind it says. Her voice is dry and sounds older than the step. "Marsh sends me maybe one a month. The ones she thinks won't be trouble." There's a pause. "She's wrong about one in three."

Bolts slide, two of them, then a bar. The door opens a foot and stops on a chain. Mother Thessaly is a short, square woman of sixty or more in a brown wool wrapper. Her grey plait is as thick as a ship's line, and she holds a lamp in one hand and, quite frankly, a rolling pin in the other. She looks James over again now that there's no grille between them. She takes in the regimental cloak, the boots, and the smell of river and eel fat coming off him.

"You've been on the bridge." It isn't a question. "Smells like the Knotted Eel. Nobody goes to the Eel sober and comes out sober." She sniffs. "You don't smell drunk, though. Mm."

Her eyes drop to the cat.

"Does he do mice?"

The cat looks up at her and blinks slowly, like a lord who has been asked whether he does stairs.

"Four silver a night for the back room. Bread and something hot in the morning, if you're up when I'm up, and I'm up at first light. Cat's free if he does mice. If he doesn't, he's a silver a night and you clean up after him." The chain comes off. "Four nights, sixteen silver. Ahead."

James counts two gold pieces into her palm. She weighs them in her hand without looking, then bites one, which is plainly a habit rather than suspicion, and sets the rolling pin down on a shelf by the door to count four silver back into his hand.

The hall is narrow and smells of lye soap and bread dough set to rise for the morning. A stair goes up steeply on the left. She takes him past it, down three steps and along a short passage to a door at the very back of the house, unlocks it and hands him the key on a loop of string.

The back room is small and clean, just as Marsh promised. A bed with a straw tick and two blankets. A washstand and jug. A peg for the cloak. One window, shuttered, giving onto a yard with a woodpile and a well, with the backs of other houses close beyond it. No window on the lane. It's quiet. The noise of the Outer City gets this far back only as a low murmur.

The cat walks in ahead of him, checks all four corners and the space under the bed, and jumps onto the blanket at the foot.

Mother Thessaly stays in the doorway with the lamp.

"Bolt on the inside. Privy in the yard. No callers after dark, and no callers in the room at any hour." She stops there, and something passes across her face that isn't about rules. "I like a man who pays ahead. Last one who took this room paid a month and stayed nine days. Went out one evening and never came back for the rest of it." She shrugs her heavy shoulders. "I kept his bag. Somebody'll come for it, I thought. Nobody has."

She doesn't wait for a reply. The lamp goes back down the passage, the three steps creak, and somewhere up the stair a door closes.

In the yard the well-rope taps once against its post in the breeze. The cat has its eyes shut, but its ears are pointed at the door.

The bolt is a good iron bar that slides home with a solid knock. James pulls on the door once and it doesn't give.

He opens the shutter a finger's width onto cold air that smells of woodsmoke and the privy. There's barely any moon, but he can make out the yard: a woodpile under a lean-to of old planks, the well with its rope looped over the post, and the privy in the far corner. A low wall at the back has a plank gate in it that opens onto an alley. The back of the next house is about 20 feet away, and it has two windows on this side. The lower one has a rag stuffed in a broken pane. The upper one looks straight across at his. Its shutters are closed but warped, and a dark gap runs down the middle where they don't meet. No light shows in either window, and nothing in the yard moves except the well-rope, which knocks against its post once in the wind.

He latches the shutter, hangs the cloak on its peg, and puts the rod and the coin under the pillow. The crossbow goes against the bedframe, loaded, where his hand will find it.

By the coin's light the scrap of wool on his knee doesn't look like much: coarse grey yarn, loosely woven, with a frayed edge where it tore. It's small enough to have come off a child's shawl. Up close the tallow-and-horn smell is still there.

*Same hands…*

The cat lifts its head off the blanket while he's still sending. Its answer comes slowly, like it's picking out each word. *Sweat was afraid.* After a moment: *Drawn for you. Not for the Fist.* Then it tucks its nose back under its tail. That's all it can tell him, and it clearly doesn't intend to say more about it.

He folds the wool away and puts out the light. *Sleep on the blanket, not under it.*

*On,* the cat agrees.

Nothing wakes him. Once, deep in the night, he half-surfaces at a dog barking two streets away, feels the cat's attention prick up and settle again, and goes back under. The house creaks as it cools. The well-rope knocks a few more times and then stops.

He wakes at first light. Grey seeps through the cracks in the shutter, and the room smells of baking bread. Somewhere on the other side of the house an oven door clanks, a pan scrapes on stone, and Mother Thessaly's heavy, steady step goes back and forth across a kitchen floor. She's up, as she said she would be.

The cat isn't on the blanket. It's sitting on the narrow windowsill with its back to the room, its nose almost touching the latched shutter. It doesn't look round when he stirs. It's looking at the shutter like there's something on the other side it wants him to see.

*(Out of game: first light is about half past five, so James slept a bit over three hours. By the rules that isn't a long rest, which needs eight. He hasn't spent anything yet, so it costs him nothing now. If you'd rather he slept the full eight hours, it would be about ten in the morning and he'd miss Thessaly's breakfast. Tell me and I'll change it.)*

1. **Bolting and testing the door:** James slid the iron bolt home and pulled on the door once. It held.
2. **Looking over the yard:** he saw the woodpile, the well, the privy, the gate in the back wall, and two windows in the next house's back wall, 20 feet away. The upper one has warped shutters and looks straight across at his room, and both were dark. Nobody was moving and nothing was hidden, so there was nothing to roll for. His passive Perception covered it.
3. **Cloak:** it's hanging on its peg.
4. **Rod, coin and crossbow:** the rod and the coin are under the pillow, and the crossbow is loaded against the bedframe, where his hand falls.

James leaves the crossbow where it is and takes the coin from under the pillow. He closes it in his left fist without lighting it. The floorboards are cold under his bare feet. He crosses the room the way he would cross a tent in a camp he didn't trust, heels down, slowly, and stops beside the window with his shoulder to the wall.

*What is it?*

The cat doesn't turn its head. The answer takes a while, and it's flat and certain, the way it is when the cat has made up its mind about something. *Outside. Ash.* Then: *Old. Before you.*

James puts his eye to the crack between the shutter and the frame.

The yard is grey and empty in the first light. The woodpile sits under its lean-to with a hatchet left in the chopping block. The well-rope hangs still, and the night's wind has dropped. The privy door is shut. The plank gate in the back wall is closed, and its latch is down. Nothing has been dropped on the ground under the window, and the hard earth has no fresh marks on it, only the old ruts of someone carrying wood. A sparrow lands on the wall, looks at nothing and flies off again.

Across the yard the upper window of the next house is just as it was in the night. The shutters are closed and warped, with a black gap down the middle. He watches that gap for a slow count of thirty. No light shows behind it and nothing moves. If anyone is standing back from it in the dark, he can't see them. Below it, the rag still plugs the broken pane, grey with old smoke.

Nothing living is out there except the sparrow, and it has gone.

He lifts the latch. The shutter swings out a hand's width on a dry hinge, and the cold morning comes in smelling of woodsmoke and the yard. The cat leans forward over the gap at once, its nose almost on the outside edge of the frame, its whiskers pushed forward.

James sees it as soon as the shutter moves.

It's on the outer face of the frame, low by the sill, at about the height of a child standing in the yard on tiptoe. Rain has washed most of it away, so it's more stain than chalk now, a pale ghost in the grain of the old green paint. The shape is still there: a circle, and inside it the Lady's coin-sign. It's drawn the other way up, the same way as the half-drowned mark on the lowest step under the bridge.

It's been there through a good many rains. It was weeks old before he ever took the room.

The cat breathes on it once and pulls back with its ears flat. Even from where he stands, with the cold air on his face, James catches it under the woodsmoke, faint and bitter: burnt horn.

On the other side of the house an oven door clanks open. Mother Thessaly's voice comes down the passage and the three steps, flat and unhurried, aimed at nobody in particular:

"Bread's out. Hot's on. I don't keep it warm."

I set a few coppers on the plank before she has to ask and give her an easy, road-tired smile.

"James Worgen. Late of Queen Zaranda's foot in Tethyr, lately of nowhere in particular." I nod at the cat on the parapet. "That's my business partner. He doesn't pay tolls, and he doesn't take advice."

I don't look at the gnome and his whispering cards. I keep my eyes on her ledger.

"Business? Honest work, if the Gate has any going. A bed, a hot meal, and somewhere a man with a steady hand and a soldier's papers might be useful." I tap the pay slip inside my coat without taking it out. "Where would a sergeant send someone like that, if she were feeling generous?"

As she writes, I glance down at the fresh chalk coin by her post, then back up to see whether she noticed me looking.

I stop a pace short of the crate, close enough to talk and too far to touch the cards, and hook my thumbs in my belt.

"Free's the most expensive price there is, friend. I gave up the game." It comes out lighter than it feels. I keep my eyes on his face, not his hands. "But I'll pay you for something else."

I set one of the silver pieces on the corner of the crate, well away from the deck.

"Someone drew the Lady's coin on the sergeant's post this afternoon. Fresh chalk, face up. You've been sitting under this lantern long enough to see who. Child, priest, anyone at all?"

While he answers, I send the cat a thought: *Go back to the post. Sniff the chalk and anything near it, then follow the trail if there is one. Not far.* I keep one eye on the gnome for the kind of tell I used to watch for across a table.

I give the gnome a two-finger salute off the brow, an old habit, and leave him to his deck.

"Keep the offer warm, friend. I won't be collecting."

I walk back along the bridge toward the cat. I don't hurry, so I look like a man who has forgotten something. At the net-mender's shack I step into the gap and crouch on the top step beside it, keeping the parapet at my shoulder. My right hand rests on the rod under my cloak, and the boots keep my steps silent.

*What is it?* I send down the bond. *Someone down there? Or just a smell you don't like?*

I don't go down yet. I look over the edge of the stair, let my eyes adjust to the dark below the span, and listen past the slap of the river. I want to know if anyone is moving, talking, or waiting on the landing, and whether there's a boat, a light, or a door in the stonework.
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

I don't like going down blind into a place the cat calls a dog's yard. I like standing on a bridge wondering even less.

*Stay up here and watch the gap behind me,* I send. *If anyone comes into it, tell me.*

I go down slowly, one hand on the wet wall and the other on the rod. The boots keep me quiet, and I test each step before I trust it. I stop on the last lit step and wait for a few breaths, listening.

Then I take the Lady's coin from under my collar, close my fist around it, and cast Light on it. I keep my fingers curled so only a thin blade of light leaks between them, enough to see the next few steps and not enough to be noticed from the river. I keep going down like that to the pale thing at the bottom step. I crouch and open my fingers just a little to see what it is, keeping the light low and pointed away from the water.

If it's cloth, I don't pick it up yet. I look for a grey shawl, chalk dust, burnt-horn residue, scuffs on the weed, anything at all.
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

I don't touch the smudge. Whatever leaves a scorched-horn stink on wood, I don't want on my skin.

First I pick the scrap of grey wool off the step by one loose thread, fold it into my handkerchief, and tuck it inside my coat. Somebody's grey shawl lost a piece here, and a child came down these steps today.

Then I close my fist tight on the coin so the light goes out, and stand in the dark beside the door. I lean in and put my ear to the planks above the hasp, not touching the smudge. I breathe slowly and listen for anything on the other side: voices, movement, water dripping, a draught through the cracks. I also check whether any light shows at the bottom edge or around the frame.

If it's silent, I open my fingers just enough to look at the padlock. I want to know whose work it is: cheap or dear, Fist issue, a smith's mark, anything scratched on it.

*Still clear up there?* I ask the cat.

I close my fist on the coin until the light is gone completely and go back up the stair in the dark. One hand on the wall, testing each step as I did coming down, quiet as the boots allow.

*Stay put,* I send. *Watch that shutter. If the door opens, or the light goes out, tell me.*

I stop three or four steps short of the top, where the parapet still hides me from the bridge and the shack wall is close enough to touch. There I crouch and listen. I want to hear what the net-mender is doing in there: talking to someone, working, moving about. Most of all I listen for whether they're heading for a door.

If it sounds like one person going about their evening, I'll climb the last steps and come out of the gap brushing off my knees, like a man who went down to the water for the usual reason and is a little embarrassed about it.
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

I let the porters pass, then step back to the shack's door, the one on the bridge side, not the stair, and knock twice like a customer, not the Fist.

When he opens it I show him an apologetic face and keep my hands where he can see them. The cat sits at my boot and looks harmless.

"Evening. Sorry to call so late. They told me at the barrier there's a net-mender here who might know about storage under the bridge." I nod vaguely downriver, as if *they* were anyone. "I've got a few crates coming up from the south. Nothing that stinks, nothing that burns, I swear on my mother. I need a dry floor for a week or two, and I'd pay better than whoever you've got in there now, if there's room."

I let the last part hang and watch his face, especially at *dry floor* and *whoever you've got in there now*. Then I give him the easy smile again.

"And if there's no room, I'll buy a length of good cord off you anyway for the trouble. A man can always use rope."

I let the smile go. It isn't doing any work, and he's earned better than a second lie.

"Nobody's been talking. That was a bad story and you caught it. Fair's fair." I keep my hands open at my sides and my voice low, below the bridge noise. "Truth is, I followed a smell down your stair. There's a piece of her shawl on the bottom step, and somebody tied a boat to your ring not long ago."

I nod at the door, not past him at the room.

"I heard you through the wall. Five coins, and a store that reeks like a tannery fire. I'm not Fist and I'm not Guild, and I don't want your money or your lease. I just want to know who's taking children down to the water in the dark." I let that sit a moment. "If they're the sort who'd do that, you already know they're not the sort who'll leave you be when it goes wrong. I'd rather it went wrong for them first."

I take two silver from my purse and hold them out, not pushing.

"For the cord you won't sell me. Who rents your store, friend? A name, a face, when they come. That's all."

[Onward]

I nod slowly and keep my voice as low as his.

"Nothing to your door tonight. I won't touch the lock, I won't leave a mark, and nobody will know I was down there except you and me." I glance at the bolt behind him, then back at his face. "You've got my word on that, for what a stranger's word is worth. I'd rather have them come back to a store that looks exactly as they left it."

I lean a shoulder on the wall beside the stove so I'm not crowding him.

"Few more questions, and then I'm gone. When did the thin man last pay you? When's he due again? How long has he had the store, since the first week with the lock? And when the boat comes after one, does anything go in or out? Crates, sacks, people?" I pause. "And the girl. When did you see her last, before today?"

I give him a short, tired smile, the honest kind this time.

"And your name, friend. If this goes bad, I'd like to know whose door to knock on to tell you so, before they do."

*To the cat:* *Go out the gap and sit somewhere high where you can see the stair and the water. Don't go down. If a boat comes, tell me.*

"Not on your stair," I agree. "Not in here. You won't see me again tonight, Gask, and neither will they."

I push off the wall and wait for him to draw the bolt. On the step I pause, half turned, and keep it low:

"If he comes early, or the girl comes up alone, don't do anything. Just be a man mending nets. That's the safest thing in the world to be."

Then I'm back on the bridge, hands in my pockets, a tired traveller who's finally found his bearings. I walk toward the Rock end, past the eel stalls where he last saw the girl, looking for somewhere I can sit for hours without anyone wondering why. A tavern or cookshop with a window or a bench on the downstream side would be best, somewhere I can see the open water below the span and the landing's side of the river. If I find one, I'll buy a bowl of whatever's hot and a small beer I'll make last, and sit with my back to the wall.

*Stay on the roof,* I send to the cat. *Rest if you like, but keep one ear on the water. When oars come, wake me. I want to see the boat, which way it comes from and which way it goes, and how many are in it. Nothing more.*

Before I settle in, I pull the hood of the grey cloak up and use the Mask to blunt my face a little. Ten years older, a broken nose, a beard going grey. Gask has seen my real face, and that's enough people for one night.

*(Out of game: if there's a decent spot, I'm happy to skip to about half past midnight. James eats, waits, and keeps quiet. If anything happens on the bridge before then that he'd notice, stop me there.)*

I take my bowl and beer over to the watermen's table. My eyes go to the jug, not to them, the way a lonely old soldier's do.

"Pardon. Couldn't help hearing." I keep my voice rough, to suit the broken nose. "Coin with a face on both sides. I knew a sergeant in Tethyr who carried one. Swore it was the Lady's own. Never lost a toss, and then one day he lost the lot." I set two silver on their table beside the jug. "Fill that on me, lads. Whose face was it, if the girl said? A woman's? And the dead one at the Seatower, Tuesday. Anybody know who he was, or where he drank?"

I listen for anything that ties back to a long-faced man with grey hands, a woman rowing at night, or a burnt-horn smell. Then I finish the beer, thank them, and go back out onto the bridge.

On the way back I find somewhere within range of the cat. Ideally that's the downriver parapet in the dark between two lanterns, about seventy or eighty feet from Gask's roof. I'll sit with my back against a pier post and my cloak around me like a drunk sleeping it off. If the parapet's too exposed, I'll take the porters' cookfire and sit facing the river side.

*I'm back,* I send once the bond comes clear. *Same orders. Oars, you wake me.*

I renew the Mask whenever the hour runs out.

Under the cloak I run my thumb along my jaw and renew the Mask now: same broken nose, same grey beard. I don't want it slipping while I'm away from my own eyes.

Then I let my head sag the last inch onto my arm, like a drunk finally losing the fight, and keep my fingers closed on the rod.

*Looking now,* I send. *Keep half an eye on the post for me.*

I go down the bond and into the cat's eyes, under the nets at the roof's edge. I stay still and quiet and just watch the landing below. I want to see how many there are, whether the hunched thing in the stern is a person, whether the girl is with them, who has the key, and what goes through that door.

I pull back up the bond, fast, and I'm back in my own skin: cold stone, cramped legs, the rod in my fist. I don't lift my head. I keep the drunk's slump and open my eyes a slit under the hood, turned toward the gap by Gask's shack 75 feet back.

*Freeze,* I send. *Be the roof. If his light finds you, be a cat and nothing more: hiss, then run up over the ridge and away along the bridge. Not toward me. Don't come to me.*

If he only looks and goes back down, I stay put and let him. If he knocks on Gask's door or starts forcing it, I'm getting up. I'll be a stumbling, loud drunk wandering his way, the kind of witness nobody wants to deal with at one in the morning. The rod stays ready under the cloak in case that isn't enough.

I keep coming, but I slow down about twenty feet short of him and stop there, swaying, one hand flat on the parapet. Close enough to be a nuisance, too far to grab. I squint at his thread of lantern light like it's the sun.

"Oi." It comes out loud and wet, loud enough to carry to the porters by the dead fire. "Oi, friend. Mother… Thessaly's. Second left past the… the barrel man." I wave vaguely uphill and nearly lose my balance. "Sergeant said. Clean, cheap, won't rob you. You know it? You look like a man who knows it."

I don't wait for an answer. I start in on the old Tethyrian marching song, the one about the quartermaster's daughter, off-key and too loud, and I lean my back against the parapet as though I mean to settle in right there in front of Gask's door for the night. That's one more drunk, two porters, and a whole bridge's worth of eyes he didn't plan on.

Under the cloak my fingers stay on the rod. Through the slit of my eyes I watch his hands, not his hood. If one goes inside the oilskin for steel, I'm not drunk anymore.

*Stay under the nets,* I send to the cat. *Don't move. Not for anything.*
