[Onward]

I finish the verse, let it trail off into a mumble, and stay slumped against the parapet for a good while longer, long enough for anyone watching from the water to lose interest in a drunk.

*Go to the head of the stair,* I send. *Low. Smell and listen down. Is anyone still on the landing? Did they leave anyone, or anything, behind the door?*

When the cat says it's clear, I get up the way a drunk does, grumbling, and stagger the few steps to Gask's door. I lean on the frame as if I need it to stand and knock twice, soft, the way he told me.

"It's the cord man," I say through the planks, barely above a breath. "Don't open if you'd rather not. Just tell me what he said to you. And did anything come out of that store tonight, or go in? The boat sat lower going away."

I keep my face turned toward the bridge, not the door, and my hand on the rod under the cloak.

*(Out of game: the log line says the Deception roll was "10 vs 15 — failure", but that was the first roll. The reroll came up 17 and the scene played as a success, so the log just needs correcting. That's one of my two rerolls spent this session, one left.)*

I lean my forehead against the planks beside the knothole and keep my voice down to a breath.

"Tell him the truth, near enough. The drunk did it. Old soldier, broken nose, grey beard, Tethyrian song. He came off the bridge last night to piss and sleep it off on your landing, and you heard him down there and ran him off with your stick. You don't know his name. He said something about Mother Thessaly's." I let that sit. "He's already seen that face, Gask. He'll believe it, because he wants an easy answer. And that face isn't mine. If he goes hunting for it, he'll find me, and I'll be ready for him."

I take ten gold from my purse by feel and slide the coins one by one through the gap under the door, where the planks don't meet the stone.

"That's for you, not for cord. If you've got a sister, a cousin, anyone this side of the river or the other, sleep there tomorrow night. Leave your lamp lit and your door bolted so it looks like you're in. If you'd rather stay, stay, and give him the drunk. Either way, I'll be on this bridge when the Rock rings one. You won't see me. He won't either."

I straighten up off the frame and drop the drunk back over my shoulders like a coat.

"Bolt it. Sleep if you can."

Then I push off and stagger away toward the city end, muttering, past the porters and into the dark between the lanterns.

*Come,* I send to the cat. *We're done here tonight. Mother Thessaly's. Back room. You can complain about the cold on the way.*

In the dark of the lane, a few doors short of the lamp, I let the Mask go. The broken nose and the grey beard fall away, and it's my own face under the hood again, tired and a day's stubble rough. I push the hood back too. The old drunk is the man I sent the oilskin to look for, and I sent him to this door. Mother Thessaly is going to meet somebody else.

I glance back once down the hill toward the barrier and the chalk coin, then look down at the cat.

*I saw,* I tell it. *Face up all night. Somebody wants me to know she's watching. Or someone is using her sign and wants me to think so.*

I give the bell-pull one short, gentle tug, the ring of a man who knows the hour and is sorry for it. Then I step back off the scrubbed step so whoever opens the door can see my hands and the cat, and nothing else.

When the door opens I keep my voice low:

"Forgive the hour. Sergeant Marsh at the Crossing said you're clean, cheap, and won't rob me, and that I should ask for the back room. James Worgen. No dice, no drink, I swear it. I'll pay for tonight and the next three, in advance, if the back room's free." I nod at the cat. "He's house-trained, and he's better company than I am."

*(Out of game: a small thing. The party line shows the cat at 8/8 HP, but my sheet gives the familiar 2 HP. Whichever you mean the cat to be is fine, I just wanted to flag it.)*

I bolt the door and try it once to be sure. Then I open the shutter a finger's width and look over the yard: the woodpile, the well, the backs of the houses, any window that looks straight into mine. I latch it again and hang the cloak on its peg. The rod and the coin go under the pillow, and the crossbow stays loaded against the bedframe, where my hand falls when I lie down.

I sit on the edge of the bed with the handkerchief open on my knee and look at the scrap of grey wool by the light of the coin. It's a child's shawl, smelling of tallow and burnt horn.

*Same hands,* I send to the cat. *The girl drew both, then. Face down on the landing weeks ago. Face up on the post today, right where I'd stop.* I turn the coin over in my fingers, the Lady's profile worn almost smooth. *A child marking the way in, or asking for help the only way she's allowed to. He holds her by the neck, Gask said.*

I fold the wool away and put out the light.

*Sleep on the blanket, not under it. If anything touches that door, the shutter, or the yard, wake me.*

Lying back, I go over the morning in my head. First, ask Thessaly over the bread about the lodger who never came back, what he looked like and what's in his bag, without seeming too eager. Then Tolliver's on Chandlers' Row: who buys a lock that good for a net-store under a bridge. Then maybe Nessa and the Water Queen's House, about a coin with the Lady weeping on one side and laughing on the other. And be back on the bridge before the Rock rings one.

I close my eyes and let a soldier's sleep take me, the kind that wakes at a footstep.

*(Out of game: a long rest, please, until first light or whenever Thessaly's morning bell goes, unless something interrupts.)*

I keep the three hours and let the long rest wait. I'd rather have Thessaly's bread and her gossip than four more hours on straw. I can sleep this afternoon, before the bridge.

I get up slowly and keep quiet, out of habit. My hand goes to the crossbow first and leaves it where it is. Then I take the coin from under the pillow and close it in my left fist. I don't light it.

*What is it?* I send, and cross to the window on bare feet. I stand to one side of the shutter, not in front of it, the way you stand beside a door you're not sure about.

I don't open it yet. First I put my eye to the crack between shutter and frame and look out at the yard in the grey light. I check the sill outside, the ground under the window, the woodpile, the gate in the back wall, and above all the warped upper shutters across the way.

If there's nothing living out there, I lift the latch and open the shutter a hand's width to see what the cat's nose has found.

*(Out of game: three hours is fine, no change needed. James has spent nothing yet, and I'll look for a proper long rest during the day.)*

**Player's note: Session 1, James Worgen**

**What worked**

- **The opening.** It was a strong hook with no quest attached. A fresh chalk coin on a Fist post, a gnome with cards right past the barrier, and a sergeant who writes down the cat. Within five minutes I had a temptation, a mystery and a tone. Using the cards temptation lightly, through Pell, was right. It never felt like a nag.
- **The NPCs.** Each had a voice and their own concerns. Gask was the best: frightened, stubborn, counting coins aloud, trying out phrases like "man mending nets." Marsh, Thessaly with the rolling pin, and Hob and Jory all felt like people with lives that didn't revolve around me. Thessaly's line about one Marsh-referral in three being trouble was perfect.
- **Consequences.** The failed Deception on Gask's doorstep changed the scene for the better. I had to switch to the truth, and that earned more than the lie would have. The oilskin man noticing the disturbed landing and promising to come back "tomorrow night" made my snooping cost something. The world moved without me.
- **Clues.** The trail built well: the burnt-horn smell, the Tolliver lock, the face-down and face-up marks, the dead-smell leaving in the boat. The drowned-men rumour arrived naturally over beer and tied loosely to the Lady's coin. The last reveal, an old face-down mark on *my* window frame from before I arrived, was a great closing beat.
- **The cat.** Terse telepathy ("Cold." "Warm room. Yes.") gave it personality without making it a talking sidekick. Hints like "same hands" and "drawn for you" make me curious what it really is.
- **Honest table management.** Flagging the 100-foot familiar range, the short rest, and the Mask's duration before they bit me was exactly right. "Show the threat before it lands" applied to rules too.

**What broke**

- **Skill modifiers on cards.** Deception and Persuasion came up as +2 instead of +7 at least four times, including after you said it was fixed. Every time I had to check the arithmetic myself, which pulls me out of the scene. Once it was fixed (the drunk act on the bridge) it was correct.
- **Log lines.** The reroll was logged as "10 vs 15 — failure" although the 17 stood. The scrap of wool was briefly logged as "In the camp." The cat started at 8/8 HP and AC 10 against a sheet of 2 HP and AC 12.
- **Sheet mismatches I noticed but didn't raise.** Healing Light is "up to 5 dice" on my sheet but "up to 4" in the records. The rapier is +5 in the files but +2 in the records. These need one source of truth before they matter in a fight.
- **My "?" question was swallowed** ("Nothing was sent: the turn waits for the card"). Out-of-game questions should go through even when a roll is pending, especially when the question is about that roll.
- **Duplicated narration.** After the failed Insight, the scene was told softly and then retold plainly in an out-of-game block. Once, said straight, is enough. The same goes for the long out-of-game notes justifying why things didn't need rolls. I didn't ask, and a single line would do.

**What was missing**

- **More of Tymora herself.** The coin warmed, but the patron's presence was mostly implied. Even a small sensation at the moment of the reroll would have helped.
- **A few more rolls, judged in my favour.** Several rolls felt like DC 15 for things a scout-trained veteran might just do. That's not a big complaint, but the dice drove a lot of the night.
- **No combat yet,** so I can't judge that side. Tomorrow at one bell looks like it will test it.

I'd play the next session. The hook is set, and I care about the girl and about Gask.

Yes, a few. One mattered most.

**At Gask's door, when the oilskin man was twenty feet away.** I could see his grey hands on the lantern shutter, and a moment earlier someone in the stern had coughed and been muffled. Everything in me wanted to drop the drunk act. I'd have cast Suggestion, *"Show me what's in your boat"* or *"Walk away from this door and forget it,"* or simply put Hex on him and opened up with Eldritch Blast. I had both slots, full hit points and a clear line.

I held back for three reasons:
- **The girl might have been in that boat.** I couldn't confirm it because the cat got dazzled. Starting a fight in the dark with an unseen rower and maybe a child within arm's reach of a man I knew nothing about felt like gambling with her life, not mine.
- **I didn't know what he was.** Grey hands, burnt horn, something dead dragged out of the store. That could be a cultist, a necromancer, or something worse. The table rule is to show deadly threats ahead of time, and I hadn't seen enough to know whether this was one.
- **Gask.** I'd promised him no trouble on his doorstep. A blast at his door would have made him the obvious target the moment I left.

I still think it was the right call, but it gnawed at me. Letting that boat row off downstream felt like folding a decent hand.

**Following the boat** was the second. I wanted to track it toward the harbour, but I had no way onto the water, and the cat can't leave my range. I never asked whether a waterman would take me out at that hour, or whether the cat could shadow it along the quays. That's on me. Next time I'll ask.

**Opening the store** was the third. I wanted badly to see behind that Tolliver lock. I have no thieves' tools, and I'd promised to leave no mark, so I didn't even look for a way in. In hindsight, the cat might have fit through a gap I never checked for.

**And yes, Pell's table.** James walked past it. I wanted him to sit down for one hand, just to feel how much it still pulled. I kept him moving because that felt true to the ban, but it was a real itch, and I'd like the game to keep pressing on it.

turns.message:
I set a few coppers on the plank before she has to ask and give her an easy, road-tired smile.

"James Worgen. Late of Queen Zaranda's foot in Tethyr, lately of nowhere in particular." I nod at the cat on the parapet. "That's my business partner. He doesn't pay tolls, and he doesn't take advice."

I don't look at the gnome and his whispering cards. I keep my eyes on her ledger.

"Business? Honest work, if the Gate has any going. A bed, a hot meal, and somewhere a man with a steady hand and a soldier's papers might be useful." I tap the pay slip inside my coat without taking it out. "Where would a sergeant send someone like that, if she were feeling generous?"

As she writes, I glance down at the fresh chalk coin by her post, then back up to see whether she noticed me looking.
turns.reply:
Your fingers find no coppers. The purse holds only gold, so a single gold piece rings on the plank instead. The sergeant looks at it, then at you, and doesn't share your smile.

"Save that for the gnome." She sweeps the coin into a tin box, counts change back onto the plank without looking at it, nine silver and eight copper, and dips her pen. "Toll's two copper. Worgen. W-O-R?"

You spell it. She writes in a square, plain hand, and you read it upside down: *Worgen, James. Human. Tethyr, ex-soldier. On foot. One cat.* She really did write the cat. The column above is all names and ticks, dozens of them, and she writes fast enough that nothing else on the page stands out.

"Work." She keeps writing. "The Fist's hiring. Pay's three months late, so the Fist is always hiring. Recruiting table's at the Seatower, mornings. Caravan masters want men with papers, they hire at the Friendly Arm, a day south. Docks pay day rates, if you don't mind a Guild man taking a cut." She blots the line. "Bed. Mother Thessaly's, up the hill, second left past the cooperage. Clean, cheap, and she won't rob you. Ask for the back room, it's quieter."

You glance down at the chalk coin by her post. When you look up, she's already following your eyes to it.

She looks at the mark a moment longer than she needs to. "Wasn't there at noon." She shuts the ledger halfway, over her thumb. "Temple brats draw those on the Lady's steps for luck. Not usually on mine." She looks at you again, more carefully this time, the way she might at a crate with a loose lid. Then her chin jerks toward the open road behind the barrier. "Go on. Next."

The cat hops down off the parapet and crosses into the Outer City ahead of you, tail up. It goes straight past the gnome's crate without a look. Behind you a porter starts arguing about his mule's toll.

As you step through, the cards stop whispering. "Soldier!" the gnome calls, bright as a bell, knuckles resting on his deck. "Steady hand, you said? Steady hands win. First hand's free for veterans of any queen you like!"

*(Out of game: the state shows only gold in your purse, no coppers, so I had you put down a gold piece and get change. If you'd sooner have paid some other way, tell me and we'll fix it.)*

turns.message:
I stop a pace short of the crate, close enough to talk and too far to touch the cards, and hook my thumbs in my belt.

"Free's the most expensive price there is, friend. I gave up the game." It comes out lighter than it feels. I keep my eyes on his face, not his hands. "But I'll pay you for something else."

I set one of the silver pieces on the corner of the crate, well away from the deck.

"Someone drew the Lady's coin on the sergeant's post this afternoon. Fresh chalk, face up. You've been sitting under this lantern long enough to see who. Child, priest, anyone at all?"

While he answers, I send the cat a thought: *Go back to the post. Sniff the chalk and anything near it, then follow the trail if there is one. Not far.* I keep one eye on the gnome for the kind of tell I used to watch for across a table.
turns.reply:
James stops 3 feet short of the crate. Pell Tumblewick watches the silver land on the corner. For a moment the bright patter stops, and the gnome looks at the coin the way a man looks at a dog he hasn't met.

"Gave up the game." He says it back slowly and squares the deck with two taps against the crate. "Well. The Lady's lost a good one, then, or found one. Hard to tell which, some nights." He doesn't reach for the silver yet. "The post. Sure, I saw. Afternoon, after the Fist changed shifts and before the fish-sellers came up. A kid. Grey shawl, too big for her, pulled up like an old woman's. She walked up to the post like she was waiting in line, crouched to fix her shoe, and when she stood up there it was." He shrugs, and his fingers start the deck moving again. "Temple brats do that. Luck-marks. Sergeant said so herself, didn't she? I heard her."

While he talks, you reach for the thread that ties you to the cat. It's already gone, a pale shape sliding back along the parapet toward the barrier. You feel it get there and drop its nose to the stone.

You watch his face the way you used to watch a man across a table with a week's pay in the pot. You see a hustler who has just lost a mark and is trying to hide that it stings. His eyes go back to your silver twice, his mouth keeps the shape of a smile out of habit, and the deck never stops moving. Nothing else stands out. If there's anything under it, you can't see it tonight.

"Off she went," Pell says, and sweeps the silver into his coat without fuss. "Back onto the bridge, I think. I had a customer. A cooper, terrible player, wonderful loser." The bright bell comes back into his voice. "Offer stands, soldier. Any night. The Lady likes a man who comes back."

Over at the post the cat has its nose to the stone. What reaches you down the bond isn't words. It's a jumble of things it noticed: plain chalk, the cheap kind sold by the stick; a child's sweat; tallow; and underneath, something sharp and bitter, like horn left too close to a fire. Then the cat moves off, low and quick, through the legs of the queue, and drags the smell along behind it like a thread.

The trail doesn't go uphill toward the city or the temples. It runs back along the last few houses of the bridge to a gap between a net-mender's shack and the parapet. There a narrow stone stair drops toward the river, to a water-landing below the span, and the bitter-horn smell goes down it. The cat stops on the top step, about 60 feet from you, tail curled tight around its feet. It doesn't go down. It looks back up the bridge, straight at you.

Below it the Chionthar slaps against the pilings in the dark.

 *(Out of game: I wrote that outcome too softly, so here it is plainly.)*

You couldn't read Pell Tumblewick. You watched his face for the whole exchange and got nothing past what any gnome hustler would show you. Whether he told you everything or left something out, you can't say. On this one the gnome beat you, and you know it. Across a table, that would have cost you the pot.

turns.message:
I give the gnome a two-finger salute off the brow, an old habit, and leave him to his deck.

"Keep the offer warm, friend. I won't be collecting."

I walk back along the bridge toward the cat. I don't hurry, so I look like a man who has forgotten something. At the net-mender's shack I step into the gap and crouch on the top step beside it, keeping the parapet at my shoulder. My right hand rests on the rod under my cloak, and the boots keep my steps silent.

*What is it?* I send down the bond. *Someone down there? Or just a smell you don't like?*

I don't go down yet. I look over the edge of the stair, let my eyes adjust to the dark below the span, and listen past the slap of the river. I want to know if anyone is moving, talking, or waiting on the landing, and whether there's a boat, a light, or a door in the stonework.
turns.reply:
James touches two fingers to his brow. Pell answers with a flick of a card, and the bright patter has started again before James has gone three steps. "One hand, friends, just one…"

The walk back along the bridge takes no effort. James looks like any tired traveller who has left something at the barrier: a glance at the queue, a pat at a pocket. The boots make no sound on the stones. The net-mender's shack leans against the parapet, its shutters closed and nets hung on pegs to dry, stiff with salt and smelling of tar. The gap beside it is barely wide enough for a man's shoulders. James steps in and crouches beside the cat on the top step, parapet at his shoulder, his hand closed on the rod under his cloak.

The cat doesn't look at him. Its answer down the bond isn't words. The bitter smell runs down the steps and stops at the water. It isn't new. Under today's trail lie older ones, faint, laid on top of each other like footprints on a path people use. Some of it comes from more than one person. There's a flat, settled wariness too, the feeling a cat has about a dog's yard. *Not now. Before. Often.*

James lets his eyes adjust to the dark and looks down past the edge of the stair.

The lantern light from the bridge stops a few steps down. Below it the stair is just slick grey edges, about twenty of them, dropping into a black stretch of wet stone. The landing is a shelf maybe 15 feet across, and the dark piers of the span rise around it. James can't tell whether the darker patches against the pier are shadow, weed or stonework. He tries for a full minute and the dark beats him. He can't make out any door or doorway from up here. There's something pale near the bottom step, low down at the waterline. It could be a scrap of sail, foam, or something else. From up here it won't come into focus.

He can make out what he hears, at least. Nobody is talking below. There's no light, no lantern hooded or bare, and no creak of a hull rubbing against stone. The only sound is the Chionthar, slapping and sucking at the pilings, and some way downstream an oar, or a loose board, knocking at slow, uneven intervals. It could be anyone on the river at this hour.

Above him on the bridge the queue moves along. Someone laughs. Nobody comes into the gap.

The cat's tail ticks once against the stone. It stays where it is.

*(Out of game: you couldn't make out the landing in this light. You'd need to go down, make light, or get closer some other way. No one seems to be there right now, as far as you can hear.)*

turns.message:
I don't like going down blind into a place the cat calls a dog's yard. I like standing on a bridge wondering even less.

*Stay up here and watch the gap behind me,* I send. *If anyone comes into it, tell me.*

I go down slowly, one hand on the wet wall and the other on the rod. The boots keep me quiet, and I test each step before I trust it. I stop on the last lit step and wait for a few breaths, listening.

Then I take the Lady's coin from under my collar, close my fist around it, and cast Light on it. I keep my fingers curled so only a thin blade of light leaks between them, enough to see the next few steps and not enough to be noticed from the river. I keep going down like that to the pale thing at the bottom step. I crouch and open my fingers just a little to see what it is, keeping the light low and pointed away from the water.

If it's cloth, I don't pick it up yet. I look for a grey shawl, chalk dust, burnt-horn residue, scuffs on the weed, anything at all.
turns.reply:
James leaves the cat on the top step. It folds its paws under itself and turns its head toward the gap and the lantern light, away from the river. Down the bond comes something like a shrug. *Watching.*

He goes down slowly. The wall under his left palm is cold and slimy with river damp, and every step is worn hollow in the middle by years of feet. He puts his weight on the edge of each one before trusting it. Twice the stone gives a gritty slide under his heel, and twice he holds still until it settles. The boots don't make a sound. On the last step the bridge lanterns still reach, he stops and breathes. The river sucks at the piers. Downstream the slow, uneven knock goes on. Nothing else moves.

The coin is warm from his skin when he draws it out. He closes his fist around it and speaks the word under his breath. Light swells inside his hand, turning his knuckles red at the edges, and one thin blade of it slips out between two curled fingers. He tilts it down at the steps and follows it.

At the bottom the pale thing turns into what it looked like: a torn scrap of coarse grey wool, about the size of his palm. It's snagged on a rough corner of the lowest step, just above where the water slaps up and runs back. It isn't a shawl, only a piece torn off one, with loose threads still hanging from the tear. He crouches without touching it, and even from a foot away he catches a faint, greasy smell of tallow and, under that, something bitter and scorched. It's the same smell the cat dragged him here by.

There's more on that step, right at the waterline. Someone drew a chalk circle on the stone, and the river has been licking at it for a long time. Half of it has washed away to a ghost. The half that's left still shows the shape clearly: Tymora's coin-sign, the same one that was on the sergeant's post. This one has been drawn the other way up, face down. Under his thin light the chalk looks old. It's been wetted and dried and wetted again, and it's weeks old, not hours.

He lets the light creep a little wider, low over the landing, keeping it away from the open water.

Bit by bit his slow sweep of the light picks the landing out of the dark.

The weed on the stone shelf has been trodden. A wide strip of it runs from the water's edge toward the pier, bruised flat and dark, and that comes from many feet over many nights, not one. Closer in, it's been torn fresh in two places, with pale green showing where a heel skidded on it. Those were small feet, as small as a child's.

At the very lip of the landing an iron mooring ring is set into the stone, crusted orange with rust everywhere except one side. There the rust has been rubbed back to bright, raw metal in a fresh band, where a rope ran through it and pulled tight under load not long ago. Whatever boat tied up here has gone.

Then he sees the door. It's set into the foot of the nearest pier, low enough that a man would have to stoop. It's made of tarred planks, black with wet, and he took it for stonework from above. It has an iron hasp, and through the hasp hangs a heavy padlock, newer than the door by years. Around the hasp, where a hand would go to work the lock, there's a dark greasy smudge on the wood. When he brings the blade of light close, the bitter scorched smell is stronger there than anywhere else on the landing.

The river slaps the piers. Up at the top of the stair the cat's attention stays fixed on the gap, steady as a held breath. Nobody has come.

I don't touch the smudge. Whatever leaves a scorched-horn stink on wood, I don't want on my skin.

First I pick the scrap of grey wool off the step by one loose thread, fold it into my handkerchief, and tuck it inside my coat. Somebody's grey shawl lost a piece here, and a child came down these steps today.

Then I close my fist tight on the coin so the light goes out, and stand in the dark beside the door. I lean in and put my ear to the planks above the hasp, not touching the smudge. I breathe slowly and listen for anything on the other side: voices, movement, water dripping, a draught through the cracks. I also check whether any light shows at the bottom edge or around the frame.

If it's silent, I open my fingers just enough to look at the padlock. I want to know whose work it is: cheap or dear, Fist issue, a smith's mark, anything scratched on it.

*Still clear up there?* I ask the cat.
turns.reply:
James takes the scrap by one loose thread, the way you'd lift a dead mouse by the tail. The wool is coarse and damp from the spray, and it lets go of the stone with a small tug. He folds it into his handkerchief and tucks the bundle inside his coat. Even through the linen the tallow-and-scorch smell clings to his fingers for a moment before the river air takes it.

He closes his fist and the light goes out. The dark under the span is total for a few heartbeats. Then the faint glow from the bridge settles over the edges of things: the pale lip of the landing, the blacker black of the pier. He steps up beside the door, leans in and sets his ear to the planks a hand's width above the hasp. The tarred wood is cold and tacky against his cheek.

He breathes slowly and listens.

Nobody is inside. There are no voices and no breathing, and nothing shifts or settles the way it would if someone were holding still in there. Water drips somewhere behind the planks, steady and slow, onto stone. Air moves through the cracks around the frame. It's a thin, chill draught, which tells him the space behind the door is bigger than a cupboard, or opens onto something. It carries tar, old rope and wet hemp, a store of nets by the smell of it. Under all that, in a cold thread, comes the burnt horn again. There's no light at the bottom edge, around the frame or through the cracks. Whatever is in there sits in the dark.

He opens his fingers a crack and lets a sliver of light fall on the lock.

It's a good lock, too good for this door. The body is heavy, blackened iron as big as his palm, and the shackle is thick enough that bolt-cutters would struggle with it. It has been oiled recently. A sheen catches the light, and there's no rust in the keyway, though the door's own hasp is scabbed with it. It isn't Fist issue either. He's seen their locks on the barrier chest, and they're cheap stamped tin with the gauntlet punched in. This one has a maker's mark sunk into the base, small and clean: a key crossed over an anchor, and around it the letters *TOLLIVER · CHANDLERS' ROW*. Someone in the Lower City made it and sold it for real money.

There's one more thing. Around the keyhole, on the face where a thumb steadies the lock while the key turns, the iron is dulled by the same dark greasy film as the hasp. The smudge is thinner here, worn into the metal by more than one opening.

*Still clear up there?*

The answer comes back almost before he's finished asking: *Gap empty.* Then it stops and corrects itself. Through the cat's eyes he sees what it's looking at. It's the net-mender's shack, right beside the top of the stair. A minute ago its shutters were dark. Now a line of yellow lamplight shows along the bottom of one of them, and a shadow crosses it, then crosses back. Someone is home, moving about inside, less than an arm's length of wall from the head of the stair.

The cat's tail has stopped ticking.

With the listening, there was nothing to miss. The store behind the door is empty and silent apart from the drip and the draught, so a roll couldn't have turned up anything more, and you heard exactly what's there. As for the padlock, reading a stamped maker's mark and seeing that a lock is good and freshly oiled is plain looking with light on it, not uncertain work. If you think one of these should have been a check, say so and I'll roll it.)*

I close my fist on the coin until the light is gone completely and go back up the stair in the dark. One hand on the wall, testing each step as I did coming down, quiet as the boots allow.

*Stay put,* I send. *Watch that shutter. If the door opens, or the light goes out, tell me.*

I stop three or four steps short of the top, where the parapet still hides me from the bridge and the shack wall is close enough to touch. There I crouch and listen. I want to hear what the net-mender is doing in there: talking to someone, working, moving about. Most of all I listen for whether they're heading for a door.

If it sounds like one person going about their evening, I'll climb the last steps and come out of the gap brushing off my knees, like a man who went down to the water for the usual reason and is a little embarrassed about it.
turns.reply:
James closes his fist until the last red edge of light around his knuckles goes out. The coin goes cold and dark against his palm, and he tucks it back under his collar.

*Watching,* the cat sends. Its attention stays fixed on the line of lamplight under the shutter.

He starts up with his left hand on the slimy wall, putting his weight on the edge of each worn step before he trusts it. In the dark the stair is only cold stone under his boots and the river's breath on the back of his neck. A few steps up, his heel finds the same gritty patch that slid on the way down.

He feels the grit shift and lifts his foot before it can skid, then puts it down again a hand's width to the left on clean stone. The climb makes no sound at all, not a scrape, not a breath he didn't choose to take. Three steps short of the top he stops. The parapet rises to his right, and on his left the shack's wall is close enough to touch, rough boards furred with salt. He crouches and listens.

It's one person. The boards creak under a slow, heavy walk, a man's weight, with a drag to one foot. A kettle or pot goes down hard on iron. Wood scrapes as a stool is pulled out. Then comes a small, dry chinking, coins counted onto a table one at a time and then counted again. The man mutters to himself, the way people do when they've lived alone a long time and stopped noticing they talk aloud:

"…four, five. Five." There's a pause and a grunt. "Five, and the whole store reeks like a tannery fire. Dry floor, they said. Dry floor." The coins go back into something cloth with a soft clink. "Not my business. Not my business what they keep."

The stool creaks as he sits. The footsteps don't come toward a door. After a moment there's the slow, steady rasp of twine being drawn through mesh, a man getting on with a net.

*Shutter,* the cat sends. *Still lit. Nobody coming.*

James climbs the last three steps and comes out of the gap brushing at his knees, his face set in the sheepish look of a man who went down to the river for the usual reason. Nobody on the bridge turns. A pair of porters goes by arguing over a wager, the fishwife is folding up her stall, and down at the barrier the queue has thinned to a wagon and two men on foot. Pell's patter drifts up from beyond them, bright and tireless. The cat drops off the top step and falls in at James's heel as if it had been there the whole time.

Behind him the twine rasps on through the mesh, unhurried. The shutter's line of yellow light stays where it was.

James waits for the porters to go by, still arguing about their wager. Then he steps around the corner of the shack to the door on the bridge side. It's a plain plank door with a scrap of net nailed over a knothole, and the line of lamplight shows under it. He knocks twice, unhurried, the way a man knocks when he wants something.

Inside, the twine stops. The stool scrapes back, and a heavy, uneven step comes across the floor, one foot set down and the other dragged after it. There's a pause long enough for someone to decide whether to answer. A bolt slides, and the door opens a hand's width, then a little wider.

The net-mender fills the gap. He's a big man gone soft in his fifties, with a grey stubble beard and a leather apron shiny from twine. A mending needle is still pinched in one fist. He looks at James's hands first, then his face, then down at the cat sitting at his boot looking as if it had never had a thought in its life. The man keeps his weight on his good leg, and the hand that isn't holding the needle stays on the edge of the door.

James gives him the apologetic face and makes his pitch: the barrier, the crates from the south, nothing that stinks or burns, a dry floor for a week or two, better money than whoever he's got in there now.

The net-mender's face changes at *dry floor*. It doesn't harden. It goes slack for a breath, the way a man's face does when he hears his own words come back to him from outside his own walls. His eyes flick past James's shoulder toward the gap and the stair, then back. At *whoever you've got in there now* his hand tightens on the door's edge until the knuckles go pale.

He isn't fooled. James can see it the way he used to see a man across the table count the cards already played and stop believing the bet. Some of the story might have passed, but the man heard two things in it that don't belong to a stranger with crates, and he isn't going to forget them.

"Dry floor," he says flatly. Then again, quieter, almost to himself: "Dry floor."

The easy smile doesn't reach him. He looks down at the cat, then at James's coat, where the folded handkerchief makes a small lump, and finally at his boots. Wet weed is still stuck in the welt from the landing.

"It's let," he says. "No room. Let for the season." The door comes in an inch. "And I don't sell cord at night. Come back when the stall's out."

He doesn't shut it yet. He stands there breathing through his nose, needle still in his fist, and the fear in him is turning into the stubbornness of a man on his own doorstep.

"The barrier didn't send you. Marsh don't send nobody my way, never has." His eyes stay on James's face. "Who's been talking about my store?"

"Nobody's been talking. That was a bad story and you caught it. Fair's fair." I keep my hands open at my sides and my voice low, below the bridge noise. "Truth is, I followed a smell down your stair. A little girl in a grey shawl chalked a mark on the Fist's post this afternoon, then went down to your landing. There's a piece of her shawl on the bottom step, and somebody tied a boat to your ring not long ago."

I nod at the door, not past him at the room.

"I heard you through the wall. Five coins, and a store that reeks like a tannery fire. I'm not Fist and I'm not Guild, and I don't want your money or your lease. I just want to know who's taking children down to the water in the dark." I let that sit a moment. "If they're the sort who'd do that, you already know they're not the sort who'll leave you be when it goes wrong. I'd rather it went wrong for them first."

I take two silver from my purse and hold them out, not pushing.

"For the cord you won't sell me. Who rents your store, friend? A name, a face, when they come. That's all."
turns.reply:
James lets the smile drop. The net-mender watches it go, and something in his heavy face shifts. It doesn't soften, but he's paying attention now. He listens to the girl, the shawl and the ring without moving, his needle still pinched in his fist. When James says *five coins* the big man's jaw works once, as if he's chewing on it. At *children* his eyes go down to the two silver in James's open palm, and they stay there.

The net-mender's breath goes out through his nose. He looks past James at the gap, then up and down the bridge at the porters and the folded stalls. He takes the two silver the way a man picks up something hot, quickly, and it vanishes into his apron.

"Inside." He steps back off the doorway, dragging the bad foot. "Not on the step. Folk see."

The shack is one room. A cot, a stove with a pot on it, a table with a net heaped over it like a sleeping dog. He doesn't sit or offer a stool. He shuts the door, slides the bolt and puts his back to it.

"Don't know a name. Never gave one. Thin fellow, long face, oilskin with the hood up even when it's dry. Comes up the stair once a tenday, pays five silver. Real silver, good weight." He rubs his thumb against two fingers. "His hands. Grey to the knuckle, like he's been in the ashes of something. Same stink as the store."

He jerks his chin at the floor, down toward the water.

"Boat comes late. After Wyrm's Rock rings one. Not every night, most nights. A woman rows. Don't see her face." He stops, and his mouth works. "The little one. Grey shawl. I seen her. Comes with him sometimes, goes up on the bridge in the day. Calls him Da." A pause. "He ain't her da. Man don't hold his own girl by the back of the neck like that."

He scratches his stubble with the needle hand.

"Put their own lock on, first week. My store, and I ain't got a key to it. Said it's a dry floor they want, for keeping things. Dry floor." He shakes his head once. "Never asked. Five silver. Leg don't mend nets fast no more."

Then he looks straight at James for the first time, and the fear is back under the stubbornness, plainer now.

"You go poking at that door and they find it poked, they know where to come. I got one way out of here and it's that." He jerks a thumb at the bolt behind him. "So what're you going to do?"

The net-mender listens with his back against the bolt. When James promises *nothing to your door*, the big man's eyes narrow a little, the way a man checks a coin's weight in his palm. He says nothing about the word. He doesn't spit on it either.

At James's boot the cat gets up, walks to the door and sits facing the bolt. The net-mender looks down at it, then at James. He grunts, slides the bolt back a hand's width and lets the door open just wide enough. The cat flows through the gap and is gone. He shuts it and shoots the bolt again.

"Cat's got manners," he mutters. "More than most."

Through the bond James feels the cat leave the doorway, go up the side of the shack, over the salt-stiff nets and onto the roof. It settles there with the river sliding black below. From the ridge it can see the head of the stair and, past the parapet, the open water down to the landing. *High. Watching.*

The net-mender scratches his beard with the needle hand and answers the questions in order, slowly, as if he's counting them off.

"Paid today. Before dusk. Came up the stair, put the five down, went back down. Girl was with him." His mouth works. "Heard oars after. Early. Not the woman's stroke. Him rowing, maybe. Don't know."

"Due again in a tenday. Same as always. Ten days."

"Had the store since the ice went off the river. Spring. Three months, four. Lock went on the first week."

He stops at the boat. His eyes go to the floor, toward the water.

"Don't look. Hear, though. Floor's thin." He breathes through his nose. "Sacks, mostly. Dragged. Something clinks, sometimes, like a crock. And twice…" He stops, and his jaw works. "Twice it was heavy. Two of them on it, going in. Grunting. Stink was worse after, three days." He shakes his head once, hard. "Not my business. Told myself."

"Girl. Four, five days back, before today. Up on the bridge, the Rock end, by the eel stalls. Chalk on her fingers. Didn't look at me." He pauses. "Thin. Thinner than spring."

Then there's the name. He takes his time with it. He looks at James's face, then at the honest tired smile, and his weight settles onto his good leg.

"Gask," he says finally. "Everyone on the bridge knows Gask. Ask anyone for the net-mender with the foot." He reaches back and puts his hand on the bolt without drawing it. "You knock twice. Like you did. Not the Fist way."

He doesn't open the door yet.

"You staying about for the boat?" His voice drops even lower. "Not in here. Not on my stair."

"Not on your stair," I agree. "Not in here. You won't see me again tonight, Gask, and neither will they."

I push off the wall and wait for him to draw the bolt. On the step I pause, half turned, and keep it low:

"If he comes early, or the girl comes up alone, don't do anything. Just be a man mending nets. That's the safest thing in the world to be."

Then I'm back on the bridge, hands in my pockets, a tired traveller who's finally found his bearings. I walk toward the Rock end, past the eel stalls where he last saw the girl, looking for somewhere I can sit for hours without anyone wondering why. A tavern or cookshop with a window or a bench on the downstream side would be best, somewhere I can see the open water below the span and the landing's side of the river. If I find one, I'll buy a bowl of whatever's hot and a small beer I'll make last, and sit with my back to the wall.

*Stay on the roof,* I send to the cat. *Rest if you like, but keep one ear on the water. When oars come, wake me. I want to see the boat, which way it comes from and which way it goes, and how many are in it. Nothing more.*

Before I settle in, I pull the hood of the grey cloak up and use the Mask to blunt my face a little. Ten years older, a broken nose, a beard going grey. Gask has seen my real face, and that's enough people for one night.

turns.reply:
Gask draws the bolt. He holds the door open just wide enough for a man and looks past James at the dark gap beside his shack. While James says his piece, the big man's jaw works.

"Man mending nets," he mutters, as if trying out the words. Then he looks James in the eye. "Go on, then."

The door shuts behind James and the bolt slides home. A moment later the twine starts rasping through the mesh again, slow and steady.

On the bridge the evening is winding down. The fishwife's stall is folded and roped. A boy is going along the lantern hooks with a taper, lighting the ones that have gone out. James puts his hands in his pockets and walks toward Wyrm's Rock at the pace of a man with nowhere he has to be.

*Stay on the roof,* he sends. *Rest if you like…*

*Roof,* the cat sends back, and he feels it settle on the ridge with its paws tucked under.

About thirty paces on, past a shuttered chandler's and a cookfire with three porters squatting around it, the bond starts to thin. The cat's steady attention fades like a voice behind a closing door. At forty paces he can't hear it at all. The cat is still there, he knows that much, but whatever he sends now won't reach it, and nothing it sends will reach him.

The eel stalls are at the Rock end, where the bridge widens around the fortress's bulk. Four of them stand in a row, two still open, their tubs of black water seething with what's left of the day's catch. There's no girl and no grey shawl, only a man with a cleaver and a woman scrubbing a board. Chalk would show up well on these stones, and there's none.

Just past the stalls, a cookshop has been built out over the downstream parapet on timber brackets. It's a low, steamy room with a painted board showing an eel tied in a knot. The back wall is mostly shutters, propped open on the river. James stops in the shadow of the doorpost, pulls up the hood of his old regimental cloak and runs a thumb along his jaw. The Mask does its work without a sound. The face under the hood gains ten years, a nose broken and badly set, and a beard going grey at the corners. A Fist veteran on half pay, if anyone asks, and nobody here will.

Inside it smells of pepper, eel fat and wet wool. A heavyset woman with her sleeves pinned up stirs a pot the size of a cartwheel and doesn't look up. "Stew's eel. Beer's small. Eight copper the pair, bowl back when you're done."

He counts eight coppers onto the board, every one he has. She slops a bowl full and draws the beer, and he takes both to the bench along the back wall. Through the open shutters the Chionthar runs black and wide toward the harbour. Riding lights on moored barges bob downstream, and further off the Seatower's beacon smears red on the water. If he leans to the left he can see back along the span toward the city end, a dark row of piers going away from him. Somewhere among them is Gask's landing. From here it's just more dark.

The stew is better than it looks. The beer is thin enough to make last all night.

At the next table two watermen with tar to the elbows are working through a jug.

"…by the Seatower, Tuesday. Fist hooked him out with a boathook."

"Coin in his teeth?"

"Coin in his teeth." The older one drinks. "My sister's girl does the floors at the Water Queen's House. Says the priestesses won't have them. Fist brought one up there in the spring, proper, for the offering, and the high one wouldn't touch it. Said it was never paid to Her." He sets the cup down. "Funny old coin, the girl said. Face on both sides."

"Face on both sides," the younger one says, and laughs, though not as if he finds it funny. "Lucky."

"Was lucky. Won forty gold on the dogs the week before, I heard."

They move on to the price of pitch. The cook scrapes her pot. Out on the river an oar dips once and goes quiet, a barge hand going home.

"Tethyr," the older one says. "Long way to come for eel." He nudges the coins toward his companion. "Jory. Go on."

Jory takes the silver to the cartwheel pot and comes back with the jug full and no change. Nobody mentions it. The older man pours for all three and pushes a cup across.

"Hob," he says, by way of a name. "My sister's girl, Nessa, that's who saw it. Fist brought one up to the Water Queen's House in the spring, wrapped in a rag like it was holy. Priestess wouldn't put a finger to it." He drinks. "A woman's face, Nessa said. Same woman both sides. Laughing on the one and weeping on the other. Like she couldn't make up her mind." He sets the cup down. "Nessa didn't like it. Said the high one went and washed her hands after, and she'd never touched it."

"Your sergeant," Jory says. "The one who never lost a toss. Did they fish him out too?"

Hob gives him a look, and Jory shuts up and drinks.

"Tuesday's one was Fenn Corlis," Hob says. "Lighterman. Worked the barges same as us, never had two coppers to rub together. Then a tenday back he puts his whole wage on a dog at the Rivington pits, a dog with three legs that works, and it wins. Then another. Forty gold by the end of it." He shakes his head. "Spent half of it at the Blushing Mermaid, buying rounds for men who never bought him one. Walking about like the Lady had him by the hand. Then Tuesday the Fist has him on a boathook by the Seatower, blue as a mussel, with a coin in his teeth."

James listens for the rest: a long face, grey hands, a woman at the oars, the smell of burnt horn. He gets most of one.

"Fenn wouldn't have gone in the water drunk," Jory says. "Swam like an eel. Showed off about it." He turns his cup round. "River's full of fools at night anyway. That skiff with no lamp, for one. Comes up under the Crossing late, woman at the oars, and goes back down toward the harbour before light. Near took my oar off in the spring, and she never said a word. Didn't even look round."

"Lots of folk row without a lamp," Hob says, not quite to Jory. "Not our business who."

About the man with grey hands, or the stink, neither of them has a word. They've moved on to the price of pitch by the time James finishes his beer. He thanks them, takes his bowl back to the cook, who doesn't look up, and goes out onto the bridge.

The bridge has emptied while he ate. The lanterns hang further apart than they seemed at dusk, with stretches of dark between them where the light doesn't meet. Walking back toward the city end, James counts doorways and finds what he wants: a stretch of the downriver parapet between two lanterns, with a squat stone post where an old chain once hung. The shack's roof is a dark hump against the sky about 75 feet back along the span. He settles onto the stones with his back against the post, pulls his cloak round him and lets his head drop the way a man's does when beer has beaten him.

The bond comes clear like a door opening onto a warm room.

*I'm back. Same orders. Oars, you wake me.*

*Roof,* the cat sends. Then, after a pause that might be disapproval: *Cold.*

Time goes by. The Mask's hour runs out a little after nine, and James renews it under the cloak with a thumb along his jaw: the same broken nose, the same grey beard, nothing a passerby would notice changing. He does it again after ten. The eel stalls shut. The porters' cookfire burns down to a red smear and the porters roll themselves in sacking beside it. At the city end, Pell's lantern goes out, and a little later the patter stops.

A little after eleven, boots come along the bridge from the barrier. Two of them, in red-trimmed gear, walking the way men walk at the end of a long shift. Their lantern swings toward the post and stops on him. One of them prods his boot with the butt of a spear.

"Oi. Grandad. You got a bed?"

James gives them what a drunk gives: a slow lift of the head, a squint into the light, a wet grumble about Tethyr and a sergeant who owed him money.

The man with the spear bends a little closer, gets a lungful of eel and small beer, and straightens up.

"Veteran," he tells his mate, and the word has years of these nights in it. "Tethyr, he says."

"Everyone's a veteran." The other one is already walking. "Leave him. Rather him here than pissing in the barrier box."

The spear-butt taps James's boot once more, almost kindly. "Don't roll off the edge, grandad. We're not fishing you out."

James plays the drunk well enough that the patrol believes him. Their lantern swings away down the span toward the Rock, and the dark between the lamps closes over him again.

*Two,* the cat sends, a little late. *Red ones. Gone.*

Back along the bridge, the line of yellow under Gask's shutter goes out not long after. Through the cat's eyes James sees the shutter go dark, and through its ears he hears the cot creak under a heavy man lying down. The twine has stopped.

At midnight Wyrm's Rock rings the hour, twelve slow strokes rolling out over the water. James renews the Mask after the last one. The bridge is empty now apart from the sleeping porters and a dog nosing at the shut eel stalls. The Chionthar goes on sucking at the piers. Downstream the loose board knocks, then stops, then knocks again. A barge's riding light goes out.

Half past twelve. The cold has worked into the stone under him and into the backs of his legs. The cat is a still warmth at the edge of his mind, turned toward the water.

*Nothing,* it sends. *Yet.*

turns.reply:
The cold works up from the stones into James's hips and settles there. He shifts his head on his arm until the gap in the parapet frames the river: the black downstream reach, the smear of the Seatower's beacon, and to the left the dark under the span where Gask's landing is. Under the cloak his fingers stay closed on the rod.

*Listen,* he sends, and gives the orders: the roof's edge, the nets, freeze if anyone looks up, never go down. Then the second part, to watch him on the post while he looks through its eyes.

The answer is slow, like a cat getting up when it would rather not. *Edge. Low. Not down.* There's a pause. *You. Also.* He feels it accept the orders, and he also feels it decide that the nets smell of tar and it will put up with them.

Time passes. A gull complains somewhere toward the Rock and gives up. The porters by the dead cookfire snore out of step with each other. Twice James feels the cat's attention prick toward the water and settle again. The first time it's a fish turning. The second time it's the loose board downstream, knocking.

Wyrm's Rock rings one. The single stroke rolls out over the water, and the bridge seems to hold still while it fades.

It doesn't take long after that.

*Oars.* The word comes with the sound itself, heard through the cat's ears before James's own catch anything. It's a soft, steady dip and pull from downstream on the harbour side, and the rowlocks make no knock. Someone has muffled them. Through the bond he feels the cat leave the ridge and flatten itself. It slides down the roof's slope toward the river side and wedges in under the fringe of a hanging net, where the salt-stiff mesh breaks up its outline. Its chin touches the edge of the boards. Below it the landing is a grey shelf in a black hole.

From the chain-post James watches the reach through the gap in the parapet. For a while there's only water. Then part of the dark moves against the rest, a long low shape with no lamp, coming upstream close under the bridge piers where the barges' riding lights don't reach. He can't make out faces at this distance and in this dark, or even clearly how many there are. There's one figure upright at the oars, rowing in short, even, practised strokes that hardly mark the water. Behind her in the stern sits something hunched and bulky that could be a person or a pile of cargo. The skiff slides out of his line of sight under the span, toward Gask's landing.

Through the cat he hears it arrive: the hiss of the hull losing speed, a soft bump of wood on stone. Then comes a rope's dry rasp as someone runs it through the iron ring and draws it tight.

Up on the roof the cat stops breathing, as cats do. Behind the shack wall, Gask's cot doesn't creak. He's awake and lying very still.

The boat is tied up at the landing. Nobody has spoken yet.

Then I let my head sag the last inch onto my arm, like a drunk finally losing the fight, and keep my fingers closed on the rod.

*Looking now,* I send. *Keep half an eye on the post for me.*

I go down the bond and into the cat's eyes, under the nets at the roof's edge. I stay still and quiet and just watch the landing below. turns.reply:
Under the cloak James runs his thumb along his jaw. The Mask goes back on without a sound: the same badly set nose, the same grey creeping into the beard. He lets his head drop the last inch onto his forearm, like a man the beer has finally beaten, and keeps his fingers closed on the rod.

*Looking now. Keep half an eye on the post for me.*

*Post,* the cat sends back. It's a grudging word, but it means yes.

Then he goes down the bond, and the bridge goes away. His own body is still there: cold stone under his hips, the rod in his hand. But it's blind and deaf now, a coat left hanging on a peg. Through the cat he has tar in his nose, the scratch of salt-stiff mesh across one ear, and boards against his chin. Below him is the landing, a grey shelf at the bottom of a black well, and the long dark shape of a skiff lying alongside it.

A cat's eyes don't do much better than a man's under that span. For a few heartbeats it's all shapes: the hull, a figure standing up in it, a bulk in the stern that moves.

Then someone lifts the hood of a lantern a finger's width.

The light is no wider than a blade, but it's aimed low across the landing, and the cat's eyes have been wide open in the dark for an hour. The glare hits them like a slap. The cat flinches, its eyes screw shut and water, and through the bond James sees nothing but a smeared orange blot with black shapes swimming in it. When the cat can see again, the moment has passed. He has nothing he could swear to: no faces, no hands, and no idea who had the key or how the lock opened. There's only a seam of lamplight where the pier door now stands ajar, and two figures on the landing with their backs to the roof. One stands upright with her arms folded, the rower. The other, longer, is bent over at the door.

The skiff's stern is still a heap of shadow. Something there shifts. It's either a second, smaller shape pressed against a sack or just the sack slumping, and the cat can't tell which. Then comes a cough, small and quickly smothered, as if a hand had gone over a mouth. It came from the stern, or maybe from the door.

James's sight fails him, but his ears still work.

The long figure doesn't go in. He straightens, and the blade of lantern light swings off the door and down onto the weed. It moves slowly across the trodden strip, the bruised green, the stretch of shelf right in front of the hasp, and stops there. He crouches and holds the lantern close to the stone, long enough for the water to slap the piers three times.

"Who's been down." It's a man's voice, thin and quiet, not quite a question.

The woman says nothing. James hears the oilskin creak as the man turns. The light goes up to the lowest step, the one with the faded chalk, and then climbs the stair a step at a time, past where the bridge's glow ends. It stops just short of the gap beside the shack. The cat is a hand's width above that gap, flattened under the nets.

"Mind the boat," the thin voice says.

A boot comes down on the first step.

Up on the parapet, James's own body is still blind and deaf, slumped against the chain-post 75 feet away. Under the nets the cat has gone so still it might be part of the roof, and its attention has narrowed to the light coming up the stair. The half of its mind that was watching the post has gone too.

*(Out of game: the cat rolled a natural 1 on the Perception check, so by our table's rule it fails, with no extra harm. The lantern light dazzled it, and James got no faces, no key and no clear look at what's in the stern. He's still looking through the cat's eyes, so his own body on the post sees and hears nothing until he breaks off. It's about 01:12.)*

turns.message:
I pull back up the bond, fast, and I'm back in my own skin: cold stone, cramped legs, the rod in my fist. I don't lift my head. I keep the drunk's slump and open my eyes a slit under the hood, turned toward the gap by Gask's shack 75 feet back.

*Freeze,* I send. *Be the roof. If his light finds you, be a cat and nothing more: hiss, then run up over the ridge and away along the bridge. Not toward me. Don't come to me.*

I breathe slow and heavy like a sleeper and listen. I want to know whether he comes all the way up into the gap, whether he looks along the bridge, and whether he goes to Gask's door.

If he only looks and goes back down, I stay put and let him. If he knocks on Gask's door or starts forcing it, I'm getting up. I'll be a stumbling, loud drunk wandering his way, the kind of witness nobody wants to deal with at one in the morning. The rod stays ready under the cloak in case that isn't enough.
turns.reply:
James pulls himself back up the bond and the roof falls away. All at once he's in his own body again: cold stone under his hips, his calves cramped, his fingers stiff around the rod. The bridge smells of old eel fat and river. He keeps his head down on his arm. Under the hood he opens one eye a slit and turns it toward the dark hump of Gask's shack 75 feet back.

*Freeze. Be the roof.* The rest of the order goes after it: the hiss, the ridge, away along the bridge, never toward him.

No words come back, only stillness, the cat holding its breath. At the head of the stair a faint orange glow grows in the gap beside the shack as the lantern comes up the steps.

Light comes up the stair a step at a time. James sees the edge of the parapet catch it first, then the salt-crusted boards of the shack, then the gap itself as a slot of orange. The man comes into it. At 75 feet in this dark James can't make out much: a tall, narrow figure stooped under an oilskin, the hood up, the lantern held low with its shutter open a finger's width. He stops on the top step and lifts the light.

The blade of light moves slowly along the shack wall. It goes up the nets hanging from their pegs and over the roof's edge, across the stiff, tarry mesh. It stays there for a breath, then another.

The cat doesn't move. Under the nets it's just another lump among the folds of tarred twine and shadow, and the light slides on over it and away. The man saw nothing on the roof. James feels the cat let out a breath only when the glow has moved off down the wall.

The man steps out of the gap onto the bridge and turns the light along the span, first toward the city end, then toward the Rock. The thin beam is too narrow to reach 75 feet and fades into the dark between the lanterns long before it gets to the chain-post. He doesn't come any closer. He looks at the empty bridge for a while with his head tilted, like a man listening for footsteps, and hears the porters snoring.

Then he turns to Gask's door.

He doesn't knock twice. He gives three flat raps with his knuckles, close together, the knock of a man who expects to be let in. Inside the shack nothing moves. He waits, then raps again, the same three.

"Gask." The thin voice barely carries. "Up."

The cot creaks under a heavy body getting up slowly. A foot drags across the floorboards.

James is on his feet before the bolt is drawn. He comes up off the chain-post the way a drunk does, all at once and badly, one shoulder bumping the stone and his cloak tangled round his knees. He lurches out of the dark between the lanterns toward the shack. The boots make no sound on the stones, so all the noise is his body: the scrape of his shoulder on the post, his breath coming out in a heavy grunt, his hand slapping the parapet as he catches himself.

At the shack the man's head comes round. The lantern's shutter snaps almost shut, leaving a thread of light, and the tall shape stands very still in front of Gask's door. He's watching the old soldier stagger toward him out of the dark, 70 feet away and closing. Behind the planks the bolt stops halfway.

turns.message:
I keep coming, but I slow down about twenty feet short of him and stop there, swaying, one hand flat on the parapet. Close enough to be a nuisance, too far to grab. I squint at his thread of lantern light like it's the sun.

"Oi." It comes out loud and wet, loud enough to carry to the porters by the dead fire. "Oi, friend. Mother… Thessaly's. Second left past the… the barrel man." I wave vaguely uphill and nearly lose my balance. "Sergeant said. Clean, cheap, won't rob you. You know it? You look like a man who knows it."

I don't wait for an answer. I start in on the old Tethyrian marching song, the one about the quartermaster's daughter, off-key and too loud, and I lean my back against the parapet as though I mean to settle in right there in front of Gask's door for the night. That's one more drunk, two porters, and a whole bridge's worth of eyes he didn't plan on.

Under the cloak my fingers stay on the rod. Through the slit of my eyes I watch his hands, not his hood. If one goes inside the oilskin for steel, I'm not drunk anymore.

*Stay under the nets,* I send to the cat. *Don't move. Not for anything.*
turns.reply:
James comes on along the parapet with a drunk's lurch, then slows about 20 feet short of the man and stops, swaying, one palm flat on the cold stone. In the thread of lantern light the tall shape doesn't move. The hood stays turned toward him.

"Oi." It comes out wet and far too loud. By the dead cookfire one of the porters snorts and stops snoring. "Oi, friend. Mother… Thessaly's. Second left past the… the barrel man." He waves uphill and nearly goes over. "Sergeant said. Clean, cheap, won't rob you. You know it? You look like a man who knows it."

He doesn't wait for an answer. He starts in on the quartermaster's daughter, the verse every Tethyrian foot-soldier learns before he learns to march. He sings it off-key and too loud, and slides his back down the parapet as if he means to settle in right here, across from Gask's door, for the night.

*Stay under the nets. Don't move. Not for anything.*

From the roof he feels nothing but stillness.

The singing holds. To the man in the oilskin, James is what he looks like: an old soldier with a broken nose, soaked through with small beer, settling in for the night in exactly the wrong place, and too drunk to remember any of it by morning. The hood stays on him through the whole first verse and into the chorus. Then the man's shoulders loosen a little under the oilskin. It isn't relief. It's a man giving up on a job for tonight.

James watches his hands, not the hood. The left one stays on the lantern and nudges the shutter open a hair wider, so the thread of light falls across James's boots and the old regimental cloak. In that light James can see the fingers on the shutter. They're grey to the second knuckle, grey like a hand that's been working in cold ash, just as Gask said. The right hand stays hidden under the oilskin, and nothing moves under the cloth.

The man turns his head toward Gask's door and puts his mouth close to the planks. Whatever he says is too low to carry over the quartermaster's daughter. The half-drawn bolt slides home again from inside.

Then he goes. He doesn't hurry and he doesn't look back. He steps into the gap beside the shack, and his light sinks down the stair a step at a time until the bridge is dark again.

*Down,* the cat sends from under the nets. Nothing has moved on the roof. Then come scraps of what it hears below, through the boards: a door dragged shut over stone, and the heavy clack of the Tolliver lock. The thin voice says something short to the woman. The cat gets a few words, flat and clear: *"…drunk. Gask keeps."* Wood knocks once on wood. The rope rasps back out through the iron ring.

From his place against the parapet, James hears the oars himself a few breaths later. They make the same soft dip and pull through muffled rowlocks, going downstream this time. The long, low shape slides out from under the span into the open reach. He can't make out who's at the oars or who's in the stern, only that the boat rides lower in the water than when it came in. It keeps close under the piers where the barges' riding lights don't reach and heads toward the harbour and the red smear of the Seatower's beacon. Then the dark takes it.

James carries on with the song for another verse, because a drunk wouldn't stop the moment the only man listening walked off. By the dead fire the porter mutters something about Tethyr and the Nine Hells and pulls his sacking over his head.

Behind Gask's planks nothing moves. There's no twine, no cot creaking. A heavy man is standing on the other side of his own door in the dark, listening the way James is.

*Gone,* the cat sends at last. Then, after a pause: *Cold. Still.*

Wyrm's Rock hasn't rung again. It's a little after a quarter past one. The bridge is empty except for the sleeping porters, and James is sprawled across from Gask's door with a face ten years older than his own.

turns.reply:
James lets the last line about the quartermaster's daughter fade into a mumble about her father's boots. Then he stays where he is, chin on his chest, hood down over the broken nose. The red smear of the Seatower's beacon wobbles on the water. One of the porters by the dead fire turns over in his sacking and swears in his sleep. A quarter of an hour passes this way. No oars come back up the reach, and no light shows under the span.

*Go to the head of the stair. Low. Smell and listen down.*

The cat comes off the roof without a sound. It slips down through the hanging nets, crosses the boards and goes flat on the top step in the gap. James feels it reach down into the dark with its nose and ears.

Nothing down there is breathing. There's no lamp, no warmth, no creak of a hull. The river sucks at the piers, and behind the pier door the slow drip goes on the way it did at dusk. The smells are close and fresh: lamp oil, wet rope, and the burnt horn, much stronger than it was at dusk, thick around the door. Under all that is something the cat doesn't like at all. It's sweet and heavy, like a rat that died under the floorboards and lay there a few days. It's faint and already thinning on the river air, like a smell that was here until recently and has been carried away.

*Empty,* the cat sends. Then, with its fur flattening: *Dead-smell. Old. Gone with them.*

It can't tell what's still behind the door from the top step. It doesn't go down to find out.

James gets up the way a drunk does: one hand on the parapet, a grumble at his knees, a lurch that nearly takes him past the shack. He catches himself on Gask's doorframe and hangs there as though the frame is all that's holding him up. He knocks twice, softly.

"It's the cord man," he breathes through the planks. He asks his questions with his face turned toward the empty bridge and his hand closed on the rod under his cloak.

For a while nothing answers. Then a board creaks right on the other side of the door. Gask never went back to his cot. He's been standing there in the dark the whole time. His voice comes through the knothole under the scrap of net, low and rough.

"Ain't opening." He breathes through his nose. "Knew it was you. Singing."

There's a long pause. When he speaks again it's slower, as if he's been saying the words over to himself for the last quarter hour.

"He put his mouth to my door. Said, *tomorrow night.* Tomorrow night, you'll tell me who." The board creaks as he shifts onto his good leg. "Didn't ask who was singing. Asked who's been down. He knows somebody's been down. You said you'd leave no mark."

James hears his breath catch and steady again.

"Went in after. Not long. Then summat come out. Dragged it over the stone, heavy. She come up off the boat to take the other end, and the both of them grunting." He stops. "Same as the two times. Only out, this time. Out and into the boat."

Through the planks James hears a big hand rubbing over stubble.

"Store'll stink less now." There's no humour in it. "Dry floor."

turns.message:
I lean my forehead against the planks beside the knothole and keep my voice down to a breath.

"Tell him the truth, near enough. The drunk did it. Old soldier, broken nose, grey beard, Tethyrian song. He came off the bridge last night to piss and sleep it off on your landing, and you heard him down there and ran him off with your stick. You don't know his name. He said something about Mother Thessaly's." I let that sit. "He's already seen that face, Gask. He'll believe it, because he wants an easy answer. And that face isn't mine. If he goes hunting for it, he'll find me, and I'll be ready for him."

I take ten gold from my purse by feel and slide the coins one by one through the gap under the door, where the planks don't meet the stone.

"That's for you, not for cord. If you've got a sister, a cousin, anyone this side of the river or the other, sleep there tomorrow night. Leave your lamp lit and your door bolted so it looks like you're in. If you'd rather stay, stay, and give him the drunk. Either way, I'll be on this bridge when the Rock rings one. You won't see me. He won't either."

I straighten up off the frame and drop the drunk back over my shoulders like a coat.

"Bolt it. Sleep if you can."

Then I push off and stagger away toward the city end, muttering, past the porters and into the dark between the lanterns.

*Come,* I send to the cat. *We're done here tonight. Mother Thessaly's. Back room. You can complain about the cold on the way.*
turns.reply:
James leans his forehead against the tarred planks beside the knothole. The wood is cold and smells of the river. He breathes the story through the gap: the drunk, the piss, the stick, Mother Thessaly's, a face that isn't his. On the other side, Gask's breathing slows as he listens.

The gold goes under the door one piece at a time, where the bottom of the planks doesn't quite meet the stone. Each coin rasps over the grit and stops. Nothing happens for a moment. Then a heavy body lowers itself to the floor with a grunt and a scrape of the bad foot, and a big hand sweeps the coins together.

They chink as he counts them, slowly, into his palm. He stops at the last one and counts them again.

"Ten." It comes out flat, the way you'd say the depth of water under a hull. "Ten gold. That's half a year of nets."

James tells him about the sister, the lamp and the bolt. Gask is quiet for a long time.

"Sister's in Rivington. Her man don't like me." The floorboards creak as he gets up again. "He'll like this." There's a pause, and his voice drops. "Lamp lit. Bolt shot. Old fool's home, mending." He seems to be trying the words out, as he did with *man mending nets*. "And you on the bridge. Where I won't see you."

It isn't quite a question, and he doesn't wait for an answer. The bolt was never drawn, so there's nothing to shoot home. Through the planks James hears him limp back across the room, and the cot doesn't creak. Gask is sitting at his table in the dark with ten gold in his fist.

James pushes off the doorframe and lets the drunk settle back over him. He takes a lurch that nearly reaches the parapet, mutters about Tethyrian quartermasters, and goes weaving off past the dead cookfire. One of the porters lifts his head out of the sacking, decides the old man isn't worth swearing at, and lies back down. Then James is in the dark between the lanterns again, and the shack falls behind him.

*Come. We're done here tonight.*

The cat drops off the roof without a sound and comes after him at a trot, tail high. It falls in at his heel about halfway to the barrier. *Cold,* it sends, as if it hasn't said so already. Then, a few steps later: *Warm room. Yes.*

The barrier at the city end is closed for the night. The plank gate is pulled across and roped, Edda Marsh's table is gone, and a single Fist man is wedged into the barrier box on a stool, chin on his chest, under a lamp with its shutter half closed. He opens one eye when the broken-nosed drunk fumbles at the rope, sees the regimental cloak and the stagger, and closes the eye again. "Pay in the morning," he mumbles, though no one is asking. James lets himself through and ropes the gate behind him, the way a drunk who remembers his manners would.

The cat stops at the post.

It doesn't sniff. It sits beside the chalk coin and looks up at him. The mark is where it was at dusk, a pale circle on dark stone, face up, unsmudged. Nobody has touched it all night. The cat holds his eye a moment longer than a cat needs to, then gets up and trots on into the Outer City as though nothing happened.

Up the hill the streets narrow and the river smell gives way to woodsmoke and middens. A dog barks behind a fence and gives up. The cooperage is easy to find: a yard of staves stacked like ribs and iron hoops hanging from a beam. Second left past it is a lane hardly wider than a cart, and halfway along it is the house. It's a tall, narrow building of three storeys, the upper ones leaning out over the lane. Its shutters are freshly painted green, and the step is scrubbed clean even at this hour. A small lamp burns low in a niche beside the door, for late lodgers or for luck. A bell-pull hangs from a bracket, its cord worn smooth. A board under the lamp reads, in careful letters: *THESSALY'S. Beds. No dice. No drink after midnight.*

Every window is dark.

Wyrm's Rock hasn't rung two yet. Under James's hood the broken nose and grey beard still hold, but not for much longer. The hour he gave them runs out a little after two.

The cat sits down on the scrubbed step and looks at the bell-pull.
